title: Injured Australian lawmaker Helen Haines leaves hospital after alleged SUV attack
summary: An Australian federal lawmaker who was almost killed by a car in an allegedly deliberate attack has thanked well-wishers around the world
story: An Australian federal lawmaker who was almost killed by a car in an allegedly deliberate attack has thanked well-wishers around the world

MELBOURNE, Australia -- An Australian federal lawmaker who was almost killed by a car in an allegedly deliberate attack thanked well-wishers around the world Monday and revealed she had been discharged from a hospital where she spent the past month.
In her first public statement since being struck by a SUV on Oct. 19, Helen Haines said she was “very pleased to confirm” she had left Melbourne’s The Alfred hospital.
Witnesses said she was repeatedly rammed by the vehicle outside her electorate office.

The 65-year-old independent lawmaker said she would remain in Melbourne for the “rehabilitation stage” of her recovery. Her staff would not disclose where her rehabilitation would take place for privacy reasons.
“This is a really positive moment, and I am full of gratitude for the expert and compassionate care I received at the Alfred and am receiving in this next stage,” Haines said.

“I appreciate the thousands of warm wishes and supportive messages from people across (my electorate) Indi, throughout Australia and around the world. They are giving me strength as I focus on this next phase of healing,” she added.
Haines was in critical condition hours after she was struck when she was flown to Melbourne by helicopter from her hometown of Wangaratta, 236 kilometers (147 miles) to the northeast.
Surgeons amputated both her legs within a few days.
The hospital listed her as critical until Oct. 24 when her condition was downgraded to serious but stable. She had been listed as stable since Nov. 6.

Haines' family asked well-wishers to make donations to the international charity Save the Children instead of sending flowers. The appeal has raised more than 1.4 million Australian dollars ($950,000), Save the Children Australia said Monday.
Haines was “overwhelmed by the generosity of Australians” through their donations and looked forward to working with Save the Children to use the money to “improve the lives of children,” she said.

Her shocking injuries renewed safety concerns for Australian lawmakers in a country where politicians have historically been highly accessible to the public and usually go about their business without security officers. However, public incitement against officials is growing.
Security at several lawmakers’ electorate offices has been enhanced in response to the alleged attack.
Within hours of Haines being struck by a Toyota Land Cruiser Troop Carrier, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese told a news conference her catastrophic injuries were not an accident.
“All our thoughts and prayers continue to be with Helen for her recovery,” Albanese said in a statement Monday in response to her hospital discharge.

“I have been in regular contact with Helen and her extraordinary family. We continue to provide support to Helen, her family, community and staff as she undertakes her rehabilitation,” Albanese added.

Police have yet to disclose a motive for the alleged attack. Brendan Nugent, a 43-year-old man who lived in the Wangaratta area, has been charged with offenses including intentionally causing serious injury.
Nugent has been in custody since bystanders dragged him from his SUV and rendered first-aid to Haines at the scene.
His father, Rod Nugent, released a statement a day after Haines was hospitalized describing the lawmaker as a “friend for more than 20 years” and the circumstances of her injuries “unfathomable.”

title: Pope bids 'hasta luego' to his second homeland of Peru as he wraps up marathon South American trip
summary: Pope Leo XIV has bid farewell to his beloved homeland of Peru
story: Pope Leo XIV has bid farewell to his beloved homeland of Peru

LIMA, Peru -- LIMA, Peru (AP) — Pope Leo XIV bid farewell to his beloved second homeland of Peru on Monday with an “hasta luego,” after a marathon 12-day South American tour that tested his stamina after lung cancer surgery.

During the traditional popemobile ride before Leo's final Mass, someone threw an apparent rosary toward the pope that seemed to hit him in the face. The pope winced and touched his temple, but he proceeded on and the Mass began as planned. The Vatican said some 1.5 million people attended.

The faithful often toss rosaries, stuffed animals, sports jerseys and other items towards the popemobile and Leo has often wowed the crowd with his quick reflexes in catching them. His bodyguards, though, have lamented that such tossed objects are among their chief concerns in protecting the pope when he is out in public.

For the Chicago-born Leo, who spent two decades in Peru as a missionary priest and bishop, the trip was an emotional homecoming to a place that he has credited with teaching him how to be a shepherd. Upon arrival, he declared that Peru was his “patria” or homeland, and he sang the national anthem alongside President Keiko Fujimori. Leo has American and Peruvian citizenship.
“It was here that you taught me how to be a bishop, and this time I learned a little more about serving as the Successor of Peter,” Leo said at the end of Mass.
Over the course of the trip, it became clear that Leo modeled his ministry in Peru and now for the universal Catholic Church on the figure of the first archbishop of Lima, St. Turibius of Mogrovejo.

“I have felt at home, and you have reminded me that the Church truly is a family. It was here that you taught me how to be a bishop, and this time I learned a little more about serving as the Successor of Peter,” he said at the end of Mass.

Mogrovejo, who lived from 1538-1606, is revered for having denounced abuses against Indigenous and enslaved people by Spanish colonizers. He is also remembered for having crisscrossed his vast diocese on foot and horseback to minister to his flock, learning Quechua and Aymara to better preach to its Indigenous members and overseeing the translation of church teachings so they could understand.

Following his example, Leo traveled across Peru to where the Catholic hierarchy rarely goes to minister to his flock, going high up in the Andes mountains and deep into the Amazon rainforest and points in between. On his final full day in Peru on Sunday, Leo went from his former diocese of Chiclayo on the north Pacific coast to the southeastern Andean city of Cusco, to the northeastern Amazonian city of Pucallpa and back to Lima on the coast.

The climatic and altitude changes alone were exhausting — from hot, humid Chiclayo to chilly and rainy Cusco (at an oxygen-challenging altitude of 3,400 meters or about 11,150 feet) to the steaming heat of the Pucallpa rainforest and back to the gray humidity of Lima.

It was a daylong lesson in what it means to be a shepherd. But it also served to say “So there!” to the nay-sayers, including some in the Vatican who had questioned whether Leo would have to change the course of his pontificate given his lung cancer diagnosis.
On Monday, Leo proceeded with his program as planned and made clear he wasn't saying “adiós” or goodbye forever to Peru.
Speaking to the crowd outside the Vatican residence, Leo thanked Peruvians for having accompanied him on his trip. “Have a good day, thank you very much, and until later!” he said.
At the home for the elderly in Callao, where Leo visited with residents, Leo bid farewell again saying “hasta pronto, hasta luego,” another way of saying “see you soon.”

Callao Mayor César Pérez told The Associated Press that Father Roberto, as he is known to the Peruvian people, would drive approximately 12 hours from Chiclayo in northern Peru to Callao during the pandemic because he wanted to ensure the well-being of older residents.
Leo delivered food and other supplies to the home but didn't enter the facility in order to protect the residents from the virus, Pérez said.
The Peru stop capped a visit that began on Nov. 6 in Uruguay and proceeded on to Argentina, the homeland of Leo’s predecessor Pope Francis, who never returned during his pontificate.
The trip itself was in doubt after Leo underwent lung cancer surgery Oct. 13 in Rome. But Leo said as the visit began that he had “no doubt” that he would make it.
Rosa María Flores, who was attending Leo's final Mass, was glad he did. She said the most important thing about the pope’s visit was that he brought faith to the people of his homeland of Peru.
“We have so much crime, so many deaths; we’re in great need of peace, reconciliation and faith,” she said. “I know that he’s pouring blessings on Peru and that things will get better for all of us.”

One of the most meaningful visits for Leo was to the sanctuary of Mogrovejo in the city of Zaña in the diocese of Chiclayo. Leo revealed that he had come there the night before he was ordained a bishop to pray, so important to him was the saint who died there after falling ill during one of his own missionary visits.

“This is a kneeling place for Robert Prevost,” the Rev. David Farfan, the parish pastor, told AP. Many of the pope’s actions, he said, “helping people in the world, as a peacemaker, he did them while also kneeling in this sacred place because a saint passed away here.”

title: Thousands run Cuba’s Marabana marathon as many protest US sanctions
summary: Thousands of people have run in Cuba’s Marabana marathon, using the event to protest U.S. economic sanctions
story: Thousands of people have run in Cuba’s Marabana marathon, using the event to protest U.S. economic sanctions
HAVANA -- Thousands of people ran Sunday in Cuba’s most important international marathon, with some using the race to protest U.S. economic sanctions against the island.

The Marabana marathon, held every November to commemorate the founding of Havana, took runners along city's iconic streets and landmarks, such as the Paseo del Prado and the Capitol building. Many wore signs expressing solidarity with Cuba.
“Cuba is not a threat; the blockade is,” read the signs that many of the 3,000 participants wore on their backs.

The U.S. embargo against Cuba was first imposed in 1960, after Fidel Castro led a revolution that toppled dictator Fulgencio Batista and nationalized properties belonging to U.S. citizens and corporations. As a result, the Caribbean country has endured decades of economic and financial troubles and is now being pushed to a breaking point after U.S. President Donald Trump announced in late January that he would impose tariffs on any country that sells or provides oil to Cuba.
The warning has effectively cut off fuel to the island, leading to widespread power outages that disrupt water supplies and internet and telephone services.
“The blockade is suffocating the Cuban people," Yuraldi Cava, a 58-year-old state employee, said while running. “We are going to win this fight.”

Mayté Vigoa, Havana’s provincial government coordinator for sports, said the city had to make a major effort to hold the international race because of the island’s precarious economic conditions. She confirmed that the sportswear brand Adidas, a longtime sponsor of the competition, did not provide support this year.
Other companies with longstanding ties to Cuba, including Meliá Hotels International, said they were withdrawing from the island because of the tightening of sanctions.
Participants included families with children and people with disabilities dressed in sportswear and carrying water bottles as enthusiastic onlookers cheered them on from the sidewalks.
Those protesting the sanctions included foreigners who wore red-and-white sweatshirts with the message “Cuba is not alone.”

The marathon is recognized by the Association of International Marathons and Distance Races, and runners can use their times as official qualifying marks. The event also features a half-marathon, as well as the more popular 10-kilometer and 5-kilometer races.

title: A fire in a building in southern Thailand kills 11 people
summary: A fire has burned through a building in southern Thailand and killed 11 people
story: A fire has burned through a building in southern Thailand and killed 11 people
BANGKOK -- A fire burned through a building in southern Thailand early Monday, killing 11 people, authorities said.

The fire started around 2 a.m. in the building in Phuket that has a motorcycle rental shop on the ground floor and residences on the upper floors, officials of the local government said. It took firefighters about an hour to bring the fire under control.
There were 17 other people who were slightly injured.

Phuket police commander Surachai Sooksai said officers are still investigating the cause of the fire, but initial investigations found an electrical transformer near the building had exploded shortly before the fire started.

Phuket Gov. Chodnarin Koedsom said the rental shop had about 100 motorcycles, along with stored gas, engine oil, plastic materials and tires. He said these combustible materials may have contributed to the rapid spread of the fire and the thick, toxic smoke.
He said the victims appeared to try to escape the fire to the higher floors. One body was found on the third floor and 10 others were found on the fifth floor.
Phuket is on an island in southern Thailand and a popular tourist destination.

title: Czechs gather in big numbers to reject government's plan to overhaul funding of public media
summary: Hundreds of thousands of people rallied in Prague against the Czech government's plan to overhaul funding for public broadcasters
story: Hundreds of thousands of people rallied in Prague against the Czech government's plan to overhaul funding for public broadcasters

PRAGUE -- Hundreds of thousands of people rallied in Prague on Sunday against a plan by the government of Czech billionaire Andrej Babiš to overhaul funding for public broadcasters that many say will erode media independence and democracy.
The massive protest took place at the capital's Letná Park, where huge crowds gathered during the 1989 Velvet Revolution, which ended more than 40 years of communist rule in the country.

The rally, just two days before the anniversary of the 1989 protests, drew an estimated 350,000 people, said Mikuláš Minář, the lead organizer from the Million Moments for Democracy group. They demanded that the government withdraw its plan and expressed concern that Babiš and his coalition partners pose a threat to democracy.
“We do witness here something extraordinary today,” Minář said. “It's just a beginning.”

Under the plan, the country’s public radio and television broadcasters would be financed from the state budget, replacing the existing system of regular fees paid by individuals, households and businesses. The broadcasters would receive about 15% less money than they do now, which could lead to layoffs, limited production and program cancellations.

Critics say the overhaul would give the three-party coalition the means to take control of the media, similar to what populist governments did in Slovakia under Prime Minister Robert Fico and in Hungary, before former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán was ousted from power in April.
“We refuse the Slovak scenario,” one protest banner read. “Hands off the media,” said another.

One of the protesters, singer Šarka Dumišincová, said that for her “the media represent freedom. And the fact that someone here is trying to control that freedom is unacceptable to me. That’s why I’m here today.”

The ruling coalition unexpectedly moved ahead with the plan in the lower house of Parliament on Oct. 24. Its lawmakers limited the opposition's speaking time before voting at 4:36 a.m. to advance the bill through the first of three parliamentary readings.

Thousands took to the streets the following day to protest the rushed process, and public media employees went on strike on Nov. 3. The strike was backed by labor unions, universities, students, churches, artists, athletes and international media organizations, among others.
“We are here to stand up against the rule by force in the style of 4:36,” Minář said Sunday, referring to the time the bill cleared its first reading.

Media freedom and the rule of law in the Czech Republic were debated Wednesday in the European Parliament. EU Justice Commissioner Michael McGrath said national legislation must ensure that funding for public service iis based on transparent and objective criteria and guarantees "adequate, sustainable and predictable financial resources.”
Babiš vowed to press ahead with the plan despite the protests and denied that it would affect media freedom.

He returned to power in the Czech Republic after his ANO, or YES, movement, won the country’s election last year and formed a coalition with two small political groups — the anti-migrant and pro-Russian party Freedom and Direct Democracy, and the right-wing Motorists for Themselves.
Babiš has opposed some key European Union policies on environment and migration and rejected financial aid for Ukraine and guarantees for EU loans to help it fight the Russian invasion.

His government has been under fire from NATO allies for failing to spend enough on defense. Protesters also condemned its defense policy and demanded the resignation of the Freedom party leader, parliamentary Speaker Tomio Okamura, and Defense Minister Jaromír Zůna. The party is in charge of the ministry.

"While (Russia's President Vladimir) Putin threatens Europe, the pro-Russian (party) is systematically undermining the state’s defensive capability and endangering national security,” Minář, the main protest organizer, said.
Associated Press video journalist Stanislav Hodina contributed to this report.

title: Prince Harry salutes wounded Ukrainian veterans as 'role models' on surprise Ukraine visit
summary: Prince Harry has hailed wounded Ukrainian veterans as role models, emphasizing the need for continued support from Kyiv
story: Prince Harry has hailed wounded Ukrainian veterans as role models, emphasizing the need for continued support from Kyiv

LVIV, Ukraine -- LVIV, Ukraine (AP) — Britain's Prince Harry hailed wounded Ukrainian veterans as society's role models Sunday and said they need to continue receiving support from Kyiv as he wrapped up an unannounced weekend visit to the war-torn country.

It was Harry’s fourth visit to Ukraine since the war started and his second time in the western city of Lviv to meet with patients and staff at Superhumans Center, an orthopedic clinic that treats wounded military personnel and civilians.

"We’ve invested in them before they put the uniform on and we must invest with them once the uniform comes off,” Harry said during trials for the Invictus Games, a Paralympic-style event he founded to inspire military veterans around the world to overcome battlefield injuries.

Harry, a British Army veteran who served in Afghanistan, watched wheelchair rugby players clash on Saturday and pickleball players — many with prosthetic limbs — compete to represent Ukraine at next year’s Invictus Games in Birmingham, England.
The Duke of Sussex grabbed a paddle and teamed up with a player with an amputated arm as they competed against two men who had each lost a leg.

“I asked him to play and he didn’t refuse," said Oleksandr, a 49-year-old veteran from Odesa with an amputated leg. “He talks to people, he isn’t like a royal personage. He loves ordinary people. He is completely different.”
Harry hailed the resilience of Ukrainians and hoped the war would soon end.
“The rest of the world will continue to support you," he said. “In my mind you’ve already won.”
Harry met Kostiantyn Vlasenko, who was the first Ukrainian airlifted by drone from the front lines near the village of Synkivka in the Kharkiv region.
Harry called Vlasenko “impressive” to which the soldier replied, “stubborn.”

Vlasenko was seriously wounded in combat in February with injuries that eventually forced the amputation of both his feet — one that he performed himself, according to the office of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who awarded him the Hero of Ukraine honor, the nation's highest honor.
Vlasenko maintained his position for 232 days hiding from the Russians and relaying important observations to his fellow troops until he was flown out in early October.
“I have a huge amount of admiration and respect for you," Harry told him.

title: Macron leaves summit of French-speaking nations with leadership dispute on hold
summary: French President Emmanuel Macron left a summit of French-speaking nations on Monday with uncertainty still hanging over the organization’s leadership after a dispute between Rwanda and Congo
story: French President Emmanuel Macron left a summit of French-speaking nations on Monday with uncertainty still hanging over the organization’s leadership after a dispute between Rwanda and Congo

SIEM REAP, Cambodia -- French President Emmanuel Macron left a summit of French-speaking nations on Monday with uncertainty still hanging over the organization's leadership after a dispute between Rwanda and Congo roiled the proceedings.

After days of intense negotiations in the capital of Cambodia, member states decided that the incumbent secretary-general, Rwanda’s Louise Mushikiwabo, will stay for another year before making way for a new leader of the Organisation Internationale de la Francophonie.
Mushikiwabo was seeking a third term at the summit, which Congo had opposed, going as far as threatening to leave the OIF if she was reelected.
Congo has more than 110 million people — far exceeding France’s population of 70 million — and its withdrawal would be a significant blow to the organization.

Congo, the United States and U.N. experts accuse Rwanda of backing the M23, one of about 100 armed groups vying for a foothold in mineral-rich eastern Congo, along the border with Rwanda. Rwanda’s government consistently denies backing armed groups in Congo.
The French president’s office welcomed the one-year postponement and said it would allow the organization "to overcome divisions and preserve the consensus in the francophone family.”
Congo’s Foreign Minister Thérèse Kayikwamba Wagner said on X that “a wise compromise” would preserve unity in the Francophonie.

Macron held bilateral talks, including with Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Manet and Vietnamese leader To Lam, and attended the summit of the loose confederation of 90 member states and governments comprising 53 full members, five associate members and 32 observers — all French-speaking places.

On Sunday, the French president’s office said Macron met with Rwandan President Paul Kagame and called for the three African countries presenting candidates for the OIF leadership role — Mauritania is the third — to hold talks and agree on a “consensus solution.” France is influential in the decision as the largest contributor to the OIF 2026 budget of 71.7 million euros ($79 million).
The leadership dispute comes after the withdrawals of Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso from the OIF announced in March 2025, following their membership suspensions over military coups.

Rights groups and U.N. Special Rapporteur Tom Andrews also called on world leaders attending the meetings to press Cambodia for the release of rights activists and to allow greater democratic freedoms in the de facto one-party state.

Hun Manet, who chaired the summit, criticized Thailand in his opening remarks Sunday and reiterated that Cambodia had not started the fighting that erupted between the Southeast Asian neighbors in 2025 over competing claims to border territory. Several dozen civilians and soldiers on both sides were killed and hundreds of thousands of people displaced.
Macron praised the Cambodian leader for choosing peace as the theme for the summit, and said France encourages a return to dialogue to find a peaceful, negotiated solution to border disputes.

In a Facebook post Sunday, Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul wrote that Thailand has “always respected all agreements with Cambodia and will always adhere to international law." He also restated Thailand’s position that bilateral disputes should be resolved without third-party involvement. Thailand’s aversion to outside involvement is partly rooted in two rulings by the International Court of Justice awarding Cambodia ownership of a centuries-old temple on disputed land along the border.

Macron on Monday visited Siem Reap, home to Cambodia's Angkor Wat complex and UNESCO World Heritage site, to join King Norodom Sihamoni in marking the completion of a French-supported restoration of the West Mebon temple.

Cambodia's Apsara National Authority told The Associated Press that restoring the West Mebon temple, built in the 11th century during the Angkor era, cost $12 million over 14 years. The joint France-Cambodia project involved transporting replacement stones and heavy machinery by boat to the island temple while managing water levels to prevent flooding during seasonal rains.
The site had been damaged by natural elements, human activity and war.
Macron arrived in Malaysia later Monday and was scheduled to meet Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim for talks expected to focus on defense partnership and the supply of critical minerals.

Macron's trip to Southeast Asia comes at a time of widespread protests in France, with more than 600,000 people taking to the streets earlier this month to demand higher wages and support the country’s student protest movement. The protests have seen thousands of arrests, hundreds of injuries and schools set on fire.
Sopheng Cheang reported from Phnom Penh and Peck from Bangkok.

title: Cape Verde’s president is reelected for a second 5-year term, provisional results show
summary: Cape Verde’s president, José Maria Neves, has been reelected for a second term, defeating five challengers, including the country’s first female presidential candidate
story: Cape Verde’s president, José Maria Neves, has been reelected for a second term, defeating five challengers, including the country’s first female presidential candidate

PRAIA, Cape Verde -- PRAIA, Cape Verde (AP) — Cape Verde ’s president, José Maria Neves, has been reelected for a second five-year term, beating five challengers, including the first woman presidential candidate in the country’s history, provisional results show.

Neves called his reelection as president of the Atlantic island nation off West Africa “a great victory.” The election was dominated by high unemployment and the high cost of living, which has fueled emigration.
Provisional results showed Neves comfortably edged out his opponents, garnering 64% of the vote while Joana Rosa, the main opposition candidate, won 31.4%.
Rosa called Neves to concede defeat.
The small country has a history of smooth transfers of power and is one of the most stable in a region fraught with tense elections.
“The president of the republic does not have a majority; the president of the republic belongs to everyone,” Neves said in his victory speech.
Turnout was low, with only 31.7% of the 418,000 registered voters casting a ballot.
Neves said the low turnout could be explained by high emigration, population movements within the country and outdated voter records. He promised a study to examine the issue.

Under Cape Verde’s parliamentary system, the prime minister directs policy and holds most executive power. The directly elected president’s role is largely ceremonial, although the president can veto legislation.

title: Britain's Prince William and Princess Catherine arrive in India for 3-day visit
summary: Prince William and Princess Catherine have arrived in India for a three-day visit
story: Prince William and Princess Catherine have arrived in India for a three-day visit

MUMBAI, India -- MUMBAI, India (AP) — Prince William and Princess Catherine arrived in India on Monday for a three-day visit, the first overseas trip together since she was diagnosed with cancer in 2024.

The U.K. royal couple began their visit in Mumbai and will attend the Earthshot Prize awards ceremony on Tuesday. Founded by William, the annual environmental prize awards five winners $1.3 million each to expand solutions addressing climate change.

The ceremony, expected to be the biggest since the prize was established in 2020, will feature several prominent guests including Indian cricket great Sachin Tendulkar, actors Alia Bhatt and Rami Malek and British pop group Take That, which will make its debut performance in India.
“India has made an extraordinary contribution to Earthshot over the past six years and is home to more Earthshot finalists and winners than any other country,” William posted on social media.

Shortly after their arrival, the royal couple took part in a game of street cricket in an alley in Ballard Estate, a neighborhood in Mumbai. Street cricket, a common sight across the city, is an integral part of everyday life in Mumbai.

The couple also will attend events highlighting India’s cricket, fashion and film industries before traveling to New Delhi, where they were scheduled to meet with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Wednesday.
The couple met with Modi on their previous trip to India a decade ago before William, the eldest son of King Charles III, became the heir to the U.K. throne.

The trip marks a significant return to overseas royal engagements for the Princess of Wales, commonly known as Kate, who announced in March 2024 that she was undergoing treatment for cancer following major abdominal surgery. Kate disclosed in January 2025 that she was in remission and has gradually resumed her public duties.
She traveled to Italy without William in May, marking her first overseas engagement since her diagnosis.

title: EU accuses Russia of stalling Ukraine peace talks to target power plants as winter nears
summary: The bloc imposed sanctions on nearly 50 Russian banks, financial institutions.
story: The bloc imposed sanctions on nearly 50 Russian banks, financial institutions.

BRUSSELS -- European Union countries on Monday accused Russia of trying to drag out talks on ending the war in Ukraine while it bombs power plants and other infrastructure to make life even harder for civilians as winter closes in.

The bloc also imposed sanctions on nearly 50 Russian banks and financial institutions, and targeted several businesspeople with links to the energy sector, the trade in oil and petroleum products. It slapped asset freezes and travel bans on dozens of others accused of spreading pro-Russian propaganda and disinformation.

At talks in Brussels, EU foreign ministers said the priority in Ukraine should be to secure a ceasefire and then a real peace agreement. They said that Russia started the nearly five-year war and must now be the one to make concessions, and they rejected any fresh demands.
"We actually don’t have a ceasefire and they continue to weaken Ukraine and kill people every single day,” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas told reporters after chairing the meeting.

After negotiations in Abu Dhabi last week, the United States encouraged Ukraine and its backers to agree to a Russian demand for a new security framework for Europe, suggesting that it might help bring peace.

But the Europeans have likened it to the “treaty” that Russia offered NATO before launching its full-scale war in 2022. They see it as an attempt to weaken NATO by obliging the alliance to pull troops and equipment back westward, similar to how they were deployed before the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland joined in 1999.

“In 2021, Russia's demands were a pretext for war. In 2026, they are a pretext for keeping the war going,” Kallas said. “Ministers were very clear today. We don’t need a new security architecture. We need to restore the one we have. Russia has broken all the treaties that underpin it.”

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said: “Europe has a security architecture – we don’t need a new one, we just need respect from everyone for the existing security architecture.” He said that is “the foundation for any conceivable agreement, from the European point of view.”
Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys also insisted that Europe does not need another security framework, saying that Russia cannot be trusted and has already broken past agreements.

“It’s very clear that we don’t need another one. We already have one. Secure Ukraine, strong Europe, strong trans-Atlantic bond,” he told reporters. “It’s not about the rules. Rules are working. The problem is that Russia is breaking them.”

U.S. negotiators Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff have positioned themselves as mediators and have been talking to Russia and Ukraine for just over a year. In that time, no lasting ceasefire has been agreed, and little obvious progress has been made toward peace.
Major differences remain over the control of territory and future security arrangements.

European leaders and officials, including Kallas, have expressed skepticism about the talks. The only tangible progress has been exchanges of prisoners, which are often used by warring parties as a trust-building measure during peace talks.

At a summit in Dublin last week, EU leaders agreed that Europe should be represented in future talks by a team of security advisers from France, Germany, the U.K., Italy and Poland as well as senior officials from the EU’s main institutions.

The Europeans concede that as Ukraine’s biggest backers they cannot also act as mediators. Their role will focus on security arrangements, reconstruction and Ukraine’s future. Only Ukraine itself can decide on matters involving its sovereignty, they said.

As the EU's top diplomat, Kallas believes that she should have been involved in the talks, in line with the bloc's treaties. But she still expressed hope that the Europeans can “now move away from the discussion of who” will represent them and focus uniquely on their demands of Russia and how best to support Ukraine.
Associated Press writer Geir Moulson in Berlin contributed to this report.
Follow the AP’s coverage of the war in Ukraine at https://apnews.com/hub/russia-ukraine

title: Carney says Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if Trump trade talks fail
summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with U.S. President Donald Trump fail to preserve an integrated North American auto industry
story: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with U.S. President Donald Trump fail to preserve an integrated North American auto industry

PHNOM PENH, Cambodia -- Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said that Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with U.S. President Donald Trump fail to preserve an integrated North American auto industry.

Carney’s comments in Cambodia on Monday came ahead of a planned meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping this week in Shenzhen, China, where Chinese auto manufacturing is expected to be discussed. The two leaders reached an agreement in January allowing tens of thousands of Chinese electric vehicles into Canada at reduced tariffs.

“We have the best auto workers in the world, and we want them fully deployed, full opportunity, in an integrated North American market,” Carney told reporters in Cambodia. “That market has become less integrated because of U.S. trade actions.”

Carney said Saturday in Manila, Philippines, that any trade agreement with Washington must leave Canada with a viable auto industry. He said Monday that negotiations with the United States remain his priority, but their outcome could determine whether Canada pursues alternatives involving European, Chinese or Japanese automakers.
Asked whether potential Chinese investment was leverage in the U.S. negotiations, Carney replied: “It’s not leverage. But action, reaction.”

“If they’re not fully utilized in a North American context, that provides other opportunities,” Carney said of Canada’s auto workers and manufacturing assets. “Canada is going to move forward either way.”

The Detroit Three — Ford, General Motors and Stellantis — operate factories across Canada, the United States and Mexico, with parts sometimes crossing borders multiple times before a vehicle is completed. Trump has repeatedly pushed automakers to move production to the United States from Canada.

Carney said any Chinese investment would have to involve substantial manufacturing in Canada rather than simply assembling imported parts. He said it would require proper labor standards, manufacturing facilities and domestic supply chains that expand over time, including Canadian critical minerals used in electric vehicles.
“It’s not just about kit cars,” he said. “There has to be a manufacturing aspect involved.”

Under the January agreement, Canada reduced its 100% tariff on Chinese electric vehicles to 6.1%, initially allowing up to 49,000 vehicles annually, with the cap increasing over time. In exchange, China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola.
Carney said at the time that he expected the agreement to attract Chinese investment in Canada’s auto industry and create jobs.

The deal drew criticism from Ontario Premier Doug Ford, whose province is the center of Canada’s auto industry. Ford warned that allowing Chinese electric vehicles into Canada could threaten Canadian jobs and jeopardize access to the U.S. market.

Trump’s tariffs have disrupted Canada’s auto industry, which relies heavily on cross-border production. Canada recently threatened to sue Stellantis after the automaker shifted planned Jeep Compass production from Brampton, Ontario, to Illinois and agreed to sell its idled Canadian assembly plant.

Carney said Saturday that he had spoken at length with Trump and senior U.S. officials and that the two countries were making progress toward a possible trade agreement, although differences remained.

title: Pakistan's imprisoned ex-leader Imran Khan appeals for urgent medical care
summary: Imprisoned former Prime Minister Imran Khan has appealed to Pakistan's top judges for urgent medical treatment for himself and his wife
story: Imprisoned former Prime Minister Imran Khan has appealed to Pakistan's top judges for urgent medical treatment for himself and his wife

ISLAMABAD -- Pakistan’s imprisoned former Prime Minister Imran Khan appealed Monday to the country’s top judges, seeking their help in getting urgent medical treatment for himself and his wife and alleging that authorities had failed to implement an earlier court order to transfer him to a hospital in the capital, Islamabad.

In an open letter and conveyed to the judges through his lawyer, Khan said his blood pressure had risen sharply and that doctors had warned him he was at risk of a brain hemorrhage and cardiac arrest.

According to the letter released to the media by Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf party and lawyer Salman Safdar, the former premier said that his wife, Bushra Bibi, also needed further eye surgery and could permanently lose her sight without it.

Khan has been in prison since 2023 after being convicted in a graft case. He was removed from office in a parliamentary no-confidence vote in April 2022. Despite his legal troubles, Khan remains a central and popular figure in Pakistan, and the PTI wants his release.
Khan's wife is also serving a prison term on graft charges.

Tariq Fazal Chaudhry, a Cabinet minister, disputed Khan’s account, saying he was receiving regular medical care and accusing him of seeking political advantage. In a post on X, Chaudhry said Khan has been taken to the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences in Islamabad eight times for examinations, where his health and blood pressure were found to be satisfactory.

He said Khan received meals of his choice and had access to books and television. The government was responsible for ensuring Khan’s medical care and protecting his legal rights, as it was for every prisoner, Chaudry said.
The latest development comes days after authorities allowed Khan's lawyers to see him at the prison.
“Today, I ask only that my wife and I be treated,” he said according to the letter. “I will only remain able to prove my innocence if I stay alive.”
The letter was addressed to the chief justices of Pakistan’s Supreme Court and other courts.
“I appeal to Your Lordships, on the most basic grounds of human compassion: give me justice before it is too late,” Khan said.

Earlier this year, Safdar, Khan's lawyer, told the Supreme Court that the former premier had lost roughly 85% of vision in his right eye. The government at the time denied the claim, and one of Khan’s sisters said his eyesight had significantly improved following medical treatment, which authorities say is ongoing.

The government of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has said that Khan isn’t being held under a government order, but as a “convicted prisoner” serving sentences imposed by the courts following judicial proceedings.

The government has rejected allegations that Khan was being held in solitary confinement or denied contact with his family, saying Khan had received more than 900 visits since his imprisonment in 2023.

title: Cape Verde election could deliver first woman president since independence in 1975
summary: Cape Verde has held a presidential election in which former Justice Minister Joana Rosa is challenging incumbent José Maria Neves
story: Cape Verde has held a presidential election in which former Justice Minister Joana Rosa is challenging incumbent José Maria Neves

PRAIA, Cape Verde -- PRAIA, Cape Verde (AP) — Cape Verde residents voted Sunday in a presidential election that could make Joana Rosa the country’s first woman head of state since independence from Portugal in 1975.

Polls closed Sunday evening in the vote in which the former justice minister is challenging President José Maria Neves, who is seeking a second term. Six candidates are competing. If none wins more than half the votes, a runoff will be held Nov. 29.

Rosa has the backing of the opposition Movement for Democracy, which governed for a decade before losing May’s parliamentary election. Women have held senior Cabinet positions, but the Atlantic island nation off West Africa has never had a woman president or prime minister.
The archipelagic country in the Atlantic Ocean, off the coast of West Africa, is battling with challenges such as a high unemployment rate and costs of living.
“I see many promises that are not fulfilled. I am tired, but I am still voting,” Aderito Cardoso, a 44-year-old resident of Villa Nova in the capital city Praia, said after casting her vote.

Under Cape Verde’s parliamentary system, the prime minister directs policy and holds most executive power. The directly elected president’s role is largely ceremonial, although the office carries the power to veto legislation.

The country of about half a million people has a record of competitive elections and peaceful transfers of power that stands out in the region. Nearly 77,000 citizens living abroad are registered to vote, accounting for almost a fifth of the electorate.

Roselma Évora, a professor of political science and gender studies at the University of Cabo Verde, said limited economic opportunities were pushing young people to leave. Many voters also feel disconnected from political leaders and want a president who understands their daily struggles, she said.
Neves, who won the presidency in 2021 with about 52% of the vote, has promised to build cross-party support to improve housing, healthcare and education, create jobs and raise wages.

His incumbency has given him greater visibility, including among overseas voters, Évora said. Rosa’s candidacy, meanwhile, challenges traditional expectations of women in a society that remains “very patriarchal.”

Rosa has focused her campaign on the balance of power, arguing that the presidency should serve as a counterweight to the African Party for the Independence of Cape Verde, which backs Neves and controls the government and most municipalities.

The party, known as PAICV, won a parliamentary majority in May, ending a decade of rule by the Movement for Democracy. A Rosa victory would again place the presidency and government in opposing political camps.
For Cape Verde-based writer Rosário Luz, party loyalties matter more than Rosa’s gender.
“We have a lot of women in politics, but we don’t have the policies for women that we should have,” she said.
Women shoulder much of the financial responsibility for their households, but government policies have failed to address that burden, Luz said.

title: Mexican drug kingpin Félix Gallardo, founder of Guadalajara cartel, dies at 80
summary: Gallardo, nicknamed the “Boss of Bosses,” died of multiple organ failure.
story: Gallardo, nicknamed the “Boss of Bosses,” died of multiple organ failure.

MEXICO CITY -- Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo, a former drug lord considered one of the godfathers of Mexico’s drug trafficking industry and a founder of the notorious Guadalajara cartel, died at a hospital in the western city of the same name. He was 80.
Félix Gallardo, nicknamed the “Boss of Bosses,” died Sunday at 2 p.m. of multiple organ failure, the Jalisco state security department said in a statement.

The notorious drug kingpin had been hospitalized since Friday after being rushed from the Puente Grande prison, where he had been held since 1989. He was serving a combined 77-year prison sentence for drug trafficking offenses and the 1985 killing of U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration agent Enrique “Kiki” Camarena.

Along with Rafael Caro Quintero and Ernesto Fonseca Carrillo, Félix Gallardo founded the Guadalajara cartel, which dominated drug trafficking in Mexico during the 1980s and eventually splintered into several criminal organizations in the country’s north, including the Sinaloa cartel.

Caro Quintero was released on procedural grounds in 2013 but recaptured in July 2022. He was extradited to the United States in February 2025 along with 28 other prisoners wanted by U.S. authorities on drug-related charges.
All three cartel founders were convicted in Mexico in connection with Camarena’s killing. The DEA agent was kidnapped and tortured before his body was found in 1985.
Félix Gallardo had sought house arrest since 2019, citing his advanced age and deteriorating health, but courts initially rejected his requests.
In September 2022, a judge granted him house arrest, but the order was never carried out because of legal challenges by Mexico’s federal attorney general’s office.

title: Lula to govern Brazil for fourth term but faces challenges. Here’s what to know
summary: Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has won a surprise reelection victory but faces significant challenges
story: Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has won a surprise reelection victory but faces significant challenges

RIO DE JANEIRO -- Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won a surprise reelection victory in late October, but he faces a multitude of challenges on issues ranging from the economy and public security to relations with the United States.

While Lula ultimately bested challenger Flávio Bolsonaro by 4.4 million votes after trailing him in the first round, the country remains deeply divided and many voters expressed dissatisfaction with the leftist president's most recent term, which began in 2023.

Bolsonaro refused to recognize the result of the election, declared himself the victim of electoral fraud without providing evidence and fled to Miami. He has vowed to lead a fortified opposition from the U.S.
As Lula prepares to begin his next term, here is a look at challenges ahead.

Lula is facing pressure from investors who had counted on Bolsonaro winning the election after the far-right candidate received more votes than Lula on Oct. 4. Markets did not react well to his loss. Brazil’s currency, the real, dropped by 12% against the dollar the day after the election, while the stock market tumbled nearly 14% and has not rebounded since.
Investors believed a Bolsonaro victory would rein in government spending and are concerned about Lula’s future fiscal policy, said Sergio Vale, chief economist at consultancy firm MB Associados.
“Lula and the government have vowed not to touch spending while keeping all the promises made these last few years,” said Vale. “Unfortunately, they’re not compatible with fiscal responsibility.”

Lula’s government recently unveiled plans to save up to 60 billion reais ($10.6 billion) in public funds through curbs on tax breaks and spending caps — a proposal that is currently moving through Congress.

During Lula’s third term, Brazil’s public debt grew from around 7.2 trillion reais ($1.3 trillion) in 2022 to 11.1 trillion reais ($2 trillion) this year, which analysts say spurred inflation and contributed to high interest rates ultimately remaining unchanged from 13.75% despite variations over the course of the term.
The high cost of living also left many Brazilians unhappy with the state of the economy despite record-low unemployment.

Lula will face a Congress that shifted further to the right in October's legislative elections. Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party secured the largest blocs in both houses, gaining an extra 23 seats in the lower house and nearly doubling its Senate seats, mostly at the expense of centrist parties.
Despite Bolsonaro’s departure for Miami, his party will remain a force to be reckoned with, retaining instruments to block governmental proposals and even challenge judicial authorities.

Bolsonaro’s congressional allies want, above all, to impeach Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes, who chaired the investigation that led to President Jair Bolsonaro serving a 27-year prison sentence for attempting a coup.

Their efforts would be helped if Rogério Marinho, Bolsonaro’s campaign coordinator, becomes Senate president. He announced his candidacy last week, promising not to focus solely on impeachment. But, he said, “we will not turn a blind eye, because no one is above the law.”
Brazilians cited crime as a top concern ahead of the election and insecurity featured prominently in the election cycle.

While Brazil's homicide rate last year fell to its lowest level since 2012, the country continues to face the expansion of criminal activities that use digital technology and online platforms, violence against vulnerable groups — including people of color, women and children — and the need to modernize security and justice institutions, according to this year’s annual report from the Brazilian Forum on Public Safety.

Drug-trafficking gangs have expanded their reach in recent years and are now present in large swathes of the country, including parts of the Amazon rainforest, while paramilitary-type militias have entrenched their power in Rio and other states.
Brazil’s Senate recently approved legislation that strengthens the government’s power to fight criminal gangs. Lula has touted the changes as key to tackling one of his nation’s biggest problems.
Navigating the rivalry between the U.S. and China will be key in Lula’s fourth term, said Ana Garcia, an international relations professor at the Rural Federal University of Rio de Janeiro.

Relations between Brazil and the U.S. fell to an all-time low during Lula’s third term, after the Trump administration imposed several rounds of tariffs. Meanwhile, ties with China deepened, displeasing the U.S., analysts say.

But Democrats' sweeping gains in the midterm election also reflected a repudiation of Trump’s tariffs, and pressure to reduce them — including those targeting Brazil — is likely to increase, Garcia said.

Garcia expects Flávio Bolsonaro and his brother Eduardo, who lives in Texas, to continue lobbying Trump administration allies against Lula’s government. But Democrats may increase scrutiny of Trump's policies abroad. In September, 31 Democratic members of Congress sent a letter to U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio accusing the Trump administration of “an apparent effort to interfere with, and potentially undermine” Brazil’s election.
“The midterms were a rude awakening for the Bolsonaros,” Garcia said.
Follow AP’s coverage of Latin America and the Caribbean at https://apnews.com/hub/latin-america

title: Africa is charting a different road to electric mobility with motorbikes and versatile 3-wheelers
summary: In Africa, the electric vehicle transition is taking a different route from wealthier markets, with motorcycles and three-wheelers emerging as practical alternatives to passenger cars
story: In Africa, the electric vehicle transition is taking a different route from wealthier markets, with motorcycles and three-wheelers emerging as practical alternatives to passenger cars

HARARE, Zimbabwe -- The electric vehicle revolution in Zimbabwe began on rural dirt paths. Three-wheeled vehicles carried cabbages to markets, women farmers to their fields and patients to clinics in communities where transport has long been scarce.
For farmer Agefi Mutambo, the owner of an electric three-wheeler since 2021, it has transformed her business and family.
Before, she walked seven to 10 kilometers (4.3 to 6.2 miles) balancing a 20-kilogram (44-pound) bucket of tomatoes on her head that she sold for $6.
“The money wasn't even enough for food. I would do a single trip a day, arrive at the market late and the produce would no longer be as fresh,” the 56-year-old said.

Now she makes two to three deliveries a week transporting 300 kilograms (661 pounds) of produce on each trip, grossing roughly $80 a trip supplying schools and clinics. She also ferries neighbors to hospital, sometimes at midnight for a woman in labor.
“When my battery is low, I simply swap it for $4, and I am back on the road,” she said.
Mutambo is among dozens of rural women entrepreneurs in Zimbabwe whose lives have been transformed by electric tricycles introduced by local social enterprise Mobility for Africa in 2019.

The company introduced the solar-charged tricycles, powered by lithium-ion batteries, mainly for rural women, under a lease-to-own scheme costing about $30 a week. Called “Hamba,” meaning “go” in the local Ndebele language, the vehicles can carry loads of over 400 kilograms (880 pounds) and travel about 100 kilometers (62 miles) on a single charge. Solar-powered charging stations and swappable batteries allow drivers to exchange depleted batteries rather than wait for them to recharge.

Across parts of Africa, motorcycles and three-wheelers are emerging as a route to electric mobility, particularly in rural communities long overlooked by conventional mobility businesses. While electric cars gain ground in wealthier markets, these smaller vehicles can operate with less extensive and expensive charging infrastructure, offering a potentially cheaper leapfrog to electrification for the continent of 1.5 billion people.
Despite holding vast reserves of critical minerals used in electric vehicle batteries, Africa remains a minor player in the global EV market.

Africa sold about 25,000 electric cars in 2025, concentrated in Egypt, Morocco and South Africa, compared with more than 20 million worldwide, according to the International Energy Agency’s Global EV Outlook 2026.
In 2026, the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa identified unreliable electricity infrastructure, limited technical capacity and weak regulation as barriers to adoption.

But the market for small electric vehicles that are relevant to everyday transport, deliveries and commerce is growing, said Hezbon Mose, an e-mobility expert. Africa’s transition is largely centered on income-earning motorcycles and three-wheelers, with Ethiopia an exception because of its car-focused policies, he said.

While two-wheelers remain dominant, a three-wheeler market is emerging. In Kenya, annual electric three-wheeler registrations rose from 39 in 2023 to 517 in 2025, reaching 1,965 by June this year, said Mose, co-founder of non-profit, E-Mobility Africa.

The shift also has potential public health benefits. Electric motorcycles and three-wheelers produce no exhaust fumes, offering an opportunity to reduce roadside pollution. In Kenya’s capital, Nairobi, where motorcycles are part of public transport culture, road transport alone is responsible for 40% of fine particle air pollution, according to the Clean Air Fund.

A 2025 study published in the World Electric Vehicle Journal also found that electrifying Nairobi’s motorcycle fleet would eliminate tailpipe particulate emissions from those vehicles, while cutting daily automotive carbon dioxide emissions by about 85%.
For entrepreneurs, the appeal lies in the economics of income-generating vehicles rather than luxury, said Mose, the expert.
“Electric three-wheelers already pay for themselves for working drivers,” he said.

A taxi electric three-wheeler in the Kenyan coastal city of Mombasa can save roughly $4 to $10 a day in running costs compared with a petrol-powered vehicle, with the higher purchase price recouped in five to 21 months, said Mose.

“They suit Africa because they are income assets, not consumer goods. The same chassis serves as taxi, last-mile delivery, waste collection, and produce haulage, widening the market well beyond public transport,” he said.

Citing industry figures, Mose said roughly 30 million Africans earn a living on two- and three-wheelers, yet fewer than 200,000 are electric. “An owner buys on daily cash flow, which is exactly where electric wins,” said Mose.
Investors are backing businesses developing electric motorcycles, three-wheelers, charging infrastructure and battery-swapping systems, especially in East Africa.
Shantha Bloemen, the Mobility for Africa founder, reckons lasting growth requires financing models that can survive beyond donor-funded projects.

“We have seen what happens with aid, how temporary it is when countries look at other priorities,” she said. “They cut Africa, their projects go to the ground. We need humanitarian assistance, but we need development finance more.”
For Bloemen, the idea was to address basic obstacles to rural economic activity: the lack of reliable, affordable transport and funding.
“When transport is scarce, produce rots in fields, children miss school and families cannot access healthcare,” Bloemen said. “Transport becomes the difference between subsistence and commerce.”
Bloemen argues that improving access to transport can help unlock the potential of rural economies often overlooked by conventional lenders.

“The rural informal economy is where most people live,” Bloemen said. “And if you look at my market, rural small-scale farmers... none of the banks will lend to them because they are deemed not creditworthy.”
Rural women, Bloemen said, are often most affected.
“We have a gender bias. We don’t take women small-scale farmers seriously, which is really not a clever thing to do because women are so entrepreneurial and the backbone of every economy,” she said.
Mutambo, the farmer, sees herself as an example. Her improved earnings have paid for one child’s teaching diploma, high school fees for another and primary schooling for five grandchildren.
“We were looked down upon,” she said. “Now we are the pride of the village.”

title: Pope Leo helps Argentines embrace Francis, the pontiff who once divided them
summary: Millions of Argentines have turned out to see Pope Leo XIV — and the words that moved them most often belonged to his predecessor, and their compatriot, Francis
story: Millions of Argentines have turned out to see Pope Leo XIV — and the words that moved them most often belonged to his predecessor, and their compatriot, Francis

BUENOS AIRES, Argentina -- Vast crowds of young Argentines, a generation that Catholic leaders had feared was abandoning the pews, packed the parks of Buenos Aires and cheered as if at a concert when Pope Leo XIV promised a church open to “todos, todos, todos” — everyone, everyone, everyone.
Those words, like all of Leo’s surest applause lines during the visit, belonged to his Argentine predecessor, Pope Francis. So did much of the week's adulation.

Francis’ fierce defense of the downtrodden made him a moral voice abroad but long embroiled him in political fights at home — controversy that many believe deterred him from returning as pope. More than a year after his death, the more measured Leo made the homecoming Francis never could, carrying on his legacy and helping Argentines embrace their once-polarizing pope as a unifying national figure.

“It’s as though it has finally become clear that Francis left a very important legacy, not just for Argentina but for the universal church,” said Pablo Forni, a sociologist at Argentina’s national research council, Conicet. “Leo is reaping what Francis sowed.”

Billboards welcoming Leo bore Francis’ face. Pilgrims waved signs declaring “Francisco y León, un solo corazón” — Francis and Leo, one heart. Even libertarian President Javier Milei, who once insulted Francis as “the representative of evil on earth," declared Francis “the most important Argentine in history” at Leo's welcome ceremony, bringing a packed hall of his political allies and foes to its feet.

As archbishop of Buenos Aires, Francis — then Jorge Mario Bergoglio — mobilized the church during Argentina’s 2001 economic crisis, sending priests into the slums and opening soup kitchens, schools and drug rehab centers as state services receded. But his concern for the poor did not make him a natural ally of Peronism, the long-dominant populist movement emphasizing social justice. He accused its leaders of arrogance and clashed with them over same-sex marriage.

Yet once Francis moved to Rome as pontiff, Peronists became some of his biggest fans, seeing their priorities reflected in his criticism of unbridled capitalism and his outreach to the marginalized. That affinity infuriated conservatives, who blame Peronism for ruining Argentina's economy and presiding over rampant corruption. However hard Francis tried to stay above the fray, even his smallest gestures — a dour expression beside right-leaning President Mauricio Macri, a relaxed lunch with left-leaning President Cristina Fernández de Kirchner — were read as proof of his political sympathies.

A homecoming would have meant treading a minefield. Francis visited more than 60 countries as pope, including four of Argentina’s five neighbors, but never returned home, despite invitations from four successive presidents.

“At first many people were thrilled to see an Argentine elected pope. But once they heard his criticism, they stopped loving him quite so much,” said the Rev. Lorenzo de Vedia, known as Padre Toto, one of the so-called slum priests who worked under Bergoglio in the capital’s informal settlements. “He became seen as a partisan pope.”

Argentines weren’t the only ones Francis provoked. His blunt, freewheeling papacy divided Catholics worldwide. He accused Vatican officials of “spiritual Alzheimer’s” and called attacks from American conservatives “an honor.” He delighted progressives by opening long-taboo debates, then disappointed them by balking at doctrinal change.

Now Leo — a Chicago-born former missionary in Peru whom Francis made a bishop and then a cardinal — is carrying the same causes forward with a gentleness that tempers his predecessor’s hard-charging style, church leaders say.

“Francis opened the way. He broke down walls. He was forceful and impetuous, firm in his principles and startling in his proposals,” said Cardinal Pedro Barreto, a Peruvian Jesuit and close ally of Francis. “Leo XIV is clearing the path Francis laid out so that it can be traveled by every baptized member of the church."

Leo called the trip “a homage” to Francis, and over four days he followed in his predecessor's footsteps: praying in Francis’ old cathedral, dispensing blessings at the prison where Francis once washed inmates' feet, embracing residents of a disability care home where he also preached and celebrating Mass at the Luján shrine he revered. Leo invoked Francis at least 26 times.
“Leo is fulfilling the promise that Francis left unfinished,” said Carlos Custer, a former Argentine ambassador to the Vatican. “Francis' presence was felt at every turn."
But Leo did more than honor Francis’ memory. In his own voice, and without the baggage of an Argentine passport, he revived the appeals that had made Francis at once beloved and divisive at home.

In Córdoba, Leo urged Argentines to keep “making a mess,” echoing Francis’ famous call for young Catholics to shake things up in their dioceses. Before an audience of garbage pickers and business leaders, he invoked Francis’ “three Ts” — tierra, techo y trabajo, or land, housing and work — the rallying cry of Argentina’s popular movements.

And in his opening address to political leaders last Sunday, standing beside a self-declared “anarcho-capitalist” president known for aggressive verbal outbursts and harsh austerity measures, he urged “careful use of words” and insisted that “the economy must be at the service of the person, not the person in the service of the economy.”

“There is continuity between them in every respect — in their message of peace, their love for the poor, their choice to go places where people are suffering, in their emotional connection to the people,” said the Rev. Carlos María Galli, a prominent Argentine theologian who was close to Francis. “Francis brought Leo to the center of the church, and Leo has now brought Francis back to us.”

Politicians scrambled to claim Leo's message as their own. Axel Kicillof, the Peronist governor of Buenos Aires province and a leading opposition figure, hailed the visit as “very necessary in these times of cruelty." Vice President Victoria Villarruel defended the concept of social justice derided by her boss and championed by Francis, blaming “ignorance and fanaticism” for its frequent association with Peronism.
Even Milei’s spokesman, Adrián Ravier, insisted Wednesday that by taming inflation, the government had put “the economy at the service of people.”
For observers, that political jockeying proved the wisdom of Francis’ decision to stay away — and the value of Leo as his messenger.

“Had Bergoglio said the same things and visited the same places, it would have been seen as far more political,” said Gustavo Morello, an Argentine sociologist of religion at Boston College. “But you can’t accuse Leo of being a Peronist. So when he speaks about workers or people with disabilities, it’s the church speaking ... and if you don’t like it, you can take it up with God.”
Associated Press writer Mauricio Savarese in Lima, Peru, contributed to this report.

title: Southeast Asian leaders open annual summit with major conflicts and their impact topping the agenda
summary: Southeast Asian leaders have opened their annual summit in the Philippine capital Manila for three days of talks
story: Southeast Asian leaders have opened their annual summit in the Philippine capital Manila for three days of talks

MANILA, Philippines -- Southeast Asian leaders opened their annual summit in the Philippine capital Manila on Sunday for three days of talks, including dialogues with world leaders led by U.S. President Donald Trump, whose crucial trip to Asia could help boost his standing after his party’s defeat in the midterm elections.

The talks by the leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and their expanded discussions with Asian and Western heads of state would focus on the world’s most troubling conflicts led by the war in the Middle East, according to drafts of post-summit communiques seen by The Associated Press.

Trump is expected to land in Manila with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday afternoon, after the main ASEAN summit meetings have concluded and Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. turns over the regional bloc’s rotating annual leadership to Singapore, Philippine officials said.

The ASEAN leaders are likely to renew calls for self-restraint and peaceful resolutions of conflicts, including longstanding disputes in the South China Sea and a civil war in Myanmar. They also are expected to press efforts to shield their economies and citizens from continuing fallout from intractable global conflicts.
“We reaffirmed our shared commitment to upholding international law, including the United Nations Charter,” the leaders’ draft statement says.

The statement also underlines the “importance of the peaceful resolution of disputes, upholding freedom of navigation and overflight and other lawful uses of the sea, including the right of transit passage in straits used for international navigation.”
Marcos said it’s crucial that despite the 11-nation regional bloc’s diversity, it has remained committed to remaining united in the face of headwinds.

“That commitment matters even more as the waters around us turn on shifting tides, geopolitical tensions, economic uncertainty, new technologies, climate change and transnational threats,” Marcos said in his opening remarks before ASEAN counterparts in a heavily secured convention center by Manila Bay.
Marcos warned problems across the world “are reshaping our region faster than any one country can respond to alone.”
But unity has been an elusive objective in ASEAN, a diverse bloc of democracies and authoritarian states, many of which are aligned with the United States or China.
ASEAN is known more for photo-ops projecting unity, cultural pomp and pageantry than for effectively dealing with the region’s conflicts, including Myanmar and the South China Sea.

Trump will join three key meetings late Tuesday, including a meeting of the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue consisting of the United States, Japan, Australia and India, a grouping largely seen as a counterweight to China. He also will take part in a special summit with ASEAN leaders over cocktails, according to Philippine officials.

Trump will meet Wednesday with Marcos, who will receive him with a red-carpet welcome and a state luncheon at Manila’s presidential palace. They are expected to renew a commitment to their countries’ decades-old treaty alliance before flying separately to Shenzhen city in China for the APEC summit hosted by Chinese President Xi Jinping.

“The short stop in Manila will help reassure allies and partners that they aren’t being forgotten before he jets off to Shenzhen to focus on meetings with Xi,” U.S.-based geopolitical analyst Greg Poling said.
He added that the midterm electoral setback suffered by Republicans will hound Trump in Asia.

“In China, the administration has been trying to lower expectations; there will be no substantive progress made between Trump and Xi,” Poling said. “With Trump politically weakened after the midterm drubbing here, it is likely that the Chinese side will be even less interested in making any compromises.”
China will be represented in the Manila summit by its premier, Li Qiang, who will meet ASEAN leaders on Monday but leave before Trump arrives, Philippine officials said.
Associated Press journalist Haruka Nuga in Tokyo contributed to this report.

title: Spain says nearly 2,200 migrants reached Canary Islands in 2 days
summary: Spain's maritime rescue service says nearly 2,200 migrants have arrived in the Canary Islands over the past two days
story: Spain's maritime rescue service says nearly 2,200 migrants have arrived in the Canary Islands over the past two days
MADRID -- Nearly 2,200 migrants have arrived by boat in Spain’s Canary Islands over the past two days, Spain’s maritime rescue service said Sunday.

The Spanish archipelago off northwest Africa is one of the main entry points for migrants into the country, as people mainly from West Africa attempt the dangerous Atlantic crossing in ramshackle boats. Of the just over 28,000 people who arrived in Spain by sea between January and the end of October, more than 13,000 arrived in the Canary Islands, according to the Interior Ministry.

The Maritime Rescue Service said it had assisted 1,324 migrants aboard 14 dinghies, most of whom arrived on the island of El Hierro. The figure was close to the daily record for this route — 1,461 people rescued on Nov. 7, 2020.

The strip of the Atlantic Ocean between West Africa and the Canary Islands is one of the world’s deadliest migration routes. The islands are roughly 65 miles (105 kilometers) from the closest point in Africa, but to avoid security forces, many migrants attempt longer journeys that can take days or weeks. The majority depart from Mauritania.
Follow AP’s global migration coverage at https://apnews.com/hub/migration

title: Zelenskyy warns Starshield restrictions threaten Ukraine’s energy defenses
summary: Restrictions on the system hamper Kyiv’s ability to shoot down Russian drones.
story: Restrictions on the system hamper Kyiv’s ability to shoot down Russian drones.
KYIV, Ukraine -- Restrictions on Ukraine’s Starshield satellite communications system are hindering its ability to intercept Russian drones, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Sunday.

He warned that limitations on the system, operated by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, could weaken defenses around Ukraine’s energy infrastructure ahead of the winter months, when Moscow has repeatedly targeted the power grid.

Ukraine’s interceptor drones continue to lose contact with their operators when flying faster than 161 kph (100 mph) along the front line and over Russian-occupied territory, leaving them unable to catch Russian Shahed drones, Zelenskyy said.

“We are counting on these restrictions to be lifted,” he wrote on social media. “The protection of lives and Ukrainian energy infrastructure before winter depends on this. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Ministry of Defense, and the President’s Office have been instructed to work closely with the American side and SpaceX. It is important to be on the right side of history. We need to help Ukraine.”

Zelenskyy questioned Saturday whether the problem was technical, saying the restrictions appeared to have been imposed by SpaceX despite earlier assurances from U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio that Starshield was more under U.S. government control.
Meanwhile, a Russian strike on Chornomorsk, a port city in Ukraine’s Odesa region, injured six people and damaged energy infrastructure, regional head Oleh Kiper said Sunday on Telegram.
The blast and falling debris also damaged a gas pipeline and nearby residential buildings, while two parked cars caught fire.
The strike hit a facility operated by DTEK Odesa Electric Networks, temporarily leaving about 41,000 customers without power, Kiper said.
Overnight Russian airstrikes on the southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia injured another six people, including a 2-year-old boy, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said Sunday.
Russia launched more than 2,300 drones, 1,590 guided aerial bombs and 15 missiles of various types against Ukraine over the past week, Zelenskyy said.
Ukrainian drone strikes damaged two electrical substations in Russia’s Rostov region, killing a chief engineer, Gov. Yuri Slyusar said Sunday.

Four people were injured when drone debris fell on their cars, Slyusar wrote on social media. A fifth person was wounded when debris struck a “production facility” in the village of Troitskoye, he said.

Ukrainian forces also targeted Russia’s Tatarstan region, officials said. Radmir Belyaev, mayor of Nizhnekamsk, the region’s third-largest city, said a “large-scale and prolonged attack” damaged its industrial zone.
Six people were injured, and heating and hot water supplies were disrupted in parts of the city, he said.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said its forces shot down 533 Ukrainian drones overnight across 13 Russian regions, the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea, and the Black and Azov seas.
Associated Press writer Katie Marie Davies contributed from Manchester, England.
