title: Trump says he may meet with North Korea's Kim Jong Un during China trip
summary: Trump's trip comes amid the Nvidia CEO scandal involving an alleged Chinese spy.
story: Trump's trip comes amid the Nvidia CEO scandal involving an alleged Chinese spy.
President Donald Trump is traveling to Asia for meetings with global leaders and for his second visit to China for a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping.
As he departed the White House Monday morning, Trump said he "may" meet with North Korea's Kim Jong Un in China as well, though he said it would ultimately be Xi's decision.
"He may come. I don't know. That's up to President Xi," Trump said of Kim Jong Un.

Trump will participate in the first-ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the U.S., China and Russia on the sidelines of the APEC Summit in China, senior U.S. officials said. The president is expected to discuss the war in Iran with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin. However, he does not intend to discuss Ukraine during the trilateral meeting, officials say.

Denuclearization will be the focus of the long-awaited trilateral meeting, though officials said they do not anticipate the leaders reaching any concrete agreement and are characterizing this meeting as an initial conversation broaching the subject.

Trump had been teasing a potential face-to-face meeting with the world's leading nuclear superpowers for some time. On Oct. 19, Trump told ABC News Chief White House correspondent Mary Bruce that he would like to meet with Putin and Xi when he visits China, saying "I would do that," and indicated a desire to discuss denuclearization.
Trump and Xi will have a bilateral meeting ahead of the trilateral, though Trump and Putin will not be meeting one-on-one separately, the officials said.
The president's trip comes as questions linger about what the administration knew about prominent tech CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.
Billionaire Elon Musk will be joining Trump for parts of his China travels. Officials did not specify his reason for accompanying the president, merely pointing to Musk's business interests in China.
An official said they expect some additional U.S. business leaders to be attending the APEC CEO Summit, but clarified that they are not part of the U.S. delegation.

Trump is expected to leave Washington in the morning of Monday, Nov. 16 and arrive in Manila in the evening of Tuesday, Nov. 17, and will head to a bilateral meeting with the other members of the Quad, a diplomatic partnership the U.S. has with Australia, India, and Japan, about peace and security in the Indo-Pacific region. The president is also expected to sign a trade deal with Thailand.
He will then participate in an ASEAN cocktail reception followed by a summit dinner.

The next day, Trump will participate in a welcome ceremony at Malacañang Presidential Palace, the official residence of Filipino President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Romualdez Marcos Jr., followed by a bilateral meeting. He will also participate in an Association of Southeast Asian Nations cocktail reception followed by a summit dinner.

After Wednesday’s events in the Philippines, Trump travels to Shenzhen, China, where it is expected that a minister will greet Trump on the tarmac. He will participate in an APEC leaders' dinner and multilateral meeting with the APEC leaders. On Thursday afternoon local time, Trump will participate in a bilateral meeting and working lunch with Chinese President Xi.
The historic trilateral Trump-Xi-Putin trilateral meeting will be the final event on the president's Asia swing.
Each of Trump and Xi’s meetings this year have been clouded by other topics.

When Trump visited China in May, the raging war in Iran overshadowed the state visit that was scheduled after a detente in Trump's tit-for-tat trade war. Also, when Trump welcomed Xi in September, the pomp and circumstance Trump had planned went without live TV coverage after his banning outlets from the press pool led to a network boycott.

Now, in the background of this trip, is the scandal involving Nvidia's CEO, Huang, who joined Trump's last trip to China earlier this year after boarding Air Force One during a refueling stop in Alaska, according to pool reports at the time. Huang was reported to have had an affair with Alice Huang, a Chinese national and tech executive who is accused of being a Chinese spy.

Officials said they do not expect Trump to raise the allegations against Alice Huang, the suspected Chinese spy, with President Xi, adding that the two presidents plan to focus on implementing aspects of their trade agreement.

"You know, I think when it comes to some of these national security matters and examinations and investigations that are going on in the U.S., it's probably not something that we're going to read the Chinese in on at this moment," a senior U.S. official said.
Huang resigned from Nvidia's board and as its president and CEO on Nov. 12.
This scandal engulfing Huang has introduced scrutiny over Trump’s ties to him and what Trump and other administration officials knew about the relationship with the alleged spy.

"Well, I've been hearing about it and I've been reading a little bit about it over a period of time. But, not too long ago," Trump told reporters during an impromptu press conference in the White House briefing room on Nov. 9.

When pressed on if he was aware of the allegations during his May trip to China, Trump said: "No, I didn't hear about it then. But a lot of people have heard about it, and Jensen totally denies that he had."

On May 12, Secretary of State Marco Rubio shared intelligence with Trump on Air Force One showing Huang was in a relationship with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy, a U.S. official and two sources familiar with the matter told ABC News. This is the second known time that Trump had been warned about the plot. Trump was briefed by Rubio shortly before Huang was set to join Trump on the trip to China, the U.S. official and sources said.

A U.S. official and a source familiar with the matter told ABC News that after Air Force One landed in China, White House officials asked for business leaders -- including Huang -- to be allowed into a meeting with President Xi. Initially, the Chinese were hesitant to adjust the program, but ultimately agreed to it.

Huang, who co-founded Nvidia, one of the world’s most-valuable companies and the maker of chips that top AI companies heavily rely on, has been a constant presence around Trump, who has invited tech executives to multiple events, both at the White House and on overseas trips. Since April 28, when Huang and his wife, Lori, attended a state dinner for King Charles III and Queen Camila, the tech CEO has participated in at least six events with Trump, including the September state dinner for Xi.
Huang has lobbied for policy positions that benefit China and Chinese companies over the past few months.

For example, the U.S. has long blocked China's access to American AI chips. However, in December 2025, after lobbying from Huang, Trump loosened those restrictions -- approving the sale of some older but still powerful chips to China as part of a remarkable deal that gave the U.S. government a 25% cut of the sales.

And in July of this year, Huang joined the social media platform X to push back against possible bans on open-weight AI models, the type that Chinese companies have embraced, and which would be cheaper for businesses and governments to adopt. The ban would benefit American companies OpenAI and Anthropic, which use closed models. The U.S. was reportedly considering those bans.
"The world needs both frontier closed models and frontier open models," Huang wrote in his first-ever X post.

This trip marks Trump's first one overseas since American voters handed him and Republicans a devastating defeat in the midterm elections. Voter Polls show voters rejected the president’s tariffs and the war in Iran -- two of Trump's key foreign policy positions.

The tariffs have been ensnared in legal challenges in count -- and Democrats, who will take the majority in January, have vowed to counter them and reassert congressional authority over trade. They don’t have a veto-proof majority, however, and Trump has vowed to use his veto pen to kill bills he doesn't like.

And the president does not appear to feel pressure to reign in his sweeping tariffs. On Nov. 12, he threatened to double tariffs on Mexico if they don't stop what he claims are caravans heading to the southern border post-midterms.

title: Microsoft identifies issues leading to global Outlook outage
summary: Microsoft executive lays out issues leading to the Outlook outage in social media post.
story: The executive laid out three main issues leading to the outage.
Microsoft is apologizing for the mass global Outlook outage last week and identifying the main causes of the problem that spanned across two workdays.

In a lengthy social media post Monday morning, a Microsoft executive said a combination of a "latent defect," increased load and lessened server capacity were among the cascading set of issues that led to users across the globe dealing with an outage on the email service.
The outage seemingly downed communications across industries last week, with reports of businesses, governments, schools and healthcare providers experiencing communication disruptions.
"A latent defect caused servers to become overwhelmed and unresponsive under certain load conditions," wrote Charles Lamanna, Executive Vice President of Copilot, Agents, and Platform at Microsoft.
The defect came from a fix that was "prepared specifically for Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers," he said.
Lamana also pointed to "a surge in load" on the networking gateway as a secondary cause of the global outage.
The executive highlighted a reduced server capacity as a third primary reason for last week's email service issues, though Lamana said the reduction "had no impact on its own."

"Taken together, the increased load and the reduced server capacity, caused the network gateway to encounter the latent bug from July. This caused requests to build up until servers ultimately stopped responding. This occurred during the peak window of traffic in the United States," wrote Lamana.

Lamana also explained the extended time period it took to recover from the outage saying, "Recovery took longer than usual because as servers returned to service, they were immediately overwhelmed by waiting traffic and became unresponsive again."
"We are deeply sorry for the impact to all our customers and recognize the impact that this has on their normal business & operations," wrote Lamana in the update.

title: Person of interest in custody after device found at Illinois plant
summary: A person of interest is in custody after a device was found at the Peoria, Illinois BioUrja Renewables facility.
story: A person of interest is in custody in connection with the device found Friday at the BioUrja Renewables facility in Peoria, Illinois, according to multiple sources familiar with the situation.
Peoria Police also confirmed a person of interest has been taken into custody and said the FBI is expected to release additional information later Monday.

Authorities were investigating a "credible" threat at the plant in Peoria, Illinois, after the device was discovered at the facility Friday night and later rendered safe by bomb technicians, according to officials.

Police determined at about 6:45 p.m. local time Friday that a package at the facility was a credible threat and established a one-mile blast radius, officials said at a press conference after the incident.
Bomb technicians "rendered the package safe" at about 9:12 p.m. local time, according to police.

No additional devices were found and the evacuation order within a one-mile blast radius of the BioUrja Renewables facility was lifted after investigators searched the facility for hours, Peoria police said Saturday.
Asked if the incident was being investigated as a terrorist threat, Dixon said that officials would not comment on the criminal investigation as it is "active" and "open."
The police chief said the search was difficult due to the facility's size, describing it as large as 44-and-a-half football fields.
This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

title: ATC routers' ability to broadcast data turned off, being investigated: Duffy
summary: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy joined "This Week" following a rare nationwide ground stop that brought air travel to a halt Friday.
story: Duffy said the router at issue is being examined at a lab in Florida.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Sunday that air traffic control routers' ability to broadcast data has been turned off as officials continue to investigate the router communication issue that prompted a nationwide ground stop Friday.

"We have that router in the L3Harris lab down in Florida," Duffy told co-anchor Martha Raddatz on ABC's "This Week" Sunday, referring to the specific router in Arkansas that officials believe caused instability in the air traffic communication system Friday afternoon. L3Harris is a government contractor that provides technology and IT support for the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA).

"Our FAA team is on site as well. We've been partnering with the FBI and other law enforcement. We're going to take a look at what happened there," he continued. "But what we've now done, we have 69 of these routers in the national airspace. We've stopped their ability to broadcast, and it was this router was broadcasting data from this this radio facility into the whole network. Once we shut the shut the ability to broadcast down on the routers, the issue is resolved. So we're going to take a hard look at it."

Duffy explained that work was being done to replace outdated copper wire with fiber cables in El Dorado, Arkansas. When the router in that area was turned on, "we saw that in Amarillo, Texas, a system we had replaced about three weeks earlier, that started to flood our system as well."
"So we're looking at those two issues and trying to find the root cause of what happened," Duffy said.
In a post on social media, Duffy said that the router from Texas was also being investigated at the Florida lab.

"If we see these inconsistencies in the network, whether it's communication with air traffic controllers and pilots or with data feeds, we're going to keep you safe," Duffy said. "We did the ground stop. We were able to isolate the issue, shut it down. Our network came back online, and from there we opened up the airspace thereafter."

At 3:54 p.m. Friday, the FAA declared a rare, nationwide ground stop, bringing air travel to a halt. While planes already in the air were able to continue flying, for more than four hours, millions of travelers awaited news about when or if their scheduled flight would be able to take off.

Shortly after the ground stop was lifted at 8:15 p.m. Friday, Duffy briefed reporters, along with Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin. Duffy said then that the nation’s aging air traffic control system routers were “overloaded with data,” causing “inconsistency in the data” that prompted officials to “shut the system down.” He called for Congress to appropriate tens of billions of dollars more to cover the cost to completely overhaul and modernize the ATC system.

Saturday morning, Duffy updated reporters again alongside FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford. The transportation secretary said officials believed that “routine maintenance” being done by government contractor L3Harris in a “remote” location prompted the communication breakdown.

“What we're working to determine was whether we had incompetence, meaning was it user error or installer error from L3Harris, or did they install a faulty router? We haven't determined what the fault was,” Duffy said Saturday. “That router that was being replaced as we switched from copper to fiber, it started flooding other routers in our air traffic control system. … What that did was gave us issues with our, our communication with airplanes, and it also caused some disruption with our radar feeds.”
In a statement, L3Harris said it was “supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand” what happened Friday.
“L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously,” the statement read.

Duffy reiterated on Sunday that officials do not see evidence that the router issues were caused by a cyberattack, but added "if the FBI comes in and says, 'No, we found something,' obviously we'll share that with the American people, but we have no indication that this was a hack."
Duffy also said officials "don't think that someone tried to sabotage the network on the install at all. But we don’t actually have the root cause, which is why we do the investigation."

Federal Aviation Administration Administrator Bryan Bedford said at a press conference Saturday that there investigators then had seen "zero evidence of anything nefarious, and zero evidence of anything AI-related. So we want to be clear that we have a equipment issue, and we're working through what this defective piece of equipment was."
Duffy again made the case for Congress to appropriate more funding to overhaul the nation's aging air traffic control system.

"What I'm doing is saying, hey, Congress, this is old. There's issues with how it operates. Let's build a brand-new system," he told Martha Raddatz, adding that "this will be the one great bipartisan bill that can pass in an era of great partisanship."
He added that telecom companies AT&T, Verizon and Lumens are "ready to start working tomorrow" on new air traffic control architecture.
"All we need is the money to say, go build a new network. That would be done by the end of 2028 or possibly the first quarter of 2029," Duffy said.
The secretary also said that while Congress appropriated $12.5 billion to the FAA in the "One Big Beautiful Bill" signed into law last year, it cannot be used to address telecom architecture.

"They gave me money for tower -- for radios, money for radar, money for systems. But I don't have any money in that $12.5 billion for a new architecture for telecom. I don't have any money given by Congress to build a new software system to manage the airspace. They’re very specific on how we spend the 12.5 and none of the money goes to this telecom that I have to build. So, they need to give me additional money to finish that project," Duffy said.
Democrats, however, are skeptical of the funding request.

"Congress approved $12.5 billion for the Department of Transportation to make necessary safety upgrades to our air traffic control system. Fifteen months later, the administration’s obligated $4.3 billion but only spent $1 billion, leaving $8 billion unobligated and $11 billion unspent. Explain to Congress, again, why they need more money?" Rep. Rick Larsen (D-Wash.), ranking member of the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure, and Rep. André Carson, D-Ind., ranking member of the House Subcommittee on Aviation, said in a statement Saturday.

title: Congressional Republicans push Howard Lutnick, Jensen Huang to testify about Nvidia
summary: Senate Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott, a Republican, sent letters to both Huang and Lutnick to publicly testify in front of the committee
story: GOP Sen. Tim Scott sent letters to both Huang and Lutnick to publicly testify.

House and Senate Republican leaders are demanding answers from former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy and whether that relationship may have influenced business dealings involving Nvidia and China.

Senate Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott, a Republican, sent letters to both Huang and Lutnick to publicly testify in front of the committee. It comes after Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia earlier this week after reports that he had an affair with Alice Huang, a Chinese national and tech executive at Megaspeed who is accused of being a Chinese spy. Jensen Huang admitted to an affair, but he didn't say with whom.
Lawmakers have raised concerns about the national security implications of Huang's reported relationship given that he ran the world's largest computer chip manufacturer.
"Secretary Lutnick has proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the Banking Committee to address their questions," said Commerce Department spokesperson Kristen Eichamer.
It's not yet clear when Lutnick will appear before the committee.
The committee is requesting Huang to appear on Dec. 3 with Chairman Scott threatening to subpoena Huang if he fails to voluntarily appear in front of the committee.
Meanwhile, top House Republicans have asked Huang to come in for a closed-door transcribed interview on Dec. 1 as the two sides have been in active negotiations.

House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast, Intelligence Committee Chairman Rick Crawford and Select Committee on Chairman John Moolenaar requested a written confirmation of Huang’s acceptance by 8 p.m. Friday, under threat of subpoena.

"Failure to cooperate with this request will result in the House Foreign Affairs Committee issuing a subpoena to compel your testimony in a format of the committee's choosing. Other committees also reserve the right to separately issue subpoenas to compel your testimony,” Thursday’s letter to Huang states.

Mast, Crawford and Moolenaar wrote in a statement that as "reports continue to come to light regarding Jensen Huang, NVIDIA, and Megaspeed, there are clear national security concerns that need to be addressed immediately."

The three chairmen also asked Nvidia’s General Counsel Tim Teter to appear for a closed-door transcribed interview on Dec. 2 "regarding AI chip smuggling, adversary military use of NVIDIA products, and recent public reporters regarding NVIDIA’s interference in U.S. export control policies and investigations, including those involving Megaspeed." Republicans requested a written confirmation of Teter’s acceptance by 8 p.m. Friday, saying they will issue a subpoena if they do not.

The requests for both men to testify come amid growing concern over potential Chinese espionage and whether any protocols at the Commerce Department were broken in their oversight of Nvidia’s chip exports to China.

Lutnick is being accused of delaying placing Megaspeed, a customer of Nvidia and Alice Huang's employer, on a list of companies that pose national security concerns, even as U.S. intelligence indicated that Megaspeed may have been diverting purchased Nvidia chips to China, something the company denies.

"Well, I want to wait and see if the allegations are true and what he has to say about it. But I'd be concerned. You know, the rumors are very concerning. The reporting is very concerning about it,” Republican Sen. Kevin Cramer told reporters on Thursday.
Republican Sen. John Curtis said "we need answers and accountability" from Huang and Lutnick "immediately."

"Jensen Huang's gross negligence exposed cracks in our national security, but Secretary Lutnick's reported stalling on export controls raises the question of whether the Commerce Department is acting in the best interests of the American people," Curtis wrote in a social media post.

House Republicans are seeking testimony on Dec. 3 from Jeff Kessler, the under Secretary of Commerce for Industry and Security "for a hearing on chip smuggling, adversary use of advanced AI chips, reported interference by private companies into export control policy and enforcement investigations, and Megaspeed."

title: Sarah Huckabee Sanders receives 2028 presidential encouragement
summary: Supporters and donors have been encouraging GOP Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders to run for president in the 2028 cycle, sources told ABC News.
story: Georgia GOP Gov. Brian Kemp is also said to be getting encouragement to run.

Supporters and donors have been encouraging Republican Arkansas governor and former White House press secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders to run for president in the 2028 cycle, according to multiple sources with direct knowledge of the situation.

​When asked about the outreach Sanders has been receiving, her communications director Sam Dubke told ABC News that “Governor Sanders looks forward to serving the people of Arkansas for the next four years.”

​Sanders, the daughter of Mike Huckabee, himself a former Arkansas governor, Repubican presidential candidate and current U.S. ambassador to Israel, won re-election as governor last week. She became the first woman ever elected Arkansas governor in 2022.

Before becoming governor, Sanders served as President Donald Trump's press secretary in his first term from July 2017 to June 2019 after having served as deputy press secretary. She was also a senior adviser to Trump's 2016 presidential campaign.

​While Sanders formally briefed the White House press corps less than her predecessors, she became one of Trump’s closest and most trusted advisers and has maintained a close relationship with him, having worked for Trump in the White House for 3 1/2 years.
Sanders has long been viewed as a rising star in the Republican Party.

In 2023, a few months after winning the gubernatorial race in Arkansas, Sanders delivered the Republican response to former President Joe Biden’s State of the Union address -- remarks usually reserved for individuals seen as on their way up in the party.

Georgia's retiring popular two-term Republican Gov. Brian Kemp is also considering a presidential bid after he leaves office in January and has been encouraged by donors and other Republican officials to run, a source familiar with his thinking told ABC News.
​In the days leading up to the midterm elections, Kemp traveled to South Carolina, one of the early nominating states for Republicans, to campaign for Gov.-elect Alan Wilson.
ABC News has reached out to Kemp's political operation for comment.
​After Republicans' midterm losses, the party is reflecting on what went wrong and how to move forward, with some of those conversations happening publicly.
​Texas Sen. Ted Cruz, who has not ruled out a 2028 presidential run, called Republicans' performance in the midterm elections a "Watergate-level repudiation" of the party.
​Outgoing Florida Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis described the election results as a "meteor strike," arguing that even a "wave" fails to capture the scale of the Republican losses.

​DeSantis is keeping his options open for another presidential run, two people familiar with his thinking told ABC News, after the governor said Florida fended off a blue wave in this year's midterm elections.

title: Van Hollen says Schumer's team trying to 'instill fear' to retain Senate leadership
summary: Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen touted his chances of becoming Senate majority leader when Democrats take control of the Senate in January.
story: "We need to earn the people's trust," Van Hollen told ABC News' "This Week."

Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen touted his chances of becoming Senate majority leader when Democrats take control of the Senate in January, accusing current leader Sen. Chuck Schumer of trying to scare Democrats into supporting his continued leadership.
"I think there's a very open lane here. The Schumer team's put out a lot of misinformation," Van Hollen told ABC News' "This Week" co-anchor Martha Raddatz in an interview on Sunday.

"They're essentially trying to instill fear in people who may say that they're going to support me as a new leader ... We just had a great day for our democracy around the country. How about a little democracy in the Senate Democratic Caucus?"

In a post on social media this week, Schumer wrote that he welcomes "any discussion about the future of our caucus," continuing to say that he has "the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader."

Schumer's optimism came as several Democratic senators and others elected in this month's midterm elections expressed the desire for new leadership in Washington, despite Schumer's efforts in recruiting candidates who led the party to overwhelming control of the Senate.

Van Hollen, who announced his candidacy to challenge Schumer on Thursday night, said voters made clear on election day that they oppose President Donald Trump, but clarified their votes weren't a ringing endorsement of his party either.
Van Hollen told Raddatz he believes this leadership vote is a chance to regain their trust.

"They rejected Trump's policy, his wars, his corruption, the high cost. But they haven't fully hired the Democrats. We have a chance, but we need to earn the people's trust. And I don't think you earn people's trust by simply going back to business as usual and status quo," Van Hollen said.

Van Hollen also responded to the resignation of Nvidia's former CEO Jensen Huang amid his admitting to an affair reported to be with an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang. Van Hollen told Raddatz he's "very concerned" about the national security implications of the unfolding scandal.

"He has gotten the president to allow Nvidia to send very high-end chips to China against the advice of folks in the national security arena," Van Hollen said, suggesting that Alice Huang may have been part of an effort to divert such chips to China.

Alice Huang was a top executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company with access to Nvidia's most powerful chips, which under U.S. law cannot be imported into China. The New York Times reported that Megaspeed has been under investigation by the U.S. since 2024 for potentially smuggling those chips into China, allegations Beijing has denied.

Huang, who admitted to having an affair last Sunday, resigned from the company he's led since founding it in 1993. His decision to step down came after reports of an additional affair with an Nvidia employee, adding to the growing controversy spawned by reports of his relationship with Alice Huang and her alleged role as a Chinese intelligence asset.

Van Hollen, who sits on both the Senate Foreign Relations Committee and Senate Banking Committee, rebutted Trump's claims that he was not briefed about the relationship ahead of his trip to China in May of this year, which Jensen Huang accompanied the president on.

"This is a president who lies to the American public all the time, and this is why we need an investigation. We need people testifying," Van Hollen told Raddatz. "I do believe he was briefed. I think all the information that I've seen suggests that this would not have escaped the attention of the president of the United States."

title: Lauren Boebert will lose her seat in Congress to Democrat Laubacher, AP projects
summary: Colorado Republican Rep. Lauren Boebert will lose her House seat to Democratic challenger Eileen Laubacher, The Associated Press projected Friday.
story: The Republican firebrand won't return for a fourth term.
Colorado Republican Rep. Lauren Boebert will lose to Democratic challenger Eileen Laubacher in Colorado's 4th Congressional District, The Associated Press projected Friday.
With 99% of the expected vote reported, Laubacher led with 48.8% of the vote, followed by Boebert's 47.9%. Laubacher led by around 3,400 votes when the AP made its projection.
In a post on X, Boebert said she had called Laubacher and offered her congratulations. As for her future, she told her followers to "Stay tuned!"

Laubacher retired from the Navy as an admiral after 34 years of service and was senior director for South Asia on the National Security Council during President Joe Biden’s administration. She is a graduate of the U.S. Naval Academy.
Boebert, 39, first gained national attention in 2019 as a gun rights advocate when she challenged then-Democratic presidential candidate Beto O'Rourke over his pledge to pursue gun control measures.

She was first elected in 2020 to represent Colorado’s 3rd Congressional District and won re-election by less than 600 votes in 2022. Two years later, she opted to run in the 4th District and won a third term.

Her time on Capitol Hill was highlighted by two attempts to impeach President Joe Biden, as she had been one of President Donald Trump's fiercest defenders in Congress before breaking with his administration last year over a discharge petition to force the release of the Jeffrey Epstein files. She was one of four Republicans who signed it, joining Reps. Thomas Massie, who co-sponsored the petition with Democratic Rep. Ro Khanna, Nancy Mace and Marjorie Taylor Greene.

Massie lost his re-election bid to a Trump-backed challenger earlier this year in the primaries; Mace didn't run for re-election to the House to launch a failed bid for governor in South Carolina; and Greene resigned from the House last January after Trump withdrew his support for her after she criticized him and his administration for their handling of the Epstein investigation, along with other matters.

Boebert also drew the ire of Hillary Clinton for leaking photos of the former Secretary of State when she sat for a closed-door transcribed interview in the House Oversight Committee’s Epstein inquiry.

title: Trump to meet with Putin and Xi in China, US officials say
summary: Trump will participate in the first-ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the U.S., China, and Russia on the sidelines of the APEC Summit in China next week.
story: The meeting will be the first between the three leaders.

President Donald Trump will participate in the first-ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the U.S., China and Russia on the sidelines at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in China next week, senior U.S. officials told reporters Friday evening.

Trump is expected to discuss Iran with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, the officials said, but he does not intend to discuss Russia's war with Ukraine during the trilateral meeting.

Denuclearization will be the focus of the long-awaited trilateral meeting, though officials do not anticipate the leaders reaching any concrete agreement and are characterizing this meeting as an initial conversation broaching the subject.

Trump had been teasing a potential face-to-face meeting with the world's leading nuclear superpowers for some time. On Oct. 19, Trump told ABC News that he would like to meet with Putin and Xi when he visits China, saying, "I would do that," and indicated a desire to discuss denuclearization.
Trump and Xi will meet ahead of their meeting with Putin but Trump and Putin will not be meeting one-on-one separately, the officials said.

Billionaire Elon Musk will be joining Trump for parts of his China travels, the officials said, but did not specify Musk's reason for accompanying the president, merely pointing to his business interests in China.
An official said some additional U.S. business leaders are expected to attend the APEC CEO Summit but clarified that they are not part of the U.S. delegation.

Trump's trip to Shenzhen, China, for the APEC Summit will be his second trip to China this year, as well and his third meeting with Xi. Before the China leg of the trip, Trump will be in Manila for the ASEAN Summit.
There are no plans for a meeting with North Korea's Kim Jung Un while Trump is in Asia, an official added.

The senior U.S. officials said they do not expect the Nvidia controversy of this week to have any impact on the president's trip or his planned meetings after former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned from the tech company over concerns that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

Officials said they don't expect Trump to raise with Xi the allegations against Alice Huang, a Chinese national and tech executive at Megaspeed who is accused of being a Chinese spy, adding that the two presidents plan to focus on implementing aspects of their trade agreement.

"You know, I think when it comes to some of these national security matters and examinations and investigations that are going on in the U.S., it's probably not something that we're going to read the Chinese in on at this moment," a senior U.S. official said.

Trump will depart from the White House on Monday morning en route to Manila, where he will participate in a series of multilateral meetings about peace and security in the Indo-Pacific region, the officials said. The president is also expected to sign a trade deal with Thailand, they added.

While in the Philippines, Trump will participate in a welcome ceremony and state visit with Philippines President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., followed by a bilateral meeting. Trump is expected to secure "commercial deals and strategic investments" during his two-day visit to the Philippines, officials said.

Trump will then travel to Shenzhen, where he will participate in an APEC leaders' dinner and multilateral meeting with the APEC leaders. On Thursday afternoon, Trump will participate in a bilateral meeting and working lunch with Xi.
The Trump-Xi-Putin meeting will be the final event on the president's Asia trip.

title: Republicans push for Jensen Huang's testimony following Nvidia CEO's resignation
summary: "I don't think he's got anything to hide now. Let it fly," Rep. Burchett said.
story: "I don't think he's got anything to hide now. Let it fly," Rep. Burchett said.
Republican lawmakers are continuing to call for testimony from Nvidia's former CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned Thursday morning following reports that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

GOP Rep. Tim Burchett said it was a "good move" for Huang to resign, adding that the former Nvidia executive should testify as lawmakers have raised concerns about the national security implications of Huang's reported relationship given that he ran the world's largest computer chip manufacturer.
"I don't think he's got anything to hide now. Let it fly," Burchett said to reporters at the Capitol Thursday morning.
Rep. John Moolenaar, the chairman of the China Select Committee, told ABC News that lawmakers have growing concerns as details of Huang's affair continue to come to light.

"The concerns are our national security, whether he was being influenced by a Chinese spy, and the Chinese intelligence was gathering information about our crown jewels of American technology, and also this issue of chip diversion," said Moolenaar, who added that he would support a congressional subpoena to compel Huang's testimony.

House Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Rep. Brian Mast and Moolenaar both say that they're still in active conversations with Huang to schedule testimony after the former Nvidia CEO had previously signaled a willingness to testify.

"We are in discussions with him right now on a date to come and meet with us. If for some reason that were not to happen, all three committees, all three chairs have said we will use our subpoena power," Moolenaar said.
Republican Rep. Jay Obernolte said he believes that Huang's affair is a distraction.

"I hope we can keep the conversation centered around the pros and cons of our export policy regarding our most advanced chips, and you know, not talk about, you know, personal peccadillos,” Obernolte said.

Before Huang's resignation, lawmakers had called for him to testify. Last week, GOP Reps. Mast as well as Rick Crawford, the chair of the House Intelligence Committee, and Moolenaar sent Huang a letter requesting he appear for a "joint, closed-door briefing." Moolenaar said Huang responded to that letter and they are discussing a "date that works."

Congressional Republicans on the Select Committee on China also sent a letter to Huang requesting that he appear for a closed-door briefing Nov. 18 concerning his relationship with Alice Huang. Jensen Huang admitted to an affair, but he didn't say with whom.
Jensen Huang has not responded to ABC News' previous requests for comment about testifying on Capitol Hill. ABC News is working to contact Huang on Thursday -- after he left Nvidia.

On the Democratic side, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer posted on social media on Thursday morning that despite Huang's resignation, Congress needs more answers from Huang, Nvidia and the administration.
"Despite Jensen Huang’s resignation, Congress must demand answers from Mr. Huang and others at Nvidia about how they may have put U.S. national security at risk," Schumer wrote.

Democratic Sens. Elizabeth Warren and Chris Coons are asking the White House and the Departments of Commerce and State to preserve all documents related to the export of NVIDIA's advanced AI chips to China following reports that some senior officials were aware that Huang may have been the target of a Chinese spying operation. The two senators wrote a letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House chief of staff Stephen Miller on Wednesday.
Coons and Warren are also requesting preservation of all materials related to the reported intelligence operation and for a briefing to members of Congress.

Some Republicans have brushed aside concerns, however, when asked whether Huang's access to President Donald Trump at state dinners and flying on Air Force One was problematic given his affair with an alleged Chinese spy was purportedly known to the intelligence community.
"I'm not concerned about -- about Jensen's access to the president. I'm sure the president can take care of that," Obernolte said.
Republicans have said they are hoping to bring in Huang before handing over majority control to Democrats in January.

"You know, it's obviously -- with him resigning -- that does change the dynamic," Moolenaar said. "He has stated he's a patriot. He has questioned people who viewed export controls as a sound policy. I would hope he would want to come in and have that discussion with us."
ABC News' Allison Pecorin contributed to this report.

title: US soldier accused of spying for Russia identified: Source
summary: US officer who was arrested in the UK on suspicion of spying for Russia is 41-year-old Lt. Col. Brandon Tyner, according to a source familiar with the investigation.
story: Lt. Col. Brandon Tyner was entrusted with sensitive information, a source said.

The U.S. soldier who officials say was entrusted with sensitive information and was arrested in the United Kingdom on suspicion of spying for Russia is 41-year-old Lt. Col. Brandon Tyner, according to a source familiar with the investigation.

Tyner, 41, was taken into custody Tuesday near Gloucester, England, as part of a British counterterrorism investigation, according to U.S. and British officials. U.S. Army officials said the officer had been entrusted with sensitive information.
ABC News has not been able to reach Tyner. It is unclear if he has retained a lawyer.

Tyner was assigned to Imjin Barracks in the United Kingdom, a military garrison that is home to the headquarters of NATO's Allied Rapid Response Corps, which manages plans for ground troops in case of a crisis.
Tyner's identity was first reported by the Wall Street Journal.

Tyner, an Afghanistan war veteran, has held numerous high-profile personnel assignments throughout his more than two-decade Army career, according to a LinkedIn account matching his name. British law enforcement officials said the investigation involves suspected violations of the National Security Act of 2023, a law aimed at combating espionage and foreign interference.

It remains unclear exactly what Tyner is accused of doing. He is expected to be formally charged by British authorities in the coming days and subsequently face separate charges from the U.S. Army, according to a source familiar with the matter.

U.S. troops convicted of crimes in allied countries can serve prison sentences abroad before facing separate prosecution in the American military justice system, according to Army court records, which, could mean a second trial and, if convicted, an additional sentence in a U.S. military prison.

U.S. troops convicted of espionage-related crimes have often been junior or mid-level service members, according to Army data, with financial gain a common motive. Cases involving senior officers are less common, and those ranks typically have greater access to sensitive military information that could be particularly valuable to foreign adversaries, though it's unclear what specific information Tyner had access to.

Brig. Gen. Sean Stinchon, who leads U.S. Army Counterintelligence Command, said in a statement following the arrest that the case is, "a sobering reminder that insider threats are real and persistent."

title: Colom’s historic Senate win could reshape Mississippi’s political future: Analysis
summary: The question is whether his victory can establish a lasting realignment.
story: The question is whether his victory can establish a lasting realignment.
Scott Colom’s victory is more than a Democrat winning in a ruby-red state. It is a breakthrough in who can represent Mississippi and could reshape expectations about who can win there next.

Mississippi sent the nation’s first two Black U.S. senators -- Hiram Rhodes Revels and Blanche Kelso Bruce -- to Washington during Reconstruction. Both were elected by the state legislature. After Bruce left office in 1881, Mississippi went nearly a century and a half without another Black senator.

That gap cannot be separated from the violent dismantling of Reconstruction, the rise of Jim Crow and generations of deliberate suppression of Black voters. Mississippi’s 1890 constitution turned racial exclusion into governing policy through poll taxes and literacy requirements.
Now, Mississippi voters have directly elected a Black person to the U.S. Senate for the first time.
“I had the courage to believe in Mississippi,” Colom told supporters at Tougaloo College in Jackson on Wednesday night.

His slim victory over incumbent Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith challenges the assumption that Mississippi’s statewide political outcomes are predetermined. Future candidates, party officials, donors and organizers will have to consider whether an electorate that has long been treated as predictable deserves another look.

For Black Mississippians, whose right to vote was obstructed for generations, this victory puts a Black man in a position to help shape the state’s future. Colom will exercise the same authority as every other senator, from voting on legislation to weighing judicial nominations.

But one victory does not establish a lasting realignment. The ultimate test is whether the coalition that elected Colom can outlast him and this political moment. The question becomes whether that coalition will support other candidates, sustain voter participation and make future elections competitive.

Colom campaigned on raising wages, protecting rural hospitals and addressing the cost of living. Those promises now become the standards against which voters will judge him. Delivering will require legislative allies and translating national debates into benefits for Mississippi communities, including those that did not support him.
“My commitment is to be someone that continues to stay in prayer, continues to have faith, and continues to work to make every Mississippian’s life better,” Colom told the audience at Tougaloo.

That promise connects the historic achievement to the work ahead. His victory gives future candidates evidence that a path to statewide office exists. His performance will help determine whether voters see that path as worth taking again.
A state that once systematically denied Black citizens political power has chosen a Black man to represent everyone. The next test is what that representation delivers for Mississippians.

title: What to know about flights after the US nationwide ground stop
summary: U.S. air travel operations are still recovering after the nationwide ground stop
story: U.S. air travel operations are still recovering after the nationwide ground stop
Officials said they expect airline schedules to fully recover by the end of the day Sunday after a nationwide ground stop that was initiated out of caution caused massive travel disruptions.
The longest flight stoppage in 25 years lasted more than four hours and ended around 8:15 p.m. ET Friday, allowing some domestic flights to take off from U.S. airports.

Of the 41,000 flights scheduled Saturday, more than 6,600 were canceled, according to FlightAware. Just over 1,300 of the more than 26,000 flights scheduled for Sunday were canceled, according to Cirium, an aviation analytics firm. That amounts to about 5.2% of scheduled flights. Prior to Friday, the average cancellation rate for U.S. departures was 3.4%.
But officials said the U.S. airspace was safe and operational and would recover well ahead of the Thanksgiving travel rush.
Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication the failure was related to a cyberattack and no lives were at risk.
Here’s what to know:

Federal Aviation Administration Administrator Bryan Bedford said the system was stable Saturday. Several thousand flights were able to fly after the ground stop, but ultimately, some 12,000 scheduled flights were unable to take off Friday, he said.
Officials acknowledged the disruption but said safety was paramount.

Bedford offered an apology for stranded travelers and thanked air traffic controllers, pilots and flight attendants for managing the fallout. He said officials were confident the system is operating safely or else they would keep airplanes on the ground.

American Airlines said in a statement Saturday night that some individual flights might still be canceled as it continued working to fully restore its operations. It urged travelers to check their flight statuses.
Airlines are obligated to offer free rebooking on another flight or a full refund if a flight is canceled.
Bedford said the administration was working closely with airlines and said they were waiving all terms and conditions.
Some airlines were allowing passengers to rebook if they had travel scheduled Friday or Saturday. Others extended the offer to people with reservations for Sunday or even Monday.
Bedford advised passengers to contact their airlines.

A contractor was replacing a section of the system’s old and discontinued copper wire with new fiber wire in a remote location Friday afternoon, Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said Saturday. That kind of work has been happening across the country and across industries for decades, he said.

But on Friday, the router in that location started overloading the air traffic control system and causing intermittent disruptions to communications and radar feeds. When officials couldn’t quickly locate the cause of the overload, they grounded flights nationwide.
“We did that out of an abundance of caution,” Bedford said. “I’m sorry that we put you through this, but we did it for the right reasons.”

Officials stressed that the ground stop was not the result of a system outage or nefarious activity by a foreign actor. Duffy said officials were investigating whether contractor error or a faulty router was the cause.

The air traffic control modernization began last year after Congress approved $12.5 billion of funding. Duffy and the White House are pushing for $30 billion more to complete the work. About 70% of copper wire has been switched to fiber already, officials said Saturday.

Microsoft said Saturday that services were fully restored after its own massive outage. There was no indication the FAA ground stop was related to the service disruption that took Microsoft services offline Thursday, according to federal officials and a company spokesperson.
Over 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps, Microsoft said on its website. Users reported Microsoft 365 services including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot were interrupted.

title: What to know about flights after the US nationwide ground stop
summary: The Federal Aviation Administration has lifted a nationwide ground stop, allowing some domestic flights to depart from U.S. airports
story: The Federal Aviation Administration has lifted a nationwide ground stop, allowing some domestic flights to depart from U.S. airports
A nationwide ground stop ended around 8:15 p.m. ET, and some domestic flights have now departed from U.S. airports.
However, normalizing air traffic after the longest flight stoppage in 25 years will be slow, authorities warned.
Officials say the system is likely to be operating normally in time to handle the Thanksgiving travel rush.
Here’s what to know.
The Federal Aviation Administration said airplane departures could late Friday evening Eastern time. Passengers should contact their airlines for information about their flights, the FAA said.
The ripple effect from the stoppage could be felt for days, however.
More than 2,500 flights were canceled in the U.S. on Saturday and hundreds more were delayed, according to FlightAware, a website that tracks flight disruptions.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy warned Americans traveling that getting air traffic back to normal won't be quick.
International flights are being handled on a case-by-case basis, according to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin.
San Francisco airport said that flights headed across the Pacific Ocean were cleared to leave the airport from Friday evening. That included flights destined for Hawaii and Asia.
Europe’s aviation agency suspended U.S.-bound departures at the request of the FAA from 5 p.m. Eastern on Friday until midnight.
Airlines are obligated to offer free rebooking on another flight for travelers who want to continue their journey, or a refund if their flight was canceled and they decide not to take the trip.
New technology being hooked up to the nation’s air traffic control system overloaded antiquated equipment, Trump administration officials said.
That caused “intermittent” communications and radar gaps, leading to the flight shutdown of more than four hours, according to officials.
Duffy suggested more disruptions might occur.
“We didn’t think we would have this kind of outage. We did,” he said.
The air traffic control modernization began last year after Congress approved $12.5 billion of funding. Duffy and the White House are pushing for $30 billion more to complete the work.
Microsoft said it had no indication that the ground stop was related to the service disruption that took Outlook and other services offline Thursday, a spokesperson for the company said.
Mullin said there is no indication the failure was related to a cyberattack, either.
“There was never any lives at risk,” Mullin added. “There was no flights at risk. FAA was able to handle it. We did it."
The ground stop was enacted “out of an abundance of caution,” he said.

title: Trump administration blames ‘overloaded’ systems for ground stop after FAA lets flights resume
summary: The Federal Aviation Administration says airplane departures can resume after the agency lifted a nationwide ground stop caused by communications problems
story: The Federal Aviation Administration says airplane departures can resume after the agency lifted a nationwide ground stop caused by communications problems

WASHINGTON -- Trump administration officials said Friday that new technology being added to the nation’s air traffic control system overloaded antiquated parts of it and caused “intermittent” communications and radar gaps, leading to the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years.
It was lifted in the evening after a five-hour stretch when most flights were not allowed to take off from airports in the U.S.

Thousands of flights and potentially over a million travelers were affected. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin told reporters at the White House that no one was in any danger as more than 3,000 flights were safely landed. But Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said he could not guarantee it wouldn’t happen again.
Mullin said the FAA was installing “new equipment, new technology” and “it was overwhelming the older system.” There appeared to be no indication of a cyberattack, he said.

A limited number of domestic flights began departing late Friday after the ground stop was lifted, but it will likely take days for airlines to fully recover because so many planes and crews were out of position. Officials said they think the system will be back to normal in time to handle the Thanksgiving travel rush.

The nationwide ground stop was the first since January 2023, when another key FAA computer system that sends notices to pilots malfunctioned, and the second since the aftermath of the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.

Asked whether he could rule out a cyberattack or rogue artificial intelligence incident, Mullin said there are no “footprints” showing an attack and that the problem appears to be “mechanically driven.” He said officials were still looking for the cause.

At least 827 flights had been diverted. By 7:05 p.m. EST, 670 flights were sent back to the airport from where they originally took off, while 157 were redirected to a different airport, according to Cirium, an aviation analytics company.

Duffy was defensive, blaming Congress for failing to approve more funding for new technology, while downplaying the fact that trying to implement new fixes overtaxed the system. He implored lawmakers to act.
“By doing nothing, you inject way more risk into the system,” he said.

Duffy said he expected flights around the country to be “back up and operational as we come into the heat of travel” next weekend ahead of Thanksgiving, but he also suggested more disruptions might occur.
“We didn’t think we would have this kind of outage. We did,” he said, while also noting, “We were able to review what went wrong, and then reboot the system and go. But, you will have more of these.”
Duffy said the problems were not linked to the FAA’s new AI-powered system the agency is rolling out to help predict problems in the sky because that isn’t connected to what failed on Friday.
“This is all the old legacy equipment. All of the new equipment that’s been deployed did not go down,” Duffy said.

The FAA has already replaced thousands of old copper wires with fiber optic lines and upgraded hundreds of radio systems as part of the overhaul that began last year after Congress approved $12.5 billion of funding. Duffy and the White House are pushing for $30 billion more to complete the work.
Many flights ended up being diverted to places including Washington Dulles International Airport, Los Angeles International Airport and Nashville International Airport.
Some 11,000 flights carrying more than 1.5 million passengers had been scheduled to take off from airports in the U.S. after 4 p.m. EST.
At the time of the ground stoppage, more than 3,500 airplanes were in the sky, Duffy said.

At Chicago O’Hare Airport on Friday, travelers passing through security learned about the ground stop when they looked up at screens that showed flight delays across the board. Some called friends or family members, debating whether to stay the night in Chicago or find another way to their destinations.
Amber McQuilkin, 27, sat on a bench, disappointed that she might miss a trip with friends to New York for the League of Legends world finals.

“There’s not really any information being passed to me,” said the Seattle software engineer. “I contemplated just abandoning the flight and driving, but then the more I thought about it, the more I’m like, that would be miserable.”

Ruth Coles was still stuck on her plane five hours after it landed at the Los Angeles International Airport from Newark even after the ground stop was lifted. She said they were told they were waiting for a gate to open up.
“The pilot keeps saying they are telling him we are next in line,” Coles said, but that was several hours ago.

NBA, NHL and college teams were left stranded as they tried to reach their destinations. Meanwhile, NFL teams were left to wonder whether the issue would be resolved in time to travel to their games this weekend.
Duffy said NCAA teams will be prioritized ahead of football games on Saturday.
“I would encourage those football teams to reach out to the FAA, to schedule their flight times and make sure they can move” to make their kickoff, he said.
Cargo flights were also delayed by the ground stop.
FedEx, the world’s largest cargo airline, said it was prepared to activate contingency plans to keep any possible disruptions at a minimum.

U.S. airlines move about 61,000 tons (55,340 metric tonnes) of goods — from letters to packages — to and from more than 220 countries daily, according to the industry trade group Airlines for America.

The problem appeared similar to a regional air traffic control communication outage in September that snarled hundreds of flights across the Northeast, although that disruption was linked to a construction crew cutting a fiber optic line. Aging equipment was also blamed for the brief radar outages last year that disrupted Newark airport.
Aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said the difference this time is that it happened on a nationwide scale that left controllers unable to reliably talk to pilots.

“If you don’t have that ability, whether it’s because the old wires that they have are just run down or for whatever reason, you’ve got to stop airplanes on the ground and not put them in the air, where you’re going to risk not being able to communicate with them,” said Arroyo, a former United Airlines pilot.

Friday’s ground stop was also different than the one after 9/11 because planes were not being told to land immediately and pilots likely were able to communicate with ground controllers at airports, Arroyo said.

Funk reported from Omaha, Nebraska. AP writers Mead Gruver in Fort Collins, Colorado; Ali Swenson in Chicago; Alex Veiga and Jaimie Ding in Los Angeles; Seung Min Kim and Aamer Madhani in Washington; Hannah Schoenbaum in Salt Lake City; and Hallie Golden in Seattle contributed to this report.
This story has been corrected to show the Sept. 11 attacks were in 2001.

title: Questions around FAA's new SMART AI system, officials say no link to ground stop
summary: The airline ground stop that has wreaked havoc on travel since Friday was not related to the FAA’s new, $875 million AI-powered system the agency is rolling out to help predict problems in the sky
story: The airline ground stop that has wreaked havoc on travel since Friday was not related to the FAA’s new, $875 million AI-powered system the agency is rolling out to help predict problems in the sky

The airline ground stop that wreaked havoc on travel since Friday was not related to the FAA's new, $875 million AI-powered system the agency is rolling out to help predict problems in the sky, according to government officials and the artificial intelligence company behind the technology.

But the timing of the ground stop, so close to the national rollout of the Federal Aviation Administration's SMART system, has raised questions about what the system does, its benefits and risks compared with the existing human system and what guardrails there are to address potential problems.

The SMART system is based in a single location near Washington where a team of experts analyzes flight schedules, weather forecasts and hundreds of other streams of data. Then that office sends recommendations to the FAA’s command center, which relays them to air traffic controllers across the country for consideration.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Friday there’s no indication the communications issues that caused the ground stop are linked to the new computer system, and the top officials at the Transportation Department and FAA reiterated that Saturday.
The startup that designed the system, Air Space Intelligence, or ASI, said the ground stop wasn’t caused by “the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC.”

But lawmakers and outside groups raised questions about the SMART system before Friday's ground stop. Last month, House Democrats sent a letter to the U.S. Government Accountability Office requesting an audit of the new software, raising concerns about safety and guardrails.

“Concerningly, the nation’s front line aviation safety workforce apparently had little to no input into SMART’s development and have received limited training and information during the current deployment process,” the Oct. 13 letter said. “The use of artificial intelligence within SMART has rightfully raised serious questions about its reliability and safety benefits, particularly on its potential to interfere with decision-making by experienced air traffic controllers or to hallucinate safety-critical information.”
SMART, however, is not — at least not yet — set up for AI to be in charge of flight control. Rather, it is making recommendations to humans who do so.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford unveiled the system in September, calling it a “cutting-edge tool that centralizes 200 data streams — including weather patterns, flight paths, traffic flow, and controller staffing metrics — into one platform.” SMART stands for Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories.

The system's AI-supported engine synthesizes the data systems and shows a “comprehensive visualization” of where planes are going, how much traffic the system can handle and where congestion or weather could cause problems, according to the announcement. The idea is for specialists to then use the platform to fix problems before they arise.

The FAA says that during the initial test of the system in the Washington area this fall, the system helped reroute 180 flights and saved an average of 10 minutes and 80 gallons of fuel per flight by diverting around weather or other issues. The agency said that one flight cut 42 minutes off its trip from Tampa, Florida, to Dallas thanks to the system's recommendations.
So SMART was expanded for use nationwide on Nov. 10 for the airspace of all 22 air traffic control centers. That was three days before the ground stop.

According to a government fact sheet on the tool, SMART can predict where air traffic is headed and identify other routes before an area becomes too congested. The system can also help reopen restricted airspace faster and better manage airport arrivals.
SMART is also supposed to help with weather-related issues faster.

Currently, the FAA blocks off portions of airspace affected by weather as “large, rectangular boxes,” according to the fact sheet, which doesn't reflect how weather actually looks, with quick-moving thunderstorms and storm systems that are “often irregular in shape, with narrow gaps or corridors that aircraft could safely fly through.”

To help with this, SMART gives the FAA and airspace operators a “clearer picture of how weather will affect air traffic over time,” allowing air traffic controllers to plan around storms and use available airspace instead of unnecessarily shutting down large areas.

No other country has a working AI air traffic tool like the SMART system, according to Michael McCormick, a former FAA airspace manager and an associate professor at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University. Eurocontrol, the European air traffic authority, has a system in testing and several manufacturers are prototyping similar tools.

While government officials and ASI, the company behind SMART, have stressed that its AI system is designed to assist humans and not run flight control, its deployment has raised concerns about relying on artificial intelligence when human lives are at stake, given that even the most advanced models are prone to hallucinations — when models fabricate false information and present it as fact.

Mike O’Donnell, a former top FAA official who worked for the agency for 17 years and now does aviation safety consulting work, said the agency “has got to make sure that this is just a tool in the toolbox and not the actual machine that’s doing the work.”
The FAA, he said, “cannot afford to be wrong on this.”

“It’s good to use it with the proper guardrails and backstops to ensure that they’re not giving wrong information to controllers based on what (AI) has come up with,” O’Donnell said. “There’s got to be a way to verify and validate what it’s doing to make sure that it’s not the wrong information.”
He cautioned against putting too much trust in AI “until we know for sure that it's proven itself time and time again. And that's going to take a while.”

The AI system's launch comes amid a longstanding shortage of air traffic controllers around the country. The National Air Traffic Controllers Association has been raising concerns about this for more than a decade, telling Congress in 2015 that the shortage was at a crisis level. It said then that the FAA had missed its hiring targets for five years in a row. The union represents about 14,000 controllers, roughly 3,000 of them trainees. That said, experts say no AI system can replace the human air traffic controllers who spend years training for this highly demanding and stressful job.
In an October interview with NPR, ASI co-founder and CEO Phillip Buckendorf said the SMART tool is designed for traffic managers who manage the entire U.S. airspace.

“The AI does the math, the AI does the computation,” Buckendorf told NPR, but it’s ultimately up to the human operator whether to take the system’s recommendation. “They make the decision, they are the decider, they are the judge.”

title: Fewer students are traveling from abroad to study at US universities, report shows
summary: Fewer international students are coming to U.S. universities to study as the Trump administration cracks down on immigration and reshapes higher education
story: Fewer international students are coming to U.S. universities to study as the Trump administration cracks down on immigration and reshapes higher education
Fewer international students are studying at U.S. universities as the Trump administration cracks down on immigration and reshapes higher education, data released Monday shows.

Overall, U.S. campuses saw a 9% decrease in international enrollment this fall compared with last year, according to a survey from the Institute of International Education. And the number of new students entering the United States for the first time fell by 15%.

“No one aspires to send their kids to get educated in the U.S.,” said Veena Dubal, general counsel for the American Association of University Professors, whose father traveled from India to attend Tuskegee University, then the Tuskegee Institute, in the late 1960s on a student visa.
“It feels like an unsafe place. That’s the message that the Trump administration has been sending to families all over the world and they’re listening.”

Last year, the enrollment decreases were partially offset by large numbers of students who stayed in the U.S. for temporary work after graduating. But after months of speculation, the Department of Homeland Security proposed requiring schools to pay a $70,000 fee for every student who participates in the optional practice training program.
Although the rule hasn't been finalized, participation in the program, known as OPT for short, dropped 6% this fall, according to the survey.

The proposed rule, which is expected to face legal challenges, is part of wider DHS efforts that include terminating the legal status of thousands of international students, along with detaining and deporting many of them.

And this summer, the administration finalized a rule that will prevent international students from staying in the U.S. for more than four years without approval from the federal government, although a judge has temporarily blocked it.
DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin has said the changes were intended to crack down on loopholes that international students were exploiting by extending their studies.
Although the U.S. remains the top destination for international students globally, the changes are having an effect, college leaders told the IIE.

Among more than 800 U.S. colleges and universities surveyed this fall, 88% blamed the visa application process and 70% blamed travel restrictions for the enrollment drops. And if OPT options are limited, 95% of schools predicted that international students would likely look to another country, according to the survey, which offers an early look at trends before full data is released next year.

Politics aren't the only reason students are looking elsewhere, said Mirka Martel, head of research, evaluation and learning for the institute. Its survey found more global competition for international students and the rising cost of a U.S. degree also contributed.

Fanta Aw, the executive director and CEO of NAFSA, an association that represents international education, said students also are worried about research funding. Last year, the Trump administration began dismantling the federal grant-giving process and attempting to exert more political influence over what projects get funded.

“They’re saying to themselves, ‘Too much uncertainty in the United States. It’s too difficult, and you know, more importantly, we have many more choices today than we did 10 years ago. Why subject ourselves to this?’” Aw said, noting that students are going to places like China.

NAFSA, in partnership with the international education technology company JB International, found that amid the enrollment decline, international students’ contributions to the U.S. economy dropped by $2.4 billion this fall.
American colleges and universities heavily recruit students from overseas as a source of tuition revenue. So the drops have punched big holes in tuition revenue at some schools.

At Cleveland State University, international enrollment has dropped by 46% in two years, from 1,542 in fall 2025 to 828 this fall. And fewer than 50 new international students started this fall, said Provost Nigamanth Sridhar, who estimated that the budgetary impact ranges from $2 million to $4 million.
Decades ago, he arrived in the U.S. on an F1 student visa and participated in OPT. Eventually, he went through the process to become a naturalized citizen.

“I am here in this position, in this job, because I had the opportunity to come to the United States as an international graduate student and then decided to stay here and build a career,” said Sridhar, who is from India. “So international education is personal to me.”

The biggest drops were at the graduate level. This fall's data shows a 15% drop in international graduate enrollment, compared to a 3% decrease at the undergraduate level. The report also found declines in international students from India, which sends more students to the U.S. to study than any other country.

Sarah Spreitzer, vice president at the American Council on Education, which represents college and university presidents, said substantial immigration bills are unlikely while Trump remains president. But she said congressional oversight might halt new policies targeted at international students.
“Those types of things could provide more certainty for our international students that there’s not just going to be these sudden or unexplainable changes,” Spreitzer said.

title: Georgia O'Keeffe painting buried in NY apartment closet is going up for auction
summary: Christie's estimates its value at $3 to $5 million.
story: Christie's estimates its value at $3 to $5 million.
NEW YORK -- The painting was buried behind coats and boxes in the closet of a Manhattan apartment for decades.
Few if anyone knew about the hidden treasure until the woman in her 90s who lived there nonchalantly told her niece one day, “oh by the way, there’s a Georgia O’Keeffe in the closet.”
The painting — an early example from a time when O’Keeffe became enamored with the American Southwest — depicts a classic New Mexico landscape with rolling hills in earth tones.
Christie’s estimates its value at $3 to $5 million. It is set to go up for auction on Tuesday.

The auction house says the painting from 1930 was likely the first in a series of three. The second is in New York's Metropolitan Museum of Art. The other, for many years, was in the collection of the Rockefeller family.
Up until now, the whereabouts of the first one had largely been a mystery.

The painting of Lobo Peak near Taos, New Mexico, is “particularly important because of its early date and its representation of the inception point of O’Keeffe’s time in the American Southwest,” said Tylee Abbott, director of American Art at Christie’s.
In 1963, a New York art gallery sold the painting for $3,800 to a woman who gave it to her daughter.
“Before that it was only known through photography that had been taken in 1931,” Abbott said.

O’Keeffe, who died in 1986 at age 98, is often called the “Mother of American modernism.” She was a pioneer with her own style of abstract art, most known for paintings of flowers and Southwestern landscapes.

She lived in Abiquiu, New Mexico, where she built a home and studio on land with breathtaking desert vistas that inspired the work of the 20th century painter. Many Native American communities trace their ancestry to the area in northern New Mexico.

The daughter of the woman who purchased the painting in 1963 kept it at her apartment in New York’s East Village, the auction house said. The family has asked the auction house not to release their identities.
But they did share with Christie's some details, including how the artwork was found.

The woman who owned the painting lived into her late 90s before dying recently. Never married, she was extremely private and incredibly smart, the family said. At one point in her life, she worked with the U.S. Foreign Service, spending time in Europe.
She collected antiques and abstract art but nothing close to the stature of the O'Keeffe.

The family believes she received the painting as a graduation gift from her mother after earning a master's degree in the 1960s. For many years, she displayed it until the mid-'80s when she noticed a guest looking at it a little too closely.

She boxed it back into the original packing crate and put it in the back of a closet, said her niece, who spent the last few years caring for her and spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity to honor the family's request for privacy.

Around 2022, the woman first mentioned to her niece that the painting was in the front closet. It stayed there until this year when they were cleaning out the apartment and getting her affairs in order.
Once unboxed, it was obvious the painting was authentic.
It has all the hallmarks of O’Keeffe’s work — including her signature marking on the back, a star with her initials “OK” scrawled in the middle.
Seewer reported from Ohio.

title: Could everything be broken? Grounded jets, Microsoft outage, AI chaos make some wonder
summary: After the Silicon Valley chaos spurred by reports of an AI billionaire's affair with a suspected Chinese spy and the Microsoft outage that upended millions of workers' days, Friday's air travel ground stop across the U.S. had many people feeling that s...
story: After the Silicon Valley chaos spurred by reports of an AI billionaire's affair with a suspected Chinese spy and the Microsoft outage that upended millions of workers' days, Friday's air travel ground stop across the U.S. had many people feeling that s...

Maybe the trouble started with the AI billionaire and the Silicon Valley chaos that followed talk of his infidelity, including with an alleged Chinese spy.
