Or maybe it was the Microsoft outage that, depending on how you looked at it, either cast millions of frustrated workers adrift or spared them from a daily, unrelenting electronic avalanche.
But by Friday afternoon, when U.S. authorities suddenly ordered every plane across the country to land immediately, it felt to many that something was up. Something was broken.

Just ask Chuck Amasio, a 68-year-old from Rahway, New Jersey, trying to fly out of Newark Liberty International Airport when his canceled flight led to a few beers with his brother in an airport bar and eventually a night in a hotel. Saturday morning, he was back at the airport to try again.
“There’s a lot of weird stuff going on,” Amasio said. “It makes one think.”
His first thought was dark: “We talk about how wars aren’t done with bombs anymore. They shut down airspace or a power grid. They can cripple an economy.”

Throw in a few more examples just from Friday – a cruise ship that overturned in New Orleans when a tanker slammed into it, suspicious drones over a U.S. air base in Britain, a bomb found near an ethanol plant in Ohio — and perhaps things seem even weirder, opening the door for a writer who has been picking at America’s fears for generations to offer his own explanation.
“The aliens have landed,” Stephen King wrote in a Friday afternoon tweet. “That’s the REAL reason for the ground stop. They don’t want to start a worldwide panic.”
The official explanations for the thousands of downed jetliners and hours of email and other computer troubles were far more prosaic.

A technology upgrade on the nation’s air traffic control system had overloaded antiquated equipment and caused “intermittent” communications and radar gaps, leading to the ground stop that lasted more than four hours, administration officials said.
By Saturday morning, air travel was already smoother and Bryan Bedford, administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration, said airline schedules should be back to normal by late Sunday.

Microsoft, for its part, said Saturday that its services had been fully restored, saying the problem “was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced” following a recent network change.
The outage is believed to have affected many millions of people around the world.

Maxine Gustafson, a 34-year-old physician assistant from Minneapolis, was in line to pick up a hastily booked rental car at Chicago’s O’Hare airport on Friday afternoon so she and colleagues could get home from a work training.
Gustafson said the week's mishaps made her feel afraid and helpless.
“It makes you think, like, is this a cyberattack?” she said. “We don’t have control over a lot of this stuff.”
Both the FAA and Microsoft said there were no signs that malicious activity had been behind the troubles.

Tori Perkins, 34, was hoping for a Saturday flight at Terminal 2 at San Diego International Airport, where 11 of the 62 flights already were listed as canceled that morning and the same number were delayed. Crowds were normal.

“It’s one of those things where I don’t necessarily believe what the government says,” said Perkins, who seemed to take the setback in stride. “I don’t know what’s true because there are so many people saying different things.”
Perkins, who lives in Hawaii, was in San Diego on a layover on her way to see family in Florida. She spent Friday night at the airport.
She was not surprised that Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy had made a plea Friday for tens of billions in more funding to upgrade the country’s notoriously outdated air traffic system.
“It sounds like more of the same,” she said.

The FAA has already replaced thousands of copper wire connections with fiber optic lines and upgraded hundreds of radio systems as part of the overhaul that began last year after Congress approved $12.5 billion in funding. The White House has been pushing for $30 billion more to complete the work.
Sometimes chaos brings out the best in people.
Corbyn Wascher was stuck on the tarmac at Charlotte Douglas International Airport for four hours while heading back to Moline, Illinois, from Miami, where he had been at an education conference.

He said everyone was cordial on the plane, talking to one another and stretching their legs. He was impressed with the American Airlines staff, who handed out water, pretzels and biscotti snacks, though they were clearly under stress.
“The stewardesses were amazing,” said the 37-year-old high school teacher.

Back at the Newark airport, Caroline Ruiz had caught a few hours of sleep by a heating vent. She wasn’t sure what time it was as she waited for someone to bring her a meal she was promised after the cancellation of the first leg of her 24-hour trip to Australia. She hoped to get started later Saturday.
It was two days in a row, she noted, where she had been betrayed by technology.
Though maybe one of those days didn’t count as a betrayal.
“I kind of got a free day yesterday” because the Microsoft systems were down.
Associated Press journalists Elliot Spagat in San Diego, Ali Swenson in Chicago, Jessica Hill in Las Vegas and Aron Ranen in Newark contributed to this report.

title: 32 Americans named as Rhodes scholars have variety of interests, from space junk to art history
summary: The 32 Americans named as 2027 Rhodes scholars include a college senior who wants to clean up debris pollution in Earth’s orbit and a student who has researched AI use in healthcare
story: The 32 Americans named as 2027 Rhodes scholars include a college senior who wants to clean up debris pollution in Earth’s orbit and a student who has researched AI use in healthcare
WASHINGTON -- A college senior who wants to clean up debris pollution in Earth's orbit and a student who has researched AI use in healthcare are among the 32 Americans named as 2027 Rhodes scholars.

The winners, who were announced on Saturday, have a variety of interests, from bioelectronics to water scarcity to art history. They were chosen from 238 finalists who emerged from more than 1,000 candidates who received formal endorsements from their colleges and universities for the honor.

The students will attend the University of Oxford in England as part of the Rhodes scholar program, which awards more than 100 scholarships worldwide each year for students to pursue two to three years of graduate studies.

Two students are the first-ever Rhodes scholars from their schools — Prairie View A&M University in Texas and The Citadel — The Military College of South Carolina. Harvard University led the way with four 2027 Rhodes scholars, followed by Yale and Princeton with three each.
The winners include:

Evan Garrison, of Webb City, Missouri, a senior at Mississippi State University majoring in aerospace engineering and mathematics. His research includes designing ways to detect objects in space, with an interest in cleaning up orbital debris known as “space junk.” He plans to study mathematical modeling, scientific computing and global governance and diplomacy at Oxford.

Asuka Koda, of New York City, a senior at Yale University majoring in mathematics and philosophy. She has researched AI adoption in healthcare and has been a health and science writer for CNN. She plans to study social science of the internet and international health and tropical medicine at Oxford.

Michael Bueker, from Wellesley, Massachusetts, a senior at Dartmouth College majoring in biomedical engineering. His research has focused on biodegradable, implantable neural stimulators and other ultrathin bioelectronic devices. He also grows giant pumpkins. At Oxford, he intends to study engineering science.

Elizabeth Koenck, of Aurora, Colorado, a senior at Georgetown University majoring in foreign service. Her research has examined water scarcity problems across the Middle East, North Africa and the Colorado River Basin. She plans to pursue degrees in migration studies and water science, policy and management at Oxford.

Sabrina Soriano, of Azusa, California, a senior at Yale University majoring in art history. Her research includes 19th-century French painting, with a focus on the relationship between art, religion and cultural identity. She plans to study history of art and visual culture and visual, material and museum anthropology at Oxford.

Named after British imperialist and benefactor Cecil John Rhodes, the scholarships were established at Oxford in 1903. The program has more than 8,000 alumni, many of whom have pursued careers in government, education, the arts and social justice.

title: Richard Sterban, member of the celebrated country and gospel group The Oak Ridge Boys, dies at 83
summary: Richard Sterban, the bass vocalist of the Grammy-award winning gospel quartet The Oak Ridge Boys and a country music hall of famer, has died
story: Richard Sterban, the bass vocalist of the Grammy-award winning gospel quartet The Oak Ridge Boys and a country music hall of famer, has died

Richard Sterban, the bass vocalist of the Grammy-award winning gospel quartet The Oak Ridge Boys and a country music hall of famer, died Saturday, his family and the band said in a statement. He was 83.
Sterban, who had been with the band since 1972, died in Hendersonville, Tennessee, due to complications from bronchitis and pneumonia after a long battle with cancer, they said.

Sterban left his job as a backup singer for Elvis Presley to join the vocal group, which perhaps became best known for its rendition of “Elvira.” Sterban toured regularly with the group until 2025, when his health deteriorated.

The Oak Ridge Boys won five Grammy awards and were nominated 23 times. They performed for presidents, on American Bandstand, at the Grammy Awards ceremony and at the Grand Ole Opry. They toured with Johnny Cash and sang backup vocals on Paul Simon's hit “Slip Slidin’ Away.”

Sterban and the band's three other members were inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 2015, joining Presley. They joined the Vocal Group Hall of Fame in 2001. And in 2011 they gained membership in the Grand Ole Opry.

A native of Camden, New Jersey, Sterban was inducted into the Philadelphia Music Hall of Fame in 1994 along with Joe Bonsall, another Oak Ridge Boys member who died in 2024 and who sang with Sterban in the Keystones.

In a statement, Country Music Hall of Fame CEO Kyle Young said Sterban “used his unmistakable bass voice to connect commercial country music to its deep gospel roots” and called him a “steady force and a foundational figure in country music.”
“He helped the supergroup achieve seventeen No. 1 hits, legions of fans the world over, and a well-deserved place in the Country Music Hall of Fame,” Young said.

The band's golden period in the ’80s and beyond included 1981's “Elvira,” the 1982 hit “Bobbie Sue” and 1983’s “American Made.” “Elvira” was a massive crossover moment for the group, reaching No. 1 on the country chart and No. 5 on Billboard’s all-genre Hot 100.
Sterban is survived by his wife, Donna; daughters Lauren and Tori; sons Rich, Doug and Chris; and 11 grandchildren and great-grandchildren.

title: Judge temporarily blocks Trump from moving ahead on Washington public golf course redevelopment
summary: A federal judge has ordered a two-week delay to any work at a historic Washington public golf course not far from the White House
story: A federal judge has ordered a two-week delay to any work at a historic Washington public golf course not far from the White House

WASHINGTON -- A federal judge on Saturday ordered a two-week delay to any work at a historic Washington public golf course not far from the White House, blocking for now President Donald Trump's push to redevelop the site along the Potomac River into a championship-level venue.

U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes issued the temporary restraining order before the East Potomac Golf Links was due to close Sunday for 15 months. Trump had announced work would begin that day despite the legal challenge initiated against the project in February by the DC Preservation League and two local golfers.

The plaintiffs argue that Trump's plan would change the character of the accessible golf course and make it unaffordable, something the Republican president denies. They had sought the stop-work order, saying that closing the course and launching work on the project would “irreparably injure plaintiffs and the public interest."

The president's public announcements on social media last month outlining the date of the closure of East Potomac Park and linking it to the renovation of the golf course weighed heavily in the decision. Trump said on Oct. 26 that “We are closing the East Potomac Golf Course Site as scheduled on November 15th in order to renovate and rebuild for Competitive (with other such projects!), Safety, Modernization, and Aesthetic reasons.” He added that the goal was to renovate and rebuild ”a World Championship Public Facility."

Reyes in her ruling Saturday noted that Trump's posts presented a problem for the government. “They indicate that the Washington National Plan is final and that NPS will close the Park to implement it,” she wrote. “Both points favor granting Plaintiffs’ motion for another temporary restraining order.”

Reyes said her order “ENJOINS the government from closing East Potomac Park and the East Potomac Golf Course during the daily hours in which they were open as of November 14, 2026. It does not order the Government to undertake any active management of either. Further, for the avoidance of any doubt, the Government remains free, as it has since the onset of this litigation, to conduct repairs on any part of the Park and Course with any notice required by the existing Preliminary Injunction.”
The judge said the order is in effect “through November 28, 2026, or further order from the Court, whichever comes first.”

The Justice Department said in a statement Saturday that the judge acknowledged that the National Park Service can limit access to its facilities where the public is at risk of harm. “Nothing in the Court’s order precludes planning for the development of a world class golf course to continue,” it said. "The Department of Justice will always vociferously defend the Trump Administration’s agenda in court.”

Catherine Carroll, a senior legal adviser at Democracy Forward, which is representing the plaintiffs, praised the ruling. “We are grateful that once again, a court has intervened to prevent irreparable harm caused by the Trump-Vance administration’s pursuit of another one of the president’s vanity projects,” she said. “The administration’s inexplicable drive to destroy East Potomac Park would have taken away a treasured park that could never be replaced."

The park’s redevelopment is one of multiple projects in the nation's capital that Trump has championed to remake the city. They include a large memorial arch, a White House ballroom and the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, among others.

Reyes had signaled throughout a five-hour court hearing Friday that she was likely to issue some stoppage for the park closure. The only issue was how expansive it might be. Justice Department lawyer Adam Gustafson argued that the entire East Potomac Park, which includes three golf courses, a miniature course, bike riding lanes and other recreational areas, was being closed because of safety factors. He also noted that the lease between the government and the current operator, National Links Trust, was ending Sunday.

Reyes pointed out that safety had not been part of the discussion over the closure for months and that ending the lease felt more like an action that provided a premise for the closure rather than an action that led to the closure of the course about 2 miles from the White House.

Even before the order, Trump lashed out in a social media post Saturday, contending that Reyes “doesn’t want us to quickly and inexpensively fix up the Course which is, also, very dangerous.” He said people who live in the Washington area would get a 50% discount on “any and all Rates charged” and that the redevelopment would “evolve into something very special, something which the Judge will be able to take great pride in seeing!”

Reyes’ order was the latest in a series of rulings in lawsuits challenging Trump’s projects that were issued just hours before construction was expected to begin. A different judge recently ordered a 14-day delay on work for the arch, a decision that came shortly after a key planning commission stacked with Trump appointees approved plans for the project.

Reyes, who was nominated to the court by Democratic President Joe Biden, had for months been reticent about approving the plaintiffs’ requests for work stoppages. The plaintiffs had argued the administration was moving ahead with work related to the project despite the pending lawsuit.
Her reluctance to issue orders ended in October, spurred in part by a tree-cutting spree by the administration over a holiday weekend with little notification to the judge or plaintiffs.

Officials and government lawyers said the tree work was part of a 2019 plan that recommended the cutting. In response, the judge confronted the administration over what she portrayed as deceitful actions over its intentions for the project.

Reyes has repeatedly expressed frustration over the minute planning details she has been asked to adjudicate, including over the trees being cut down at the 106-year-old park. The Justice Department filed a request that Reyes be removed from the case because of what it called her “egregious behavior” and questioned her impartiality. Reyes has not recused herself.
The restraining order was one of two issues Reyes took up during Friday's hearing.

She announced plans last week to name Jessie Liu, a former U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, to examine whether officials with the Interior Department and the National Park Service and attorneys with the Justice Department had violated ethics or misled her during the course of the case.
Associated Press writer Eric Tucker contributed to this report.

title: Rare North Atlantic right whale population drops, alarming scientists
summary: The population of one of the world’s rarest whales has fallen after trending upward in recent years
story: The population of one of the world’s rarest whales has fallen after trending upward in recent years
PORTLAND, Maine -- The population of one of the world's rarest whales has fallen after trending upward in recent years, worrying scientists who fear the animal could still be at risk of extinction.

The North Atlantic right whale now numbers 382 animals, according to a consortium of scientists that released its annual population estimate for the animals on Monday. That represents about a 2% decline from last year's estimate, which showed a recent slow but steady climb in the whales' population continuing.

The whales were decimated by centuries of commercial whaling that mostly ended in the 1930s. The enormous animals have been slow to recover, and today they are threatened by entanglement in fishing gear and collisions with ships.

Those threats, combined with a warming ocean, have conspired to hold the population down, said Heather Pettis, chair of the North Atlantic Right Whale Consortium. Pettis said the warming of the ocean has caused the whales' food — tiny organisms called copepods — to move, and the whales have followed them into areas of ocean not protected from ship strikes and entanglements.

“We know that this population can and will move around to find food and if we aren't protecting them throughout their range, we may see another situation where we have this tremendous decline again,” Pettis said.

The whales' population fell about 25% from 2010 to 2020 during a time when years of poor reproduction coincided with high mortality. Recent years have been slightly more encouraging, but scientists and conservationists have warned that the whales need years of high birth counts coupled with new protections to have a chance to rebuild.

The loss in population last year underscores the need to spare the whales from entanglements and ship strikes, said Nora Ives, a marine scientist on the environmental group Oceana’s right whale campaign.

Oceana was one of several environmental groups that opposed a proposal in Congress to delay new right whale protections until 2035. The proposal, which has passed the U.S. House of Representatives, is intended to protect commercial fishing interests from regulations that members of the industry describe as burdensome.

“The latest numbers are disappointing and make the road to recovery longer for critically endangered North Atlantic right whales. This iconic whale will not escape extinction if its population cannot grow,” Ives said.

The right whales, which can weigh 150,000 pounds (68,039 kilograms), give birth off the Carolinas, Florida and Georgia in the winter and venture north to feeding grounds off New England and Canada. Large groups of the animals that sometimes include a fifth of the entire population are sometimes seen off Massachusetts in spring. Last year was one of the most successful calving seasons on record with more than 20 babies born.

The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration has said the last nine years have also been a time of unusually high numbers of injuries and deaths for the whales. The population is down to just 73 reproductive females, which makes replenishing the stock difficult.

They were hunted heavily because they tend to live fairly close to shore and floated when killed, and they yielded a high volume of oil. Some sources say they got their common name from the perception that they were the “right” whale to hunt.

title: Handwritten draft of MLK's 'I Have a Dream' speech on display before sold at auction
summary: A handwritten draft of Martin Luther King Jr.'s “I Have a Dream” speech is going on display before being auctioned in January
story: A handwritten draft of Martin Luther King Jr.'s “I Have a Dream” speech is going on display before being auctioned in January
ATLANTA -- Words scrawled in blue pen — and others scratched out — give an intimate peek into the writing of what would become the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr.'s most famous speech.

Delivered Aug. 28, 1963, from the steps of the Lincoln Memorial, the “I Have a Dream” speech reflects on the shameful legacy of slavery, segregation and discrimination and looks forward with hope to future equality for the country's Black citizens. A handwritten draft of that speech goes on display in King's hometown Monday before it is sold to the highest bidder at auction in January.

“It shows a genius at work, that these words didn't just spill out perfectly,” said Jill Savitt, president and CEO of the National Center for Civil and Human Rights in Atlanta, where the draft is on display through Sunday.

The words that became most famous do not appear in the draft. The “I have a dream” refrain was added by King as he stood before a crowd of tens of thousands of people gathered on the National Mall for the March on Washington. Watching footage from the speech that day, it is “almost like an electric charge goes through him and he is overcome and he goes on the riff about ‘I have a dream’ — that was ad-libbed from the stage,” Savitt said.

Other key parts of the speech, titled “Normalcy — Never Again,” are there in the civil rights icon's own handwriting, including the opening lines and the powerful finish invoking an African American spiritual.

The seven pages from a pad of yellow, lined paper are displayed in two cases in the Atlanta museum’s gallery devoted to the March on Washington. Video of King delivering the speech is projected on the wall behind them.

King completed the handwritten draft in his hotel room in the wee hours of the morning, less than 12 hours before it was delivered, according to Christie's, which will handle the sale of the manuscript. It was then given to assistants to be typed and sent to the media.

Peter Klarnet, a specialist in books and manuscripts at Christie's, said he was “just blown away” when he first saw the draft, which is so close to the final typed version that it must be the final handwritten draft, he said.
“It’s such an important piece of American history and it’s a part of world history,” Klarnet said. “This is a speech that inspired all of us to do better.”

Speechwriter Edward Clayton was among the multiple advisers who helped King hash out the content of the speech. His wife, Xernona Clayton, who worked alongside him in the civil rights movement, discovered the draft in the late 1990s, three decades after her husband's death. It was in a drawer of his desk, tucked inside an envelope labeled “speech.”

“The two of them gelled with writing and words,” Xernona Clayton said in a Christie's news release. “They would go back and forth and there was such respect. Dr. King, who was a great thinker, said Ed was so good at getting his words on paper and putting them in the right place at the right time.”
Clayton knew the document was important but didn't realize it was the only remaining handwritten draft and stuck it back in the drawer, finding it there again just two years ago.

Clayton, who established the Still Marching Irrevocable Charitable Unitrust to advance causes important to her, decided after consultation with trusted advisers to sell the draft to support charities that advance her own legacy and that of King. Christie's expects the draft to fetch more than $10 million. The organizations that will benefit include the Xernona Clayton Foundation and the King Center in Atlanta.
“I am so grateful for the opportunity to give this amazing speech new life, and to give new life to people who are in need,” Clayton said. “And we cannot wait to give that first gift.”

King's two remaining living children, the Rev. Bernice King and Martin Luther King III, said in the Christie's release that they are grateful the sale will support the legacy of the movement their father helped build.

“It is poetic that the past will protect the future,” Martin Luther King III said. “We are grateful that this treasure was preserved over decades by the Clayton family. It is a remarkable piece of history that shines a light on our father’s process as he prepared to make a speech that so profoundly affected the course of the Civil Rights movement and our nation. Now, for the first time, the public will have the opportunity to be inspired by this document.”

The draft is being publicly displayed for the first time at the National Center for Civil and Human Rights in Atlanta from Monday through Sunday. It will be shown at Christie's in New York from Jan. 15, King's birthday, through Jan. 21 before being offered for auction on Jan. 22. Klarnet said they are also trying to arrange additional showings of the draft before the sale.

title: 2 planes collide on the ground in Miami, only minor injuries reported
summary: Federal aviation safety officials are investigating a minor collision between two planes at a taxiway intersection at Miami International Airport
story: Federal aviation safety officials are investigating a minor collision between two planes at a taxiway intersection at Miami International Airport

MIAMI -- Federal aviation safety officials on Sunday were investigating a minor collision between two planes at a taxiway intersection at Miami International Airport, where one aircraft's wingtip struck the nose of another, authorities said. Two people reported minor injuries.

The accident happened at about 9 p.m. Saturday and involved a Copa Airlines Boeing 737 passenger aircraft with 172 people aboard and a UPS Boeing 767 cargo plane, according to the National Transportation Safety Board and Copa Airlines. The wing of the Copa flight and the nose of the UPS plane collided, the NTSB said.
Photos taken at the scene show the UPS plane nose with a horizontal gash on one side and a larger hole in the middle.

On audio recorded by ATC.com, a pilot on the UPS plane told air traffic control that he went too far at the intersection and his plane was clipped by the Copa flight. Air traffic control told the UPS pilot that he was supposed to yield to the Copa aircraft.
The NTSB said it was gathering information and may provide an update on Sunday.
The Copa plane had just arrived from Panama City and the UPS plane was headed to Bogota, Colombia, officials said.
In a statement on social media, Copa called the collision minor and said two of its passengers were treated at the scene for minor injuries.
UPS said it was working with authorities to determine what happened.

“We cannot speculate on the details of the incident,” UPS said in a statement. “The National Transportation Safety Board is responsible for investigating incidents like this and will control the flow of information.”
The mishap came two months after an Amazon cargo plane careened off a runway at Miami International and smashed into a van carrying workers for a company that cleans airplanes, killing five people.

title: Isaac, a cat missing since the Brooklyn building collapse, has been reunited with his young owner
summary: A cat missing since last week’s deadly Brooklyn building collapse has been found alive and reunited with his young owner
story: A cat missing since last week’s deadly Brooklyn building collapse has been found alive and reunited with his young owner
NEW YORK -- A cat missing since last week’s deadly Brooklyn building collapse has been found alive and reunited with his young owner, New York City officials said Sunday.
Allie Taylor, director of the Mayor’s Office of Animal Welfare, said her office worked with the veterinary nonprofit Flatbush Cats to locate Isaac and reunite him with 13-year-old Zariah Coleman.

It was a bit of good news amid the tragedy of Wednesday’s collapse, which killed 8 people, injured 18 others and forced the evacuation of several nearby buildings, including one next door where Zariah lives.

Zariah and her mother told The New York Times on Sunday that workers found Isaac on Sunday in a cabinet under the kitchen sink of Zariah’s apartment after hearing a soft meow. Zariah and her family hadn't been allowed in since the collapse, which tore off the side of her building and left a hole where her bedroom wall had been.

Waiting outside, Zariah hugged the cat’s cage as workers brought him out of her apartment building. Isaac had gone four days without food or water. After his rescue, he was taken to Flatbush Cats’ veterinary clinic for a checkup.
“I had it in my heart they would find Issac,” Zariah told the Times. “I knew they would.”
Zariah tearfully spoke about her missing cat at a news conference on Friday, telling reporters: “I just really hope they come and get our cat. He’s hiding from them, and I think he’s scared.”
Mayor Zohran Mamdani heralded Isaac and Zariah’s reunion in a social media post. He thanked Taylor’s office, the city’s Buildings Department and the nonprofit for the happy outcome.
“Isaac is now receiving the veterinary care he needs,” Mamdani said. “We’re grateful to everyone who helped bring them back together.”

title: Huge waves pummel the California coast, forcing the closure of iconic piers
summary: The California coast is being pummeled again by huge waves that inundated beaches, flooded local streets and forced the closure of iconic piers
story: The California coast is being pummeled again by huge waves that inundated beaches, flooded local streets and forced the closure of iconic piers
SAN FRANCISCO -- The California coast was pummeled again Sunday by huge waves that inundated beaches, flooded local streets and forced the closure of iconic piers.
The National Weather Service office for the Bay Area warned that surf up to 35 feet (10.6 meters) was possible, along with dangerous rip currents and sneaker waves.
“Stay out of the water, stay off rocks and jetties, and never turn your back on the ocean!” the weather service said on social media.

On Saturday, waves above 50 feet (15.2 meters) were recorded in San Mateo County, just south of San Francisco. Surfers weren't deterred, taking advantage of giant waves at the famous Mavericks Beach near Half Moon Bay.
Farther south, the Santa Cruz County Sheriff’s Office issued an evacuation warning near the coastal town of Capitola that took the brunt of the powerful surf.
In Southern California, several piers, including ones in Ventura, Manhattan Beach, Huntington Beach and San Diego's Pacific Beach, were closed during the weekend as they were slammed by waves.
Several inches of water submerged the strand in Orange County's Seal Beach and flooded beachfront homes.
At La Jolla Cove near San Diego, famous for its lounging sea lions, water overflowed the beach and crashed up a staircase leading to the sand.
Conditions were calming by Sunday afternoon, but large waves were expected all week, forecasters warned.
The ongoing super El Niño has warmed the ocean, causing seawater to expand.

title: Officials say a tanker's steering failed before it crashed into a cruise ship in New Orleans
summary: U.S. government safety officials say a preliminary finding indicates a tanker's steering system failed, keeping its rudder in a position that sent it crashing into a cruise ship docked in New Orleans last week
story: U.S. government safety officials say a preliminary finding indicates a tanker's steering system failed, keeping its rudder in a position that sent it crashing into a cruise ship docked in New Orleans last week
A tanker’s steering system failed and kept its rudder in a position that sent it crashing into a cruise ship docked in New Orleans, U.S. government safety officials said Sunday.

The preliminary finding from National Transportation Safety Board officials provided the first official word on what caused Friday's crash of the Atlantic Asphalt tanker into the American Heritage cruise ship, which sent passengers, crew and two police officers plunging into the Mississippi River.
NTSB officials said during a briefing in New Orleans that it's not yet clear what caused the steering failure.
“It could be many different things,” NTSB accident investigator Bart Barnum said. “That is something that we're investigating very closely.”
The tanker, measuring about 520 feet (160 meters) long, had a crew of 19. The cruise ship, about 300 feet (91 meters) long, had 140 passengers and 50 crew onboard.

Officials said 32 people were taken to the hospital, including the two police officers who were thrown into the river when the boat rolled, but none of the injuries were critical. As of Sunday, six people remained hospitalized, the city of New Orleans said in a statement.

The tanker's steering problem caused its rudder to remain in a starboard position, to the right, which sent the tanker veering toward the east bank of the river, where it hit the cruise ship two minutes after the rudder became stuck, Barnum said.

As the tanker approached the river's east bank, the ship’s data recorder captured audio sounds “consistent” with the ship’s whistle going off, along with warnings and requests for assistance broadcast over the vessel’s marine radio, Barnum said. He added the data included commands to deploy the vessel anchors and emergency ship handling orders.

NTSB Member John DeLeeuw urged people with photos or video of the crash to submit them to his agency to help with its investigation, which is expected to result in a preliminary report within 30 days. He also praised the “the excellent response” from federal, state, local and private vessels that helped rescue people immediately after the crash.
The cruise ship capsized in 22 minutes, DeLeeuw said.

Just hours after the crash, the Board of Commissioners of the Port of New Orleans filed a federal lawsuit saying that the tanker caused at least $1 million in damage to its terminal. A judge issued a warrant Friday giving federal officials control of the ship for now.

title: Rubio acknowledges 'people are struggling' economically in speech after GOP midterm wipeout
summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio has acknowledged that Americans are struggling in the current economy
story: Secretary of State Marco Rubio has acknowledged that Americans are struggling in the current economy

WASHINGTON -- Secretary of State Marco Rubio gave a sweeping speech to fellow conservatives on Friday evening acknowledging that Americans are struggling in the current economy, while also railing against what he called the “weaponization” of international law to constrain the U.S. from acting in its own interests.
His comments to the conservative Federalist Society touched on a core issue of the midterm elections — economic pain — that U.S. voters cited in delivering massive losses to Rubio's Republican Party.

“I think we have to recognize that people are struggling. There’s no doubt about it,” he said. “The health of our economy has nothing to do with the stock market. The health of their economy is whether they have enough money to be able to afford the things they need.”

President Donald Trump often points to the stock market as evidence that the economy is doing well. But voters angry over higher costs gave Democrats control of Congress after blaming Trump for his tariffs, his war in Iran and his unfulfilled campaign promise two years ago to bring down prices.

Rubio's remarks had the overtones of campaign speech, though the former Florida senator has consistently refused to discuss whether he would seek the presidency in 2028 in a race that could pit him against Vice President JD Vance. Rubio gave another wide-ranging speech last month in Greece that focused on Western values and also appeared to reflect his political aspirations beyond being America’s top diplomat.

Rubio on Friday defended the Iran war, arguing that it was necessary to stop the threat of the Islamic Republic obtaining a nuclear weapon. But he acknowledged that the unpopular conflict has driven up gasoline prices for Americans and other connected costs.

“It’s not easy to address these things because it’s not popular to address them," Rubio said. “It’s difficult. And oftentimes it inflicts, you know, pain, economic pain and otherwise. So we recognize that.”

He also pointed to the need for American leaders to continue a tradition of ensuring the next generation is better off than those before them. Economic prosperity is “not self-perpetuating,” he said, but an enormous undertaking that requires years and decades and is not accomplished “election cycle to election cycle."

“That’s the challenge before us now, because I do think there’s a legitimate fear that we will be the first generation to leave the next worse off, and that can’t happen. That’s un-American,” he said.

Rubio also hit back hard on critics of Trump administration policies such as deadly strikes on alleged drug-smuggling boats in Latin America, the January capture of then-Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and strict immigration policies.
He accused other countries and international organizations of trying to stymie the U.S. from acting in its own best interests by accusing the Trump administration of violations of international law.

“We’ve heard the concept international law invoked against nearly every major foreign policy decision or action of this administration,” he said, describing it as “the weaponization of international law.”

Rubio also condemned the United Nations, the International Criminal Court, the “global elite” and organizations staffed by “international activists and bureaucrats,” all of which he said want to weaken the United States.

“They lecture us on the importance of sovereignty, even as they demand that nations surrender control of their borders and outsource their immigration laws to unelected international courts,” Rubio said. "They oppose, they say, all forms of imperialism, of conquest, of domination, but they seek to exercise authority over every country and every government on earth.”
AP Diplomatic Writer Matthew Lee in Washington contributed.

title: Trump is taking Elon Musk on his Asia trip, but he plans to avoid talking about Nvidia scandal
summary: President Donald Trump plans to take the world’s wealthiest man, Elon Musk, with him next week when he travels to the Philippines and China
story: President Donald Trump plans to take the world’s wealthiest man, Elon Musk, with him next week when he travels to the Philippines and China
WASHINGTON -- President Donald Trump plans to take the world's wealthiest man, Elon Musk, with him next week when he travels to the Philippines and China.

As the head of SpaceX and Tesla, Musk has economic and national security interests that make him a valuable adviser to Trump, according to administration officials who insisted on anonymity as a condition for previewing the president's plans on a Friday call with reporters.

The journey comes as the fallout spreads from Jensen Huang being ousted as the CEO of Nvidia for having an extramarital affair with an alleged agent of the Chinese government. Beijing denies that Alice Huang is a spy. Her company Megaspeed was accused last year of shipping Nvidia's advanced computer chips into China.

But Trump does not plan to confront Chinese leader Xi Jinping on the matter and administration officials do not expect Chinese retaliation for any follow-up actions to prohibit China from smuggling or using advanced computer chips, officials told reporters.

The administration believes the situation with Nvidia should not have any bearing on the trip, as the U.S. does not make its use of export controls subject to negotiations with foreign countries. Trump's aides are discussing the possibility of closing loopholes in existing trade measures, including the use of export licensing and preventing the ability of Chinese firms to use advanced chips over the internet through remote access.

The trip will be capped with a historic trilateral meeting with Xi and Russian leader Vladimir Putin, where efforts to limit nuclear weapons will be a chief topic. Still, there are no plans for Trump to meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, whose nuclear arsenal has been a source of consternation to the U.S. and its allies.

Trump is set to arrive Tuesday in the Philippines to meet with his counterparts in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations. While in Manila, he intends to sign a trade deal with Thailand and meet with the Quad, an alliance composed of the U.S., India, Australia and Japan.

On Wednesday, Trump will leave for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, where he’ll have his third in-person meeting this year with Xi. Afterward, Trump and Xi will hold their joint meeting with Putin.

The leaders are expected to talk about the Iran war, but Russia's war in Ukraine is not expected to be part of the agenda, officials said — and Musk, whose Starlink system has been integral to Ukraine's ability to fight back against Russia's invasion, will not be part of the trilateral meeting.

title: The European Union says Europe will send a team of diplomats from across the continent to the Ukraine peace talks
summary: The European Union says Europe will send a team of diplomats from across the continent to the Ukraine peace talks
story: The European Union says Europe will send a team of diplomats from across the continent to the Ukraine peace talks
DUBLIN -- The European Union says Europe will send a team of diplomats from across the continent to the Ukraine peace talks.
THIS IS AN APNewsAlert. Check back for updates. AP's earlier story is below.

European nations are seeking an envoy to represent them in talks on ending the Russia-Ukraine war, concerned that a U.S.-backed process will leave them sidelined and Kyiv vulnerable as Moscow and Washington decide the fate of a conflict that has roiled the continent.

Whether Europe should be represented by one person or a team — and who should take on the role — was debated Friday as leaders of the 27-nation European Union met at a summit in Dublin. Senior EU officials and politicians have been suggested, but there is no consensus yet.

What the job might entail is also unclear and contested. But there is broad agreement by governments from the U.K. to Ukraine on the need for Europe to join the ongoing negotiations involving Moscow, Kyiv and Washington.

“I would hope that today’s discussions bring clarity around this,” Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin said as he arrived. “It needs to be, in my view, finally decided upon within the next week or two.”

Ukraine is eager for support from its European allies. It's reluctant to leave the talks solely in the hands of a U.S. administration that has often seemed to lean toward Moscow’s views. Russia does not want European countries involved in direct negotiations, complaining they are financing and supplying Ukraine’s military effort.
European leaders also distrust U.S. President Donald Trump to negotiate on their behalf after a series of tense standoffs over trade, Greenland and conflicts in Iran and Ukraine.
“Without Europeans, there is no support for Ukraine,” French President Emmanuel Macron said Thursday at a meeting of the European Political Community in Dublin. “There is no more U.S. support.”
“At the end of the day, we will be the ones to define and decide for our future security as Europeans,” he said.

After Thursday’s meeting of the EPC, a larger group than the EU with members including the U.K. and Ukraine, Macron's office published what he called a “historic declaration” by 40 European nations affirming support for Ukraine and the continent’s collective security.
It affirmed that “the path to peace in Ukraine should be decided with Ukraine and that any matter affecting European security should be decided with the Europeans.”

European leaders fear Russian President Vladimir Putin will press Trump to back a peace settlement that weakens not just Ukraine but broader European security. Putin has demanded NATO troops be pulled back from Russia’s borders and that no European forces be deployed in Ukraine.
As envoys from Washington, Moscow and Kyiv met in Abu Dhabi, several European countries, including the U.K., France and Germany, attended discussions nearby.

U.S. envoy Jared Kushner and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said after they met in Dublin late Thursday that Europe would be part of the next round of talks. Zelenskyy said Europe would send a negotiating team, adding, “They will have a voice.”
“We cannot conclude this deal without the Europeans being at the table,” Kushner said. He said Putin “is willing to give it a try.”
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Thursday that Europe must first name a representative. “The Europeans squabble like spiders in a jar.”

Supporters of a single envoy, such as Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, argue that the absence of a united European voice has allowed individual countries or small groups to engage in freelance diplomacy.
“There are too many different groupings discussing the issue,” she said.

Meloni has criticized a series of seemingly uncoordinated initiatives, including an October call to Putin by Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, that she said could undermine European interests.
Martin said that European representation at the negotiations “can't just be European Union.”
“It's a European continentwide issue,” he said, pointing to the role of Norway and Britain in supporting Ukraine.

The question of who represents Europe is an old one. Europe itself is loosely defined. Is it the 27-nation EU, the 32-nation NATO military alliance made up mostly of European countries, the 29-nation Schengen zone, or the 47-nation European Political Community?
That has long frustrated Washington.

After this week's U.S.-brokered talks between Ukraine and Russia in the United Arab Emirates, Kushner said that “if Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf, that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiation.”
That echoes the famous question often misattributed to former U.S. Secretary of State Henry Kissinger: “Who do I call if I want to call Europe?”

France, Germany and the U.K., the region’s top three economies, collectively known as the European trio, or E3, have so far been the most engaged European group in negotiations. But while London is deeply involved with Ukraine, the U.K. left the EU in 2020.

An E3 envoy would leave out the other 25 EU nations and rankle smaller nations, like those bordering Russia and Belarus on the bloc’s eastern flank, which face constant hybrid threats, including influence campaigns and disruptive drones.
Some back a top EU official for the job. Even inside Brussels, however, there are two leading contenders: European Council President Antonio Costa and the EU's top diplomat Kaja Kallas.

“European security cannot be discussed without a European voice at the table,” Costa said in Dublin on Thursday. “That European voice needs to be a team effort between European nations, the European Union and NATO.”
Earlier this year, Costa faced criticism within the EU after his office set up a hush-hush back-channel with Moscow.
Kallas, a former prime minister of Estonia, laid claim to the envoy role Friday, saying, “I’m the one who is representing Europe in the foreign and security policy.”

“I know that the Russians don’t want me, but, you know, do we have a say, who is representing Russia?” she said. “We can’t send any person that has no institutional role like the Americans are sending.”
Another name that has been floated is Stubb, the Finnish president. He has warm relations with Trump and met in Oslo last month with Witkoff and Kushner.
But some leaders deeply distrust the U.S.-brokered talks.

“In my opinion, calling them negotiations is an exaggeration,” Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Thursday. “We will not build a new security architecture simply because the Russian president, or someone in the United States, wishes it.”

With Trump due to head to Beijing next week to meet Putin, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said European leaders feared another “Anchorage moment,” a reference to the Alaska summit where they were stunned by Trump's overtures to the Russian leader in the absence of Ukrainian or European envoys.
“Please, no surprises,” Merz said. “Continue to play in team Europe and in the team with Ukraine.”
Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs noted that Europe is larger than Russia in population, economy and military might.
“We as Europe have to grow some bigger balls," he said.
Associated Press writers Geir Moulson in Berlin, Lorne Cook in Brussels and Colleen Barry in Milan contributed to this report.

title: Democratic political group launches new push to shape AI agenda ahead of 2028
summary: A Democratic political group is launching a new push to find ways to meet voters' concerns about artificial intelligence ahead of the 2028 presidential election
story: A Democratic political group is launching a new push to find ways to meet voters' concerns about artificial intelligence ahead of the 2028 presidential election

DENVER -- A Democratic political organization is announcing a new effort to shape how to talk with voters about artificial intelligence, deepening its investment on an issue that an increasing number of party leaders believe creates a stark contrast with President Donald Trump's opposition to regulating the powerful technology.

Tomorrow Together was one of several groups that tried to counter the industry's huge campaign war chest during the midterms. It pushed for new limits on artificial intelligence and data centers and spent $6.5 million on behalf of candidates calling for more regulation.

The latest research initiative, pegged at $1.1 million to start, begins as Democrats meet in Denver for the What's Next conference, a two-day opportunity to celebrate their sweeping wins in midterm races and chart a course toward the next presidential campaign. It also comes in the wake of fresh warnings that the technology poses risks to humans as companies begin a new phase of development that will allow AI to build new versions of itself.

“We expect getting this right is going to be critical to winning people's votes,” said Maddie Kriger, the group's chief program officer. “It's also not out of the realm of possibility we will see more and worse AI incidents in the next year, and we want to be prepared to move to help people and take action if that does happen.”
Democrats believe Trump has embraced a wildly unpopular position and handed them an opportunity to become the party that pushes for guardrails on AI development.

“I really think we're watching the birth of a new political issue before our eyes,” David Shor, a prominent party data analyst, told the Denver crowd as he described AI as the rare issue where voters of both parties embrace regulation.
Karthik Ganapathy, a co-founder of Together Tomorrow, agreed.
“I'd rather be us than them,” he said of Republicans on the issue.
Some Republicans have distanced themselves from Trump's pro-industry stance, most notably Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, who is widely believed to be preparing another run for the presidency.
Rob Flaherty, the other co-founder of Together Tomorrow, expects his party to still have the edge.

“At the beginning of the cycle, this was a jump ball. Voters didn't know who to trust,” he said. Now, thanks to Trump, he argued, Democrats have the lead. “Regulating technology is where the voters are.”

title: Investigation says understaffing and unexpected fire behavior led to firefighter deaths
summary: Unexpected fire behavior, chronic understaffing, a lack of trained employees and a new policy to quash fires quickly were among the factors that contributed to the deaths of four helitack firefighters as they battled a blaze in western Colorado in June
story: Unexpected fire behavior, chronic understaffing, a lack of trained employees and a new policy to quash fires quickly were among the factors that contributed to the deaths of four helitack firefighters as they battled a blaze in western Colorado in June

Unexpected fire behavior, chronic understaffing, a lack of highly trained employees and a new policy to quash fires quickly were among the factors that contributed to the deaths of four helitack firefighters as they battled a blaze in western Colorado in June, according to a report released by the U.S. Department of the Interior.

The firefighters, working for the U.S. Forest Service and the newly created U.S. Wildland Fire Service, were part of an interagency response to the Knowles fire that merged with others to form the Snyder Fire on the Colorado/Utah border. The Rifle Helitack crew had been dropped in a remote area to work on a fire line, but became trapped when strong winds blew the fires in their direction and overtook them.

Their deaths came after the Trump administration revived a previously discredited policy to stomp out all wildfires quickly. Decisions on how to fight the Knowles fire were driven by the desire to prevent the spread of cheatgrass and protect sage-grouse habitat and a downwind community, the report said.

These factors “established an organizational posture to aggressively suppress new starts while small,” the report said. “This policy framing drove the decision to insert helitack firefighters onto small wilderness starts on a day with extreme fire weather conditions forecast.”

Emily Barker, Nick Hutcherson, and Sydney Watson were killed at the scene while Nathan Matthews sustained burn injuries and died on July 24. A fifth firefighter on the team sustained burn injuries but survived.

Ron and Lisa Hutcherson, Nick's parents, said the crew should not have been sent out ahead of the fire because dangerous winds were in the forecast. After meeting with investigators and visiting the site, they said they believe the deaths were preventable and were caused by a failure of leadership and oversight.

“Telling us how the fire reached our son does not answer why he was still there,” Ron Hutcherson said in an email to The Associated Press. “Who was watching the bigger picture? Who was responsible for bringing those firefighters home while there was still time?”
Lisa Hutcherson added: "My son depended on the people responsible for tracking the fire threatening him and making the decisions needed to keep him safe. We want answers, and we want accountability.”
The Serious Accident Investigation report detailed the circumstances that led to the decision to send out the helitack team and the many problems that led to their deaths.
Multiple lightning fires ignited on June 27 in Colorado's Black Ridge Canyon Wilderness. The region was experiencing extreme drought conditions, and the winds were picking up.

An incident team orchestrated coverage of the various fires by calling in aircraft and crews. At one point, the official in charge ordered all aircraft to the Jones fire, but constant high winds challenged all pilots that day, with many saying it was the most difficult flying of their careers, the report said.
By the early afternoon, communication systems broke down, with many trainee dispatchers trying to coordinate operations. There was also confusion over who would track aircraft.

“Dispatchers simultaneously tracked up to 16 active aircraft, three emerging incidents, multiple new starts, county river evacuations, and non-stop media inquiries, leading to severe cognitive task saturation,” the report said. “Due to constant radio congestion and workload strain, dispatchers felt they were unable to transmit the mandatory scheduled 1000 Fire Weather Forecast broadcast across the zone.”
The incident commanders on the Snyder and Jones fires did not have clear information about the location of the firefighters on the Knowles and Gore fires to the east, the report said.

“Because no operational role was assigned to continuously map personnel location against the emerging fires’ trajectories, overhead did not recognize that firefighters were positioned directly in the fire’s line of advance,” the report said.

A large fire about eight miles to the west of the helitack crew was observed three and a half hours before the entrapment, the report said. In less than three hours, the fire ran over complex terrain and reached the five firefighters, who were forced to deploy fire shelters, because a helicopter was unable to reach them in time.

The Hutcherson family met with fire investigators in Grand Junction on Oct. 26 for a three-hour official readout of the report, they said. The review described a failure of lookouts, communications, escape routes and safety zones, they said.

An aging mobile radio system and software crashes compromised official channels during critical operations, the family was told. Overlapping transmissions and confused radio traffic forced firefighters to use cellphones to communicate.

The Knowles fire was in a remote location, the family said, so the central question remains: “What justified keeping this crew exposed as communications, observation, and extraction options deteriorated?”

Timothy Ingalsbee, executive director of the nonprofit Firefighters United for Safety, Ethics and Ecology, said the problem can be traced back to the Trump administration's full-suppression policy, which has prompted crews across the country to take unreasonable risks.

“It was outrageous to have a full-suppression policy on a lightning-caused fire in the wilderness to prevent the spread of cheatgrass,” Ingalsbee said. “The policy driving this aggressive attack of all fires is an obsolete paradigm that is just humanly or ecologically unsustainable. And unfortunately this crew paid the ultimate price, ultimate sacrifice.”

title: US gives states another 6 months before they have to remove people from Medicaid for not working
summary: President Donald Trump's administration is giving states another six months before they must remove beneficiaries from Medicaid rolls for failing to meet new work requirements
story: President Donald Trump's administration is giving states another six months before they must remove beneficiaries from Medicaid rolls for failing to meet new work requirements
President Donald Trump’s administration told states Friday that they can wait until July before removing people from Medicaid for failing to meet a work requirement.

The requirement is scheduled to take effect nationally on Jan. 1, and states have been scrambling to put in place the staffing, training and technology to implement it by then. The administration clarified that while states still have the option to take action at the beginning of the year, they won't have to kick anyone off or deny coverage for failure to meet the requirement until July 1.

Medicaid is the joint state-federal health insurance program for lower-income people. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services told state Medicaid directors on Friday that they'll still need to determine whether many enrollees and applicants for benefits are meeting new requirements that they are working, in school or volunteering.

The move announced Friday gives state social service departments more time to make sure complicated changes are ready to run before there are consequences. CMS said that states are making progress but have implementation challenges.

“I think these extra six months are going to give states the ability to respond to the change, and there will be fewer people that lose their coverage due to administrative failures” resulting from states’ inability to prepare, Kathy Hempstead, senior policy officer for the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation, told The Associated Press.
Still, she said it's not clear which states will opt to use the additional time.
Kate McEvoy, executive director of the National Association of Medicaid Directors, said state Medicaid leaders “appreciate the additional flexibility that CMS is providing."

The decision also could give some breathing room to Congress to consider changes to the requirement. Democrats who are taking control of both chambers in January after their sweeping election victories last week have said they want to roll back the requirements.

The news comes after Democratic Sen. Ron Wyden, of Oregon, and Rep. Frank Pallone Jr., of New Jersey, wrote to CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz this week, asking to delay implementing the work reporting requirements. Their letter cites, in part, a recent decision out of a Boston federal court that determined medically frail people should not be bound by the work requirement qualification rules.

“The practical reality is that this significant implementation issue may not be definitively resolved for months, creating untenable uncertainty for states that need a final resolution of this issue before going live with work reporting requirements,” the letter states. “The court ruling is an important victory for the millions of medically frail people who rely on Medicaid for their health care coverage."

Under the policy, many Medicaid beneficiaries must work or volunteer at least 80 hours a month or be in school at least half-time. The new policy applies only to people who receive Medicaid under a voluntary expansion that 40 states undertook and which was intended to get health coverage to more lower-income adults who don’t have kids at home. There are exceptions for those who are over 64, caring for kids under 14 or deemed too medically frail to work.
Critics say that most enrollees covered by the mandate are already working and that people are more likely to lose coverage because of the paperwork to prove it rather than failing to work.

The federal government is pushing states to use data from other government departments or elsewhere to verify whether beneficiaries are working as a way to reduce the burden on the beneficiaries to show proof.
A few states have launched the work requirements early.
The first of them was Nebraska, where they started in May.

Preliminary data presented to the state’s Medicaid Advisory Committee showed that more than 9 in 10 people subject to the work requirement and due to have their benefits renewed in July and August qualified.

But 533 people were denied continuing coverage. For most of them, it was over paperwork: They didn’t show that they were working or were exempt from the requirement. Of those denied, 43 lost coverage because they did not meet the new requirement.

Similarly, most of the new Medicaid applicants who were denied coverage due to work requirements from May through August did not get the coverage because they did not provide information to verify whether they were complying.
Among both groups, it’s not clear how many people didn’t provide information because they weren’t working — or how many might meet the requirements but failed to show it.
“There are likely people who are still eligible for coverage who lost it,” said Amy Behnke, the CEO of the Health Care Center Association of Nebraska.

title: Bigger and more-frequent wildfires threaten water supplies across the US
summary: A record number of wildfires burned more than 9 million acres in the U.S. this year, leaving behind charred trees and scorched vegetation
story: A record number of wildfires burned more than 9 million acres in the U.S. this year, leaving behind charred trees and scorched vegetation

Wildfires leave behind charred trees and scorched vegetation that impact the streams and rivers providing drinking water to much of the country, and new studies show that contamination could remain for more than a decade.

These findings about the longevity of contamination in the nation's drinking water supplies are especially concerning as climate change and increasingly strong El Niño weather events, which intensify drought conditions, have led to bigger and more frequent wildfires in the U.S. So far in 2026, there have been 68,179 blazes burning more than 9.5 million acres (3.8 million hectares).

After a wildfire sweeps through hillsides and forests, rains carry ash and organic matter into the streams that feed water treatment plants for towns and cities alike. Communities are working to adapt, but it can take years and require stopgap solutions.

People in the City of Las Vegas, New Mexico, went without water for months after the Hermit’s Peak/Calf Canyon wildfire contaminated the Gallinas River in 2022. In the four years since, they’ve had to give residents bottled water and ship tanks in from nearby towns as they collected funds to build a new treatment plant.
Karen Pettine, who has owned the Hillcrest Restaurant for 50 years, said the water crisis forced them to close, sometimes for a week at a time.

“It’s hard to run a restaurant without good water,” she said. “We used some paper plates at times. They brought in semi-truckloads of bottled water. You could pick up four cases at a time. The water situation is ongoing because when it rains, it floods and it brings dirty water down the stream.”
Las Vegas Mayor David Romero said climate change has made the things that used to be reliable less predictable.
“It’s a scary situation that we’re all going to encounter,” he said.

Wildfires are a natural part of forest ecosystems, but an increase in their severity has made areas that capture, filter and regulate the flow of water, known as watersheds, vulnerable, said Amanda Hohner, an assistant professor at Montana State University who specializes in wildfires and water quality.

Forested watersheds provide water to nearly two-thirds of municipalities in the U.S., according to Carli Brucker, lead author of a University of Colorado Boulder study that assessed wildfire-affected water quality in hundreds of burned basins and compared them to unburned areas. Their study found that the impacts can last up to eight years.

Garrett McKay, an assistant professor of civil and environmental engineering at Texas A&M, said utilities are extremely concerned about the impacts wildfires have on water. They’re reaching out to experts like him for help finding different water sources or to learn how to treat the organic matter coming into their plants.

Water treatment facilities that rely on streams and rivers typically treat high quality water, aided by trees and soil that act as a natural filtration system, Brucker said. But wildfires cause spikes in heavy metals or dissolved organic matter, which the plants aren't built to handle, she said.

This can force treatment facilities to shut off the incoming water and resort to other sources, which may not be immediately available, Brucker said. Some have groundwater or reservoir backups, but even those can be impacted.

Reservoirs can serve as a “sedimentation basin” where particles can settle, said Kyle Shimabuku, an assistant professor of civil engineering at Gonzaga University. But sediments from burned vegetation are rich in nutrients, like nitrogen and phosphorus, and as they sit in still water, algal blooms can grow, he said. The algae can make people sick and kill the fish.

Chlorine, routinely used to treat water, also is impacted by wildfires, said McKay at Texas A&M. When facilities add disinfectants, like chlorine, to water, they react with the dissolved organic matter left behind by the fires to form “disinfection byproducts,” which are regulated by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency because they can cause illnesses, including cancer.
Since plants can't remove the disinfection byproducts, they must get rid of the organic matter before disinfecting the water, which can cause delays in the water supply.

When a 2020 wildfire burned the area around No Name and Grizzly creeks, the primary water sources for the city of Glenwood Springs, Colorado, officials scrambled to protect against sediment expected to wash down the slopes when spring rains arrived. They sought help from the Colorado Water Conservation Board. Within two months, the board authorized an emergency loan of $8 million for improvements to the treatment system.

Fort Collins faced a similar challenge that year when ash and sediment from the Cameron Peak fire forced the city to close its river intake and pull water from the Horsetooth Reservoir, which was safe to use because it's fed by a different watershed.

Las Vegas, New Mexico, was hit harder when the Hermit’s Peak/Calf Canyon fire damaged the Gallinas River watershed in 2022. A massive rainstorm swept ash and sludge from the burn scar into the river and reservoirs, forcing the town to shut down its water treatment plant while they installed additional filters and looked for additional water sources.

As they worked on solutions, a massive flood in 2024 carried more burn debris into the town’s two reservoirs, leaving them with only a few days of safe water. As businesses closed and residents bought bottled water, the town hired trucks to bring 2.2 million gallons (8.3 million liters) of water from nearby towns of Santa Fe and Santa Rosa.

They were hit again in February 2025. Burn scar debris coupled with bad weather and equipment failure caused a pressure drop, which resulted in a monthlong boil-water advisory and more water shipments.
“The February event was probably the scariest,” Romero said.

Ultimately, the state and federal governments allocated $148 million to rebuild the town's treatment plant and help support their efforts to find other options, including drilling wells and reusing water. Groundbreaking on the first phase of their new water treatment plant is slated for Nov. 18, the mayor said.
“We’ve been doing a lot of work for other sources of water and we know with climate change and what we experienced in the past, the Gallinas River is something we can’t depend on forever.”

title: Brother of Mexican cartel leader sentenced to 22 years for drug trafficking plot
summary: A man whose brother led one of Mexico’s most violent drug cartels has been sentenced to more than 22 years in U.S. prison for his role in a sprawling drug trafficking conspiracy that brought cocaine and methamphetamine to American streets
story: A man whose brother led one of Mexico’s most violent drug cartels has been sentenced to more than 22 years in U.S. prison for his role in a sprawling drug trafficking conspiracy that brought cocaine and methamphetamine to American streets

WASHINGTON -- A man whose brother led one of Mexico’s most violent drug cartels was sentenced Friday to more than 22 years in U.S. prison for his part in a sprawling drug trafficking conspiracy that brought cocaine and methamphetamine to American streets.

Antonio Oseguera Cervantes, brother of the late Jalisco New Generation co-founder known as El Mencho, pleaded guilty to drug trafficking charges in July after the Mexican government handed him over to U.S. authorities last year alongside other high-ranking cartel leaders.
His case is part of a broader Trump administration effort to crack down on powerful cartels such as Jalisco New Generation, also known as CJNG, that have helped fuel America's drug epidemic.

“Oseguera Cervantes’ sentence sends a clear message to criminals around the world that the Department of Justice is committed to the total elimination of drug cartels and transnational criminal organizations, including the CJNG," Assistant Attorney General Tysen Duva, who leads the department's Criminal Division, said in an emailed statement.

Antonio Oseguera Cervantes, 68, of Michoacán, Mexico, worked for cartels with his brother Nemesio Rubén Oseguera Cervantes, the drug lord known as El Mencho, who was killed by the Mexican army in February, according to federal prosecutors.
Antonio Oseguera Cervantes was a leader of the Milenio Cartel and later reported directly to his brother after El Mencho became the CJNG’s top leader, according to prosecutors.

Prosecutors in Washington's federal court had recommended a 30-year prison sentence, noting that his duties included receiving CJNG drug proceeds, managing the cartel's money laundering activities and supervising meth laboratories.

“Rival cartels rarely settle disputes through diplomacy alone," prosecutors wrote in court papers. “And while there may be no nonviolent drug cartels in Mexico, (Oseguera Cervantes) was a member of particularly brutal cartels."

Antonio Oseguera Cervantes' attorneys requested a 20-year prison sentence, saying in court documents that he accepts full responsibility for his crimes and “blames no one except himself.” They noted that he already has spent several years behind bars in Mexico for essentially the same conduct to which he pleaded guilty in the U.S.
He expressed remorse in a letter addressed to the court, saying he is “deeply sorry for my actions and for the harm they caused.”

“One of my greatest fears is that I will die far away from my family," he wrote. "I love my children and my family very much, and I hope that I may one day have the opportunity to spend the remaining years of my life with them.”
Associated Press reporter Alanna Durkin Richer contributed from Washington.

title: Survivors of the deadly Brooklyn building collapse recall shock, terror and grief
summary: Survivors of a Brooklyn apartment building collapse are desperate to know what caused the catastrophe that killed relatives and neighbors and destroyed their homes
story: Survivors of a Brooklyn apartment building collapse are desperate to know what caused the catastrophe that killed relatives and neighbors and destroyed their homes

NEW YORK -- One man's pregnant wife was pulled alive from the rubble, while two of his roommates perished. A woman living next door woke from a nap to bright daylight flooding her bedroom because her apartment wall was suddenly gone.
Survivors of the Brooklyn apartment building collapse that killed eight people wept as they recounted their terror and grief during a news conference Friday.

New York officials, from building inspectors to prosecutors, say they're investigating what caused the three-story building to come crashing down as workers were digging at an adjacent construction site.
Those who lost family, neighbors and their homes demanded answers.

“As they’re taking me, evacuating me from the building, I could see my neighbors coming out on stretchers,” said Ciahola Lawrence, whose apartment building next to the one that collapsed had a shared wall ripped away, exposing an abyss of dust and debris below.
“We didn’t deserve this,” said Lawrence, who sobbed in her husband's arms as she spoke with reporters.
Among the dead were two children, ages 9 and 10, according to city officials. Another 18 people were injured, including four firefighters.

Mamadou Mouctar Balde stepped out to buy groceries Wednesday, leaving his pregnant wife and two roommates, 31-year-old Mamadou N’Diaye and 23-year-old Mamadou Barry, at home. Barry was cooking and N’Diaye was sleeping on the couch, he said.
He returned to find firefighters, police and neighbors gathering outside and assumed there had been a traffic accident. Then a woman told him a building had collapsed.
“I didn’t see my wife. I didn’t see my friends,” Balde recalled, a tear streaking his cheek. “I no longer knew where I am.”
First responders found the bodies of N’Diaye and Barry while combing the wreckage. Balde's wife, Fatoumata Bah, was pulled alive from the rubble. He said she and their unborn child were doing OK.
N’Diaye and Barry were Guinean nationals who came to the U.S. about five years ago from Conakry, the capital of the West African nation. Their uncle said their family is heartbroken.
“We ask the city and the Guinean community to stand for us, to have a justice for this tragedy,” he said.
Other victims came from Mexico, Colombia, Ecuador and Trinidad, New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said.

New York police identified the others who died as Nicole Daniela Salvada Rodriguez, 9; Juan Daniel Salvada Guzman, 31; Kevin Santiago Reyes Gonzalez, 10; Gabriel Siguencia, 22; Edgar Sapon, 26; and Jose Luis Caguana Cosquillo, 26.
Ahmed Tigani, commissioner of New York's Department of Buildings, said Friday that his office is conducting “an exhaustive investigation” of the Brooklyn collapse.

The city has ordered inspections at more than 160 sites in New York that are associated with six entities linked to the construction and demolition site next to the fallen building, Mamdani said, significantly raising an earlier count of sites subject to renewed scrutiny.
“I think it is always an outrage when eight New Yorkers lose their lives, when 18 New Yorkers are hospitalized, and when families are shattered as a result of all of this,” Mamdani said.
If investigators uncover “any evidence of criminality,” Mamdani said, “it is one that we follow through to the fullest extent of the law.”

One witness who works across the street said he watched bricks fall minutes before the disaster. A woman in a neighboring building said she and fellow residents blamed vibrations from the construction for cracks that appeared in their apartment walls.
Lawrence said the construction work had been a source of constant disruption, producing noises so loud that “you would hear that thumping and movement in your soul.”

A security camera above Lawrence’s door recorded video of her apartment’s shared wall and the building next door collapsing in a clattering rumble and a thick cloud of dust. Inside her apartment, a closet filled with hanging clothes and bags was exposed to the outside.
The security video shows Lawrence leaving her damaged home with a firefighter, who held her hand as they descended a stairway overlooking mounds of wreckage below.
“This feeling is indescribable,” Lawrence said. “I was right there.”
