title: Transcript: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Nov. 15, 2026
summary: The following is the transcript of the interview with Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Nov. 15, 2026.
story: The following is the transcript of the interview with Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Nov. 15, 2026.

MARGARET BRENNAN: For more, we go now to the Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy. Good morning to you, Mr. Secretary. Will the country be back to fully operational with a full flight schedule by the end of today?

SEC. SEAN DUFFY: So we have some delays in the airspace right now, but as we look to the end of the day and into tomorrow, we should be running at full capacity. What happens with a ground stop, like on Friday, we have airplanes and crews that are out of position, so it takes a little bit of time for the airlines to get back and choreographed and at full capacity and operations, but we're well on our way.

MARGARET BRENNAN: So I know that there was a router in El Dorado, Arkansas, as I understand it, that became an issue on Friday. You said on another network this morning there was a second issue at a radar site in Amarillo, Texas. Are those two things related? And if so, why did they both become problems on Friday?

SEC. DUFFY: Yeah, so the- the Amarillo facility- that work had been done weeks ago, and so why- when we did the install in El Dorado, did that start to broadcast data into our network? But then also the- the facility in Amarillo- why did that happen? We're investigating that right now. We actually have both routers with L3Harris, who operates and owns our network. FAA is on site as well. FBI is offering support. We're looking at that right now, and when we know what the root cause of this issue was- was it- was it the install from L3Harris? Was it the router? I'm going to tell you and the American people what we find.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So, was the issue old infrastructure or was it new equipment?

SEC. DUFFY: So first off, the- the- the telecom in El Dorado, it was an old copper wire that basically was- it was going to be decommissioned. They said it can't be used anymore. So we were forced by the telecom provider to actually update that copper to fiber, and we brought in our routers and did the work, and that's when we saw the- the flooding of the network. So this was- this is part of our maintenance that we do on this really old architecture of a telecom network that was- I mean, this goes back decades. By the way, the rest of the world, every institution, every company, not just in the U.S. but around the world, they've all switched over to digital and fiber. It's just the FAA is still using this really old telecom network that has to be updated, upgraded, and I think built brand new.

MARGARET BRENNAN: So the union that represents aviation safety specialists, PASS, as they're called, said the issue was isolated to two contractor-owned and maintained routers that were being updated in the middle of the day, and they said their technicians were not involved in the upgrades. So I wonder, did the FAA do a risk assessment in advance and know that something like this was- happened, or were you totally caught off guard?

SEC. DUFFY: So let's be clear, the union that works at the FAA, they'll do the work on the radios- our equipment, or the radar- our equipment. They do all of the work on FAA-owned equipment. This union doesn't do any work on telecom, and it's our telecom contractor and providers like L3Harris in this situation. They're the ones that actually do the work. So the FAA lets L3Harris into our- into our sites, and then L3Harris will do the telecom work. But our- this union only works on our equipment. This telecom is not our- is- that's not our equipment. It's L3Harris's network. So just to clarify that, this- this was done appropriately, which by the way, it's been done thousands of times by us, by others, and other companies. This has never happened, and so that's why when you have a remote location like this, we felt comfortable doing it in the middle of the day because it's been done thousands of times. We've never had this situation. We're going to have to reevaluate now when we do this work. Now, normally, if you have a big facility, a Newark or an Atlanta or an LA, we have work to do, we do that at night, but in a remote location, we can do it during the day because the risk historically has been very low. Obviously, on Friday we saw no, it flooded our network, and we had to take the extraordinary step of issuing a ground stop.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So there was not a risk assessment, or there was a risk assessment, and this was just not foreseen as an issue?

SEC. DUFFY: Oh no, no- listen, we do risk assessments on everything, right? And if you want to talk about a risk assessment, the GAO has done a risk assessment on my network, on all of the old equipment, and they'll say, "Hey, this is- this is risky America. Make the investments and fix American air traffic control systems." And by the way, the Congress gave me $12.5 billion dollars.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.

SEC. DUFFY: I've- I've got ordered new radar, new radios, new voice switches. We're doing all of that, but it's also risky to say we're operating on a 1980s network with copper wires. So we've done a risk assessment- assessment: How do you switch over from copper to fiber? We keep airplanes safe in the sky. That's our number one priority. We've done that, and which is why it's worked thousands of times when we've made the switch over.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, when--
SEC. DUFFY: --this time it- it didn't- and the- go ahead.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah. So you just mentioned the- the Government Accountability Office. They also, in a September report, concluded that there is a push to modernize quickly, and that the FAA is buying delivery speed at the risk of cost uncertainty and potential disruptions. So, should you have seen this coming?
SEC. DUFFY: Well, first off, with regard to the GAO, my number one priority is safety, which is why we shut down the airspace on Friday, right? We did the closure--
MARGARET BRENNAN: They're saying speed.

SEC. DUFFY: No, I'm going to get to that. But I want to make sure that- that Americans get from point A to point B safely. They get back to their loved ones. I want them to be on time, but I want them to be safe, which is why we issued the ground stop. In regard to speed, we are going I think at the- at the right speed, we- we have to get off old network, old telecom. By the way, that's why I've already switched over 70 percent of copper to fiber without incident, without issue. Almost 470 radios have been switched over. New- new- new electronic flight strips and towers. We're doing incredible work, and just- let's be clear about one thing.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.

SEC. DUFFY: For decades, this work in the FAA has not been done. It hasn't been done because it's hard. I don't want to be dishonest. It's a hard problem to solve. The Trump administration, with my leadership, we are solving the problem. We're building and deploying new technology. One of the problems I have is I need more money to- to build a new--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.
SEC. DUFFY: --telecom network. I need new software, but we're doing the right thing by- by way of the American people by fixing this really really old system that was left to us.

MARGARET BRENNAN: But respectfully, the American people have put a lot of money into infrastructure upgrades. In 2021, it was $25 billion for upgrades under Biden. Under your administration, the Trump administration, as you just said, $12.5 billion for upgrades. Democrats say the lion's share of the money that was provided to you- you just have not obligated or spent. Why? And if the White House has allowed for reprogramming of funds, why do you keep saying Congress is stopping you from spending the money they're giving you?

SEC. DUFFY: So first off, there was a lot of money that was given to the FAA in the past, and I can't answer for other secretaries or other FAA administrators. A lot of money was given, not a lot of work was done. So when I asked for a massive amount of money to fix the system, what the Congress did is they said, "Okay, we'll give you a partial funding, $12.5 billion dollars," in One, Big Beautiful Bill. And they were very specific in how we spend it. Now I can't- I can't go buy radar off the shelf. This is a massive order. So we've asked those who won the contract, I want them to build the radar in America. They'll start to deliver those radar to us in the spring. All of them will be deployed by the end of 2028. So all that money hasn't been spent, but it's been obligated to radar. Radio is the same thing. I'm buying radios, but they're not on the shelf. They have to be built. They specifically said how I spend the money, and I've- and I've got it all spent, ready to be deployed by the end of the- the president's tenure in office. But what I don't have money for is a new telecom system. I don't have money for new software. Those- those are critical pieces to the infrastructure, and it's been historically underinvested in. I'm making the case to the American people and the Congress. For the first time, the FAA is taking your money, and we're actually building with your money. Let me continue. Let's finish the job. Let's not see what happened on Friday. Let's not let it happen again
MARGARET BRENNAN: Is $50 billion the total ask?--
SEC. DUFFY: Let's make sure we keep the American people safe- yeah, $50 billion.
MARGARET BRENNAN: All right, Mr. Secretary. I'm told you have to get to another network. Thank you for your time this morning. 'Face the Nation' will be back in one minute. Stay with us.

title: Transcript: Rep. Jim Himes on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Nov. 15, 2026
summary: The following is the transcript of the interview with Rep. Jim Himes, Democrat of Connecticut, that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Nov. 15, 2026.
story: The following is the transcript of the interview with Rep. Jim Himes, Democrat of Connecticut, that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Nov. 15, 2026.

MARGARET BRENNAN: We're joined now by the top Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee, Connecticut Congressman Jim Himes, who joins us from Greenwich. Good morning, Congressman. You just heard the secretary ask for $50 billion in funding for upgrades. There are 16 working days left in the House. Are you going to consider that funding request?

REP. JIM HIMES: Yeah. Well, Margaret. I mean, look, you- you- you had the right question. This is not a Congress money problem. You pointed out that there was $50 billion sent in the Biden administration and 12 and a half billion appropriated that has not been obligated. For the American people watching, obligated is a fancy D.C. word for spent, right? So this is not immediately a spending problem. It is a prioritization problem, and it's payback, by the way, for you remember when Elon Musk was standing on a stage spinning his chainsaw around, cutting government willy-nilly. Well, part of that chainsaw got 1,300 employees of the FAA to resign or to retire. They fired 400 probationary employees. These are the technical specialists and the maintenance people. So what you're seeing here, apart from a lack of prioritization of improving our- our- our FAA system, what you're seeing is the wages of what Elon Musk did, where he just gutted an entity that- that affected millions of Americans last Friday.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So you're a no on the 50 billion?

REP. HIMES: Well, no, I'm not a no. Look, if- if- if- if they- I'm not on the transportation committee. But if they came and said- my first question would be, well, what about that other 12 and a half million that's sitting in your bank account right now? How about if you spend that before we- we put more money in that bank account?

MARGARET BRENNAN: Understood. I want to ask you about what is happening with this arms race with China and chips. You were one of the rest of the Gang of Eight who were briefed this past week on what is going on with Nvidia, that chip maker. CBS has reported U.S. intelligence agencies believe Alice Huang, the Megaspeed CEO who was linked to Jensen Huang of Nvidia, was indeed an asset of China's Ministry of State Security. However, when President Trump was asked about the scandal, he put it this way:
[START SOUND ON TAPE]

PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: The big thing is: was the woman a spy? And I don't know if that's been determined yet. But if the woman was a spy, yes. If the woman was not a spy, perhaps it would be different.
[END SOUND ON TAPE]
MARGARET BRENNAN: So, how certain is U.S. intelligence that she was an asset of Chinese intelligence, and is that the central issue?

REP. HIMES: Margaret, I don't- I don't even know how to respond to the president's statement. Remember, it was March when- March or April when the Secretary of State Marco Rubio circulated a memo to all of the senior people, including presumably the White House, saying we have concerns that this woman is a spy. It is now November, and the President of the United States had no interest in understanding whether, in this most essential technology, the technology which could end millions of jobs or cure cancer, and/or create, you know, a real tool for terrorists and, you know, I mean, the fact that the president in November is saying we don't know if she's a spy that- that actually sort of perfectly illustrates my concern. Now, here's what I can tell you based on what I know. I don't think that we know. I don't think that we know. And when we say spy, spy is a pretty imprecise term, right? It's possible, based on what I know, that Alice Huang had no idea that she was maybe being monitored or- or- or working for the Chinese. That's possible. We don't know the answer to that question. It's also possible on the other end of the spectrum that she was a fully paid up, you know, intelligence asset and actually communicating. But the point of all of this is, how is it possible that we don't know this around the single most important technology of our lifetime? So, as you might imagine, Margaret, I'm going to spend a lot of time getting to the bottom of this, and I'm happy to report that actually, as you've observed, Republicans in Congress are interested too.

MARGARET BRENNAN: They are indeed. You referenced there a memo CNN reported Marco Rubio, as national security adviser and secretary of state, drafted this based on CIA intelligence, and then briefed the president. It also drew on intercepted communications between Alice Huang and Jensen Huang. Has that memo been shared with the Gang of Eight?

REP. HIMES: That memo has not been shared, and again, the only information that has come our way, and I'm speaking, I think, on behalf of the whole Congress here, because I was with the Gang of Eight last week. The only information that has come our way was sort of a glancing, not on the agenda discussion in that meeting. So we have a lot of work to do. But I mean, the fundamental question is: number one, has the FBI, and I don't know the answer to this question, the FBI, as you know, is the entity that does this counterintelligence work, figuring out what Alice Huang is and what she sent to the Chinese, if anything, right? We don't know that. We don't know if they launched an investigation. We're worried about it, right? Because the president, his buddy buddies, and apparently Howard Lutnick, the commerce secretary, who has responsibility for keeping chips that could help build you know Chinese AI out of China. You know these guys are palling around. Jensen Huang is, you know, writing $25 million checks for the ballroom. We got to get to the bottom of this, and we haven't even begun to get the facts we need here.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Two law enforcement sources told CBS that DOJ's National Security Division is investigating Megaspeed. That's the Singapore company that Alice Huang was CEO of. She's since left that position, as I understand it, and they're looking at that. But it sounds like you are also saying Jensen Huang needs to be looked at with more scrutiny here, and whether he was indeed a target. If- if he was a target of Chinese intelligence, why wouldn't the United States tell him that?

REP. HIMES: Well, let's take that piece by piece. Megaspeed is an entity that sort of didn't exist 10 years ago in any meaningful way, and now they appear, and I want to say appear, to be doing possibly two things. Number one, they may be a way of getting these chips to China. You know, Nvidia could sell them to Megaspeed, Megaspeed gives them to China. Or more interestingly, and we know that this goes on, China wants to train its models so it doesn't even buy the chips, but it just uses Megaspeed's data centers, right? So China is, you know, training up their frontier models simply online, if you will, right? So that's the question around Megaspeed. The question around Alice Huang is what, you know, was she a witting agent of the Chinese government, or was she just sort of being monitored? And then the really important question is what information, and- and this is where you know Mr. Huang, Jensen Huang comes in. What information made its way from the CEO, Jensen, to her, to the Chinese? What influence was exerted, right? I mean, if you look at the behavior of the Commerce Department in particular, it looked like somebody was standing up for Nvidia. Why? Was that influence on the part of Jensen Huang, $25 million in money handed over for a ballroom sounds like a pretty good way to build influence to me, at least.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Has Secretary Lutnick, whose Commerce Department would be in charge of overseeing some of this, did he respond to your request to meet with the Intelligence Committee?

REP. HIMES: Well, that- that request just went out Friday of last week, so you know he- he will respond. And as you probably know, there's also been a bipartisan request for him to appear in the Banking Committee in the Senate. But again, if you read the reporting here, it looks like he has been the barrier inside the government to stopping the flow of these Nvidia chips to China, and the question is, why?

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, sort of to that point, I want to ask you about what the treasury secretary, if I could ask you to put your financial services hat on for a moment here and bridge both worlds. The treasury secretary was on Fox this morning, and he floated that more Nvidia executives should be removed. He said there's a culture of non-compliance that might need to be looked at, and whether they boosted potentially illicit sales of chips. He- which sort of suggests as part of a larger smuggling operation that you may have just touched on there. And he cited reporting that only 1% of the computer chips imported to Singapore stayed there, even though Nvidia said Singapore accounted for 20% of their sales. Now, if a bank were entangled in those kind of activities, there would be very strong action taken. What action needs to be taken here in terms of answering all these questions the treasury secretary just laid out?

REP. HIMES: Yeah, yeah. So I mean, let's be super clear here, right? Nvidia makes chips. They get wealthy when they sell chips. So of course they have an incentive to sell these chips to the Chinese. That's nothing new. Lots of companies would love to sell everything to the Chinese. It's the government's job, it is the commerce secretary's job, and the president's job to stop that from happening through things like the entity list, which you know prohibit American companies from doing business with anybody on that entity list. Lo and behold, Megaspeed was not on that entity list. Actually, the treasury secretary has been saying that. But yes, what you're talking about, were banks facilitating a smuggling operation. I don't know what the treasury secretary was talking about, but yes, it should not just be Jensen Huang. It needs to be his people who apparently were doing exactly everything that he- that- that they were told to do. It needs to be the commerce secretary who was not doing apparently, according to the treasury secretary, enough. And yes, if banks were facilitating this stuff, they too, you know, need to be called to account.

MARGARET BRENNAN: The treasury secretary was very clear that enforcement comes to commerce, and that commerce was not taking the action there. We have to leave it there, Congressman. Thank you for your time this morning. We'll be right back.

title: Judge temporarily blocks closing of historic D.C. golf course
summary: U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes ruled that the Trump administration cannot close East Potomac Park in Washington, D.C., for now.
story: Washington — President Trump says his administration will appeal a federal judge's move to temporarily block the closure of a historic golf course and park in Washington, D.C., that Mr. Trump wants to overhaul into a new "world class championship" course.

U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes on Saturday ruled that the Trump administration cannot close East Potomac Park and its golf course, but said that the Trump administration was not required to actively manage either.

She sided with a D.C. preservation group and two local golfers who argued that closure of East Potomac Park, set for Sunday, Nov. 15, was part of the Trump administration's plan to redesign and replace the course with a championship-style venue designed by golf course architect Tom Fazio.
Mr. Trump said in a social media post on Sunday that the golf course is in "a terrible state of disrepair" and it needs work.

"They don't call it Trash Island for no reason! Why would a judge want to delay taking a terrible and very unsafe golf course, one that is mocked all over D.C.(and far beyond!), instead of quickly turning it into a great and admired one?" he wrote. "'INTERIOR' has the absolute right to do so, and will immediately appeal, on an expedited basis, this highly destructive and political decision of the judge. Time is of the essence, or golf seasons, jobs, prestige, and much money, will be lost!"

Reyes said that the Trump administration's justifications for the proposed course closures were pretextual, and said, "the Government reverse-engineers additional justifications for the Park's closure… All while it continues to assert that it will close the Park to follow the President's directive."
Her order will last until Nov. 28.

"We are grateful that once again, a court has intervened to prevent irreparable harm caused by the Trump-Vance administration's pursuit of another one of the president's vanity projects," said Catherine Carroll, senior legal adviser at Democracy Forward. "The administration's inexplicable drive to destroy East Potomac Park would have taken away a treasured park that could never be replaced, and we are honored to work with this coalition to secure this temporary relief."

"The Court has acknowledged that the National Park Service can limit access to its facilities where the public is at risk of harm," a Department of Justice spokesperson told CBS News. "Nothing in the Court's order precludes planning for the development of a world class golf course to continue. The Department of Justice will always vociferously defend the Trump Administration's agenda in court."

Reyes has for months been overseeing a challenge to the president's plans for East Potomac Golf Links, a public course in Washington that opened in the 1920s. The dispute escalated last month when the National Park Service notified the judge that it would be removing trees on the course and went on to cut down more than 500 trees in the span of a weekend.

Reyes then issued an order blocking the Trump administration from felling any additional trees, and required the Justice Department to provide her with notice of any future actions the National Park Service planned to take at the golf course.

Mr. Trump, meanwhile, announced last month that East Potomac would close Nov. 15 to allow work on the new design by Fazio to begin, with the renovated "world-class, championship course" expected to open in roughly 15 months.

But in a court hearing Friday, Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward said he "would be shocked to learn there is a contract" with Fazio or any affiliated entities finalizing the new course plans and future construction.

Following Mr. Trump's announcement, the Justice Department notified the court late last month that the Interior Department was working on a plan to close the course and would also temporarily shut off the public's access to all of East Potomac Park, which encompasses not only the golf course, but also a road, playground and recreational space.

The Trump administration argued that the entirety of the park had to be closed because of a deteriorating sea wall, safety risks at the golf course, and because the organization that was overseeing the course, the National Links Trust, would cease operating it as of Nov. 15.

There is no plan currently in place to fix the sea wall, according to the National Park Service, and it's unclear how long East Potomac Park will be closed for. The new sea wall is expected to cost more than $300 million and take at least two-and-a-half years to complete, according to a proposal for the new golf course that the National Park Service submitted to the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts last week.
The Trump administration said in a notice published Friday that it will be soliciting a contract for work related to 20,700 linear feet of shortline and sea wall infrastructure.

Lawyers for the preservation group and golfers said the Trump administration had manufactured a situation where the course would no longer have an operator, the National Links Trust, as of Nov. 15, and found areas of disrepair in East Potomac Park that needed to be fixed, effectively reverse-engineering the decision to close the area.

Reyes, too, pushed the Justice Department on whether Mr. Trump's order to shutter the park to overhaul the golf course was the real reason for the Nov. 15 closure date, or whether it was because of a longstanding need for repairs at the park, and the Trump administration was simply closing the park to effectuate those fixes.

"If this is such an emergent situation… why wasn't [East Potomac] closed immediately?" Reyes asked the government, noting that thousands of runners participating in the Marine Corps Marathon ran through East Potomac Park just last month.
Fazio's new course design shows it taking up the entirety of East Potomac Park, eliminating the existing road around the peninsula and recreational space at its southern end.
Adam Gustafson, a Justice Department lawyer, said that the government has "limited resources and discretion" and "when the president talks, the agencies listen."
"The agency has said consistently that it will comply with the law in reaching a final position on the deposition of this park," Gustafson said.

He argued that closing the park does not mean the Trump administration will immediately begin renovating the course, since the National Park Service still has to continue a legal analysis and assessments under federal environmental and historic preservation laws. The Commission of Fine Arts and National Capital Planning Commission must also conduct their own reviews, Gustafson said.
The NCPC is set to consider the proposal for the new course at a Dec. 3 meeting.

Separately, Reyes has also opened an inquiry into whether top Trump administration officials in the Department of Interior, Justice Department, and National Park Service misrepresented facts to her in recent court hearings and documents and violated ethics rules.

Reyes said she intends to appoint a former U.S. attorney in Washington, D.C., Jessie Liu, to lead the probe, which will include whether government lawyers told Jessica Bowron, the acting director of the National Park Service, and Kevin Griess, superintendent of National Mall and Memorial Parks, to omit or include certain information in declarations about work at the golf course.
The Justice Department opposes the appointment of a special master.

title: Ground stop shows "we have to get off old network," Duffy says
summary: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said that "we have to get off old network, old telecom" after a telecommunication outage led to a nationwide ground stop on Friday.
story: Washington — Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Sunday that "we have to get off old network, old telecom" after a telecommunication outage that officials said stemmed from overloaded routers prompted the Federal Aviation Administration to order a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday.
"For decades, this work in the FAA has not been done. It hasn't been done because it's hard," Duffy said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."

The ground stop resulted in thousands of canceled flights and stranded travelers, creating chaos in the nation's airports at the start of the weekend. Officials said that FAA telecommunications contractor L3Harris Technologies had performed maintenance updates at a remote facility to replace aging copper communications lines with fiber optic connections. And as the router was being switched, it started flooding other routers and overloaded the system.

Duffy said the FAA is looking into why, when it conducted the installation in El Dorado, Arkansas, it started to broadcast data, but also why a second issue occurred at a facility in Amarillo, Texas, where work had been conducted weeks earlier. He said along with L3Harris, which operates and owns the network, the FAA is on site and the FBI is offering support.

"We're looking at that right now, and when we know what the root cause of this issue was — was it the install from L3Harris, was it the router — I'm going to tell you and the American people what we find," he said.

Duffy said for the telecom in El Dorado, it was an old copper wire that had become unusable. He said, "We were forced by the telecom provider to actually update that copper to fiber, and we brought in our routers and did the work. And that's when we saw the flooding of the network."
"So this is part of our maintenance that we do on this really old architecture of a telecom network," Duffy said.

The transportation secretary said the work was done "appropriately," noting that it's been done thousands of times and "this has never happened." He explained that normally, work is done on big facilities overnight. But for remote locations, that work can be conducted during the day, "Because the risk, historically, has been very low."
"Obviously, on Friday we saw no; it flooded our network, and we had to take the extraordinary step of issuing a ground stop," he said.

Duffy stressed that upgrades are necessary, saying the system should be "built brand new," while noting that "the rest of the world — every institution, every company, not just in the U.S. but around the world — they've all switched over to digital and fiber."

The transportation secretary said over 70% of copper lines have been switched over to fiber "without incident," pointing to almost 470 radios having been switched over and new electronic flight strips and towers.

On Friday, Duffy said the FAA needs $50 billion from Congress to overhaul the telecom network. On Sunday, Duffy reiterated his pitch, saying that although the FAA received funds when Congress allocated money under the One Big Beautiful Bill, Congress was "very specific in how we spend it."

"They specifically said how I spend the money, and I've and I've got it all spent, ready to be deployed by the end of the president's tenure in office," Duffy said. "But what I don't have money for is a new telecom system. I don't have money for new software. Those are critical pieces to the infrastructure, and it's been historically underinvested in."

Duffy said he is "making the case to the American people and the Congress — for the first time, the FAA is taking your money, and we're actually building with your money. Let me continue. Let's finish the job, let's not see what happened on Friday — let's not let it happen again."
President Trump also weighed in on Sunday, urging Congress to approve the funding.

"Much of our current air control system is 50 years old - RIDICULOUS!" he said in a post on Truth Social. "We have already started the work, but it should be done all at once, not in drips and drabs. Congress must approve."
Rep. Jim Himes, a Connecticut Democrat who also appeared on "Face the Nation" on Sunday, said, "This is not a Congress money problem."
Himes pointed to the One Big Beautiful Bill funds, saying, "How about if you spend that before we put more money in that bank account?
"This is not immediately a spending problem," he said. "It is a prioritization problem."

As for the continued impacts of Friday's ground stop, Duffy said, "We have some delays in the airspace right now, but as we look to the end of the day and into tomorrow, we should be running at full capacity."
Duffy said, with airplanes and crews out of position due to the ground stop, "It takes a little bit of time for the airlines to get back and choreographed and at full capacity and operations."
"But we're well on our way," he said.

title: Army whistleblower alleges officials ignored warnings before Kuwait attack
summary: Maj. Stephen Ramsbottom filed a complaint with Congress on Friday, saying Army leaders dismissed concerns about a U.S. command post in Kuwait. He will appear on 60 Minutes tonight.
story: A U.S. Army soldier who survived a deadly Iranian drone attack filed a whistleblower complaint to Congress alleging senior military officials ignored warnings and did not plan properly for anti-drone defenses ahead of the war with Iran.

The whistleblower, Army Maj. Stephen Ramsbottom, spoke exclusively with 60 Minutes' Norah O'Donnell about his complaint, which was submitted to the House and Senate Armed Services Committees on Friday and obtained by CBS News.

He alleges Army leaders dismissed concerns over thin fortifications at a U.S. command post in Kuwait where six American soldiers were killed by an Iranian drone in the first 24 hours of the conflict, the deadliest attack on U.S. troops in the war.
The complaint also claims the post — known as Port Shuaiba — "had no physician, no fixed aid station, and only one ambulance."

"I feel this is a tactical failure by the Army, our leadership, and myself — all the way down to my level," Maj. Ramsbottom told 60 Minutes. "We just did not plan this well, and this needs to be a lesson that we learn."

Ramsbottom spoke with 60 Minutes as part of an eight-month investigation into the March 1 attack at the command post, known as Port Shuaiba. The day after the attack, in a press conference, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth insisted the troops there were well protected.

"Every once in a while you might have one, unfortunately, we call it a squirter that makes its way through," Hegseth said. "And in that particular case it happened to hit a tactical operations center that was fortified. But these are powerful weapons."

The eyewitness accounts, along with photos and videos of the attack's aftermath, offer a staggering look at the thinly fortified Kuwaiti port facility when it was hit one day after the U.S. and Israel launched Operation Epic Fury.

Sen. Richard Blumenthal, a Democrat from Connecticut and the ranking member on the Senate's Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, issued a series of demands to Hegseth after reviewing the whistleblower complaint.

In a letter dated Nov. 15, the senator called on Hegseth to appear in a classified briefing and provide "all force protection assessments" for Port Shuaiba. Democrats have signaled they will probe the administration's handling of the war with Iran when they retake both houses of Congress next year.
"The families of the six fallen servicemembers, the wounded survivors, and the American people deserve transparency and accountability," wrote Blumenthal.
A Pentagon spokesperson declined to comment on Ramsbottom's allegations, including on whether adequate force protection was in place at Port Shuaiba.
This story published first on CBS News at 11:07 a.m. on Nov. 15, 2026.

title: Outcome of Alaska Senate race could take weeks to determine
summary: The Senate race in Alaska, which has garnered widespread attention with two candidates named Dan Sullivan, remains in limbo.
story: Washington — The Senate race in Alaska remains unresolved more than 10 days after Election Day as a contest that has garnered widespread attention over the two candidates named Dan Sullivan faces a lengthy ballot-counting process.

Incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola are facing off in the race, which also has two other candidates on the ballot: an independent candidate and retired teacher Daniel J. Sullivan, and another Republican, Gerald Heikes.
With 97% of the vote in as of Sunday, Nov. 15, the race is leaning Democratic, according to CBS News estimates, with Peltola's lead growing to more than 3 percentage points ahead of Sen. Sullivan.

The count in Alaska could stretch on. Alaska has a ranked-choice voting system, which allows voters to rank as many or as few candidates as they'd like in order of preference. If no candidate secures support from more than 50% of voters as their top choice, the count goes to a second round.

The ranked-choice tabulation doesn't occur until the last counting of ballots 15 days after Election Day, meaning the process could drag on for weeks if one candidate does not secure more than 50% of first-place support on the ballot.

The results in Alaska will come after Democrats already secured enough seats to take control of the Senate, winning in several states that President Trump won by double digits in 2024. It is the final Senate race to be decided, after the seat in Mississippi went to Democrat Scott Colom by a narrow margin.
Speaking to reporters in the early hours after Election Day, Peltola said, "The results are not going to be fast."
"But Alaskans are patient," she said. "We just want to make sure the folks [in] the Lower 48 know it won't be hours, it won't be days, it will be weeks."
Sen. Sullivan likewise emphasized to supporters, "We're going to have a long night," adding, "We're probably going to have some long weeks."

title: Van Hollen will challenge Schumer for Senate majority leader
summary: Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland announced Thursday that he will challenge Sen. Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader.
story: Washington — Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland announced Thursday that he will challenge Sen. Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader.

"In this election, Americans called on us to unrig an economy rigged against working people & fueled by political corruption. To deliver, we need new leadership. This isn't about any one person – it's about answering that call," Van Hollen said in a post on X. "That's why I'm running for Senate Majority Leader."

The decision by Van Hollen, who said earlier this week he was in "listening mode" about running for majority leader, marks the most significant step by a high-profile Democrat to challenge the party's existing leadership since it decisively won last week's midterms.

Independent Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont quickly threw his support behind Van Hollen on Thursday. Some other Democrats have not yet committed to voting for Schumer in leadership elections, which are expected early next month, but haven't explicitly endorsed another candidate.

Van Hollen, 67, has been in the Senate since 2017 after representing the state in the House for more than a decade. The Maryland Democrat has gained attention from progressives in recent years. In 2024, he vocally supported restricting weapons shipments to Israel and criticized the Biden administration's posture toward the war in Gaza. Van Hollen also gained attention when he traveled to El Salvador last year to meet with Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran national who lived in Maryland and had been sent to the country's notorious CECOT prison.

Supporters see Van Hollen as someone who's willing to speak to the issues progressives hold most dear. Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed told NPR in an interview this week that Van Hollen is "willing to take risks when it matters," citing his trip to El Salvador.
Schumer, 75, responded to Van Hollen's announcement in a post on X, saying he welcomes "any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead."

"I'm proud of what we've accomplished together — 55 seats and counting is an amazing result — and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader," he wrote. "I look forward to leading our new Democratic majority and delivering for the American people."
Schumer has led Senate Democrats since 2017, when he succeeded retiring Sen. Harry Reid of Nevada.
Democratic Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand of New York, who chairs the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, defended Schumer at a news conference earlier this week, crediting his "strategic leadership."

"You will see, despite all the grumblings, enormous gratitude for the hard work he has done to get us to this position," Gillibrand said. "We are about to win nine Senate seats — that has never happened in my political history."

Democratic Sen. Jacky Rosen of Nevada endorsed Schumer late Thursday, praising his work ahead of the midterms and writing, "I know he has the experience and the fight to continue leading our diverse caucus at this crucial moment."

The challenge comes as Schumer is still widely expected to hold on to the top leadership post, especially after the strong showing for Democrats in the midterm elections. Despite a Senate map that appeared unfavorable for the party heading into the cycle, Democrats flipped at least eight Senate seats — with one race remaining up in the air in Alaska — securing a sizable majority in the new Congress.

With the election results, Schumer has appeared to improve his position with the caucus, following a tumultuous tenure in recent years. The pushback took hold after the New York Democrat maneuvered to avoid a government shutdown in early 2025, prompting frustration from his party's left flank.
Later that year, he changed course and kept Democrats largely united through a record-breaking government shutdown as they sought to prevent the expiration of health insurance tax credits.

In an interview with MS NOW announcing his run for majority leader, Van Hollen acknowledged he is an "underdog," but said he has spoken with caucus members and believes the race is "very much in flux."

Asked what he would do differently from Schumer, Van Hollen suggested the current leader hasn't taken a firm enough stance on using the power of the purse to force the Trump administration to end the Iran war. He told host Jen Psaki that Democrats should use the Dec. 11 deadline to fund the government as leverage, saying it "should not be a finger-in-the-wind issue."
Van Hollen also criticized Schumer for, in his view, moving behind the scenes to back certain candidates in Democratic primaries — a longstanding point of contention for progressives.

"On the political side of the equation, we shouldn't have a Democratic leader who is getting involved in picking sides in open Democratic primaries. … We have two senators right now in the United States Senate who wouldn't be there if the current majority leader had his way," Van Hollen said, referring to El-Sayed and Minnesota Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan.
Some members of the Democratic caucus — including both progressives like Sanders and moderates like Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton of Kansas — have called for new leadership.

Sanders endorsed Van Hollen in a social media post late Thursday, writing: "The American people voted for change. They want a Democratic Party that will stand up to powerful special interests, take on the billionaire class and fight for working families."

Two days earlier, Sanders announced in a news conference he would not support Schumer. Sanders was flanked by the more moderate Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan, who said she was "not actively seeking this job" but is "seeking change."
"Whoever wants my vote is going to have to show me a concrete plan that's definitively different," Slotkin said. "I'm a no until and unless I see that from anyone."

title: Hegseth awards medal to soldier who reprimanded group near tomb
summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth awarded a medal to the service member who reprimanded his group for making noise at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier​.
story: Washington — Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth awarded a medal on Thursday to the service member who reprimanded his group for making noise at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier on Veterans Day.

Hegseth posted a series of photos on X with the soldier, Spc. Thomas Iglesias, and other members of the unit who guard the tomb at Arlington National Cemetery around the clock. One of the photos showed Hegseth pinning a medal to Iglesias' chest.
"We love soldiers. We love standards. Well done, Specialist," Hegseth wrote. "Carry on Patriots."
We love soldiers.We love standards.Well done, Specialist.Carry on Patriots. pic.twitter.com/Uk6ek6oOso

A Pentagon official said Hegseth "welcomed the 3rd U.S. Infantry Regiment, the Old Guard, to the Pentagon where he proudly awarded Specialist Iglesias the Joint Service Commendation Medal for the execution of his duties at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier on November 11, 2026."

Iglesias was guarding the tomb following a Veterans Day event that included Hegseth, President Trump and other administration officials. Footage showed Hegseth, his wife, his chief of staff and other aides posing for photos near the tomb. Someone laughed, and Iglesias shouted: "All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times."

In the aftermath, Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell told CBS News: "The Secretary and the entire Department have always honored-and will always honor-the sacrifices our military men and women have made to keep America safe. While commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum."

Soldiers reminding visitors to maintain decorum at the tomb is not uncommon. One member of the regiment that guards the tomb said in an Army interview in 2022 that sentinels react to the crowd two or three times per day.

title: Right whale population drops, alarming scientists
summary: The population of one of the world's rarest whales has fallen after trending upward in recent years, worrying scientists who fear the animal could still be at risk of extinction.
story: Portland, Maine — The population of one of the world's rarest whales has fallen after trending upward in recent years, worrying scientists who fear the animal could still be at risk of extinction.

The North Atlantic right whale now numbers 382 animals, according to a consortium of scientists that released its annual population estimate for them on Monday. That represents about a 2% decline from last year's estimate of 384, which was an increase of 2.1% from the previous year and showed the continuation of a prior slow but steady climb in the whales' population.

The whales were decimated by centuries of commercial whaling that mostly ended in the 1930s. The enormous animals have been slow to recover, and today are threatened by entanglement in fishing gear and collisions with ships.

Those threats, combined with a warming ocean, have conspired to hold the population down, said Heather Pettis, chair of the North Atlantic Right Whale Consortium. Pettis said the warming of the ocean has caused the whales' food — tiny organisms called copepods — to move, and the whales have followed them into areas of ocean not protected from ship strikes and entanglements.

"We know that this population can and will move around to find food and if we aren't protecting them throughout their range, we may see another situation where we have this tremendous decline again," Pettis said.

The whales' population fell about 25% from 2010 to 2020 during a time when years of poor reproduction coincided with high mortality. Recent years have been slightly more encouraging, but scientists and conservationists have warned that the whales need years of high birth counts coupled with new protections to have a chance to rebuild.
Stronger safeguards needed, environmental groups say

The loss in population last year underscores the need to spare the whales from entanglements and ship strikes, said Nora Ives, a marine scientist on the environmental group Oceana's right whale campaign.

Oceana was one of several environmental groups that opposed a proposal in Congress to delay new right whale protections until 2035. The proposal, which has passed the House of Representatives, is intended to protect commercial fishing interests from regulations that members of the industry describe as burdensome.

"The latest numbers are disappointing and make the road to recovery longer for critically endangered North Atlantic right whales. This iconic whale will not escape extinction if its population cannot grow," Ives said.

The right whales, which can weigh 150,000 pounds, give birth off the Carolinas, Florida and Georgia in the winter and venture north to feeding grounds off New England and Canada. Large groups of the animals that sometimes include a fifth of the entire population are sometimes seen off Massachusetts in spring. Last year was one of the most successful calving seasons on record, with more than 20 babies born.

The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration has said the last nine years have also been a time of unusually high numbers of injuries and deaths for the whales. The population is down to just 73 reproductive females, which makes replenishing the stock difficult.

They were hunted heavily because they tend to live fairly close to shore and floated when killed, and they yielded a high volume of oil. Some sources say they got their common name from the perception that they were the "right" whale to hunt.

title: SpaceX pulls off first Starship recovery from orbit in spectacular fashion
summary: It was the first recovery of a Starship from orbit, a major milestone for a rocket SpaceX founder Elon Musk says will dramatically lower launch costs.
story: After a 22-hour stay in space, a SpaceX Starship rocket plunged back to Earth Saturday, enduring the blazing heat of reentry while homing in on its Texas Gulf Coast launch site, flipping vertical at the last moment and settling into the grasp of two huge mechanical arms on its launch gantry.

Throngs of SpaceX employees gathered nearby cheered and applauded as the rocket restarted three of its six methane-fueled Raptor engines to flip upright, rapidly slowing to a near hover as the robot arms moved in for a mechanical embrace, catching the rocket a moment before engine shutdown.

"This is so incredible to see!" said SpaceX commentator Jessie Anderson. "One of the most incredible and historic engineering feats of all time has just happened right in front of our eyes. Congratulations to our teammates at SpaceX, and to everyone who supported the Starship program."

It was the first such recovery of a Starship from orbit — previous test flights ended with planned ocean splashdowns — marking a major milestone in SpaceX's drive to develop the first fully reusable orbit-class rocket, a vehicle company founder Elon Musk says will dramatically lower the cost of launching payloads to Earth orbit, the moon and, eventually, Mars.

The Starship was launched atop a Super Heavy booster Friday using the same pad at SpaceX's Starbase facility on the Texas coast. Standing 407 feet tall, the two-stage rocket is the most powerful launcher ever built, generating some 16 million pounds of thrust at liftoff from 33 first-stage Raptor engines.
After propelling the Starship upper stage out of the lower atmosphere, the Super Heavy first stage attempted its own return to the launch site for capture by the gantry's mechanical arms.

Going into the giant rocket's 15th test flight, SpaceX had successfully recovered the first-stage boosters used in three previous launches. But the Super Heavy launched Friday was diverted to an offshore splashdown because of a guidance problem. The vehicle ran out of fuel and exploded moments before hitting the water.

While a disappointment to the SpaceX team, Musk said in a posting on the social media platform X the problem was a "slight underperformance of engines," adding that "these early ships and boosters are already outdated by improved designs in production or on the test stand."
"This booster loss does not change our timeline to reach high volume, fully reusable Starship flights," he said.
The Starship upper stage did not disappoint.

Beaming down crystal-clear views from cameras mounted on its steering fins, the spacecraft's belly, covered in heat-shield tiles, glowed red as the ship heated up in a fireball of atmospheric friction.

Crossing the Baja Peninsula and then northern Mexico, the big rocket rapidly descended before flying just north of the launch site, banking and dropping belly first out of low clouds, restarting its engines to flip upright and then falling at an angle toward the gantry, slowing to a near standstill as the arms closed around it.

"The room behind me going absolutely insane," SpaceX commentator Dan Huot said from the mission control center. "These people have done so much to earn this. ... I mean, that was the missing link. That was the holy grail of spaceflight, plummeting through fire to be snatched out of the air by steel. We caught a Starship, and now everything changes."

But SpaceX will need to successfully launch and recover a large number of Super Heavy-Starships to demonstrate the statistical reliability needed for crewed flights. And the company will need to demonstrate its ability to autonomously refuel Starships in Earth orbit and keep their propellants from boiling away in the space environment.

While the system is designed to be fully reusable, the Starship upper stage uses most of its propellant getting into Earth orbit. NASA wants to use a variant of the Starship to carry astronauts to the lunar surface in 2028 and multiple Super Heavy-tanker flights will be needed to refuel the lander in Earth orbit before it can head for the moon.

SpaceX plans to begin orbital fueling tests in the next several Super Heavy-Starship flights. But the rocket's development has taken longer than initially expected and the space agency is now hedging its bets, saying it's open to using Blue Origin's Blue Moon Mark 2 lander depending on which spacecraft is ready in time.

title: Vulcan rocket fails in major setback for United Launch Alliance
summary: The loss of its new Vulcan rocket was the first outright failure for United Launch Alliance, a major setback in the commercial launch industry.
story: In a major setback for United Launch Alliance, the company's new heavy-lift Vulcan rocket carrying 40 Amazon Leo internet satellites malfunctioned during the climb to space on Sunday, dooming the payload and throwing a costly wrench into both companies' launch schedules.

"Based on data received by our Launch Director, we confirm that the Vulcan vehicle launched from Space Launch Complex 41 (at the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station) suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit," ULA said in a statement some 50 minutes after liftoff.
"We will work closely with our customer and other appropriate organizations to find the cause, determine the appropriate corrective action and return to flight as quickly as possible."
It was the first outright failure of a United Launch Alliance rocket since the company, a partnership between Boeing and Lockheed Martin, was formed in 2006.

It wasn't immediately known what went wrong, but the Vulcan, the rocket replacing ULA's fleet of Atlas 5 rockets, will face a potentially significant grounding while engineers review telemetry and implement fixes for whatever caused the mishap.

"There is risk with any launch, and that's especially true for inaugural missions like LV-01," Amazon Leo said in a post on X, using a designation meaning Leo Vulcan flight 1. "ULA has been a trusted partner for Amazon, and we believe they'll learn from this mission and deliver on their long-term plans for Vulcan."

It was only the fifth flight of a Vulcan rocket and the first in nine months as ULA and booster-supplier Northrop Grumman worked to resolve problems with nozzles used by strap-on solid-fuel boosters that marred two earlier flights.

The solids appeared to work normally Sunday, helping boost the rocket out of the dense lower atmosphere before burning out and falling away. The two methane-burning BE-4 engines powering the Vulcan's first stage then continued the climb toward orbit, but they appeared to fire longer than expected based on ULA's pre-launch timeline.

After stage separation, the Vulcan's hydrogen-fueled Centaur upper stage engines took over for a planned 12-minute and 15-second burn. According to ULA's update, something went wrong during that Centaur firing, but no additional details were immediately provided.

Sunday's launch was the first of 38 Vulcan flights purchased by Amazon to launch its Leo satellites, designed to compete head-to-head with Elon Musk's Starlink and other space-based internet providers. ULA has already launched eight Leo flights using Atlas 5 rockets.

Amazon has also booked 24 Leo launches aboard Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket, 24 aboard the European Ariane 6, and 13 aboard SpaceX's Falcon 9. More than 3,300 Leo satellites will be needed to complete the constellation. Sunday's flight would have pushed the total number launched to date to 436.
But it was not to be.

Instead, Amazon Leo will now have to wait on ULA's failure investigation to run its course before trying again with a Vulcan. The company also is waiting for Jeff Bezos-owned Blue Origin to get its New Glenn rocket flying again after a catastrophic on-pad explosion last May.

That failure was caused by a problem with an oxygen valve in one of New Glenn's seven BE-4 first-stage engines. The BE-4, also built by Blue Origin, powers the Vulcan's first stage, but the engines used Sunday had been retrofitted with a fix by Blue Origin engineers.

While the cause of the failure is not yet publicly known, "ULA is committed to full transparency with our customers, and they will have visibility into the investigation process, which utilizes rigorous methodology and corrective action," the company said.
NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman promised assistance if needed.

"Appreciate you quickly keeping the public and your partners informed," Isaacman wrote on the social media platform X. "The team at @NASA is available to assist in all matters related to the investigation and remediation effort. Artemis, Moon Base, and the nation need ULA. We are in your corner and here to help."

The 214-foot-tall Vulcan blasted off from pad 41 at the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station at 12:40 p.m. ET, thundering away on a northeasterly trajectory atop 3.8 million pounds of thrust from six Northrop Grumman strap-on solid-fuel boosters and two methane-burning BE-4s.

A launch attempt Friday was scrubbed after problems knocked out a gaseous nitrogen plant that serves multiple launch providers. Another delay was ordered Saturday because of network problems between the Vulcan and ground systems.

On Sunday, launch controllers called a hold at the T-minus 20-second mark because of an unexplained technical issue with the rocket. Re-targeting the end of the launch window, ULA resolved the problem, and the rocket roared to life and climbed away at the end of the launch window.
It's not yet known if the problem that interrupted the countdown played any role in the subsequent failure.

In any case, the strap-on boosters helped propel the rocket out of the dense lower atmosphere, burning out and falling away about a minute and 40 seconds after liftoff. But the first stage appeared to burn longer than called for in the company's pre-launch timeline.

The first stage also appeared to separate from the rocket's hydrogen-fueled Centaur upper stage later than expected, and telemetry-driven animation showed the Centaur making unusual orientation adjustments early in the burn.

ULA's launch commentators, however, did not mention any problems and the launch broadcast came to an end without confirming whether the Centaur's first planned engine firing went for the full duration.

ULA spent months working to resolve problems with the strap-on booster nozzles that occurred during two earlier flights, one in 2024 and the other this past February. While ULA was free to proceed with commercial flights, the U.S. Space Force put Vulcan launches of national security payloads on hold pending further analysis.

"We've identified three credible causes (of the nozzle issue), and we have taken positive steps to mitigate all of those," ULA CEO Mark Peller told Aviation Week & Space Technology magazine in a pre-flight interview.
The boosters appeared to work normally Sunday.
As for the BE-4 engines, Peller said Blue Origin developed a "design improvement" to resolve the valve issue and carried out a "retrofit" on the engines installed on the Vulcan Leo 1 rocket.

"They were down at our facilities probably a couple months ago and implemented that retrofit kit on the engines on this upcoming mission," Peller said. "And they're working with us to work through our inventory of engines."

title: SpaceX pulls off first Starship recovery from orbit in spectacular fashion
summary: It was the first recovery of a Starship from orbit, a major milestone for a rocket SpaceX founder Elon Musk says will dramatically lower launch costs.
story: After a 22-hour stay in space, a SpaceX Starship rocket plunged back to Earth Saturday, enduring the blazing heat of reentry while homing in on its Texas Gulf Coast launch site, flipping vertical at the last moment and settling into the grasp of two huge mechanical arms on its launch gantry.

Throngs of SpaceX employees gathered nearby cheered and applauded as the rocket restarted three of its six methane-fueled Raptor engines to flip upright, rapidly slowing to a near hover as the robot arms moved in for a mechanical embrace, catching the rocket a moment before engine shutdown.

"This is so incredible to see!" said SpaceX commentator Jessie Anderson. "One of the most incredible and historic engineering feats of all time has just happened right in front of our eyes. Congratulations to our teammates at SpaceX, and to everyone who supported the Starship program."

It was the first such recovery of a Starship from orbit — previous test flights ended with planned ocean splashdowns — marking a major milestone in SpaceX's drive to develop the first fully reusable orbit-class rocket, a vehicle company founder Elon Musk says will dramatically lower the cost of launching payloads to Earth orbit, the moon and, eventually, Mars.

The Starship was launched atop a Super Heavy booster Friday using the same pad at SpaceX's Starbase facility on the Texas coast. Standing 407 feet tall, the two-stage rocket is the most powerful launcher ever built, generating some 16 million pounds of thrust at liftoff from 33 first-stage Raptor engines.
After propelling the Starship upper stage out of the lower atmosphere, the Super Heavy first stage attempted its own return to the launch site for capture by the gantry's mechanical arms.

Going into the giant rocket's 15th test flight, SpaceX had successfully recovered the first-stage boosters used in three previous launches. But the Super Heavy launched Friday was diverted to an offshore splashdown because of a guidance problem. The vehicle ran out of fuel and exploded moments before hitting the water.

While a disappointment to the SpaceX team, Musk said in a posting on the social media platform X the problem was a "slight underperformance of engines," adding that "these early ships and boosters are already outdated by improved designs in production or on the test stand."
"This booster loss does not change our timeline to reach high volume, fully reusable Starship flights," he said.
The Starship upper stage did not disappoint.

Beaming down crystal-clear views from cameras mounted on its steering fins, the spacecraft's belly, covered in heat-shield tiles, glowed red as the ship heated up in a fireball of atmospheric friction.

Crossing the Baja Peninsula and then northern Mexico, the big rocket rapidly descended before flying just north of the launch site, banking and dropping belly first out of low clouds, restarting its engines to flip upright and then falling at an angle toward the gantry, slowing to a near standstill as the arms closed around it.

"The room behind me going absolutely insane," SpaceX commentator Dan Huot said from the mission control center. "These people have done so much to earn this. ... I mean, that was the missing link. That was the holy grail of spaceflight, plummeting through fire to be snatched out of the air by steel. We caught a Starship, and now everything changes."

But SpaceX will need to successfully launch and recover a large number of Super Heavy-Starships to demonstrate the statistical reliability needed for crewed flights. And the company will need to demonstrate its ability to autonomously refuel Starships in Earth orbit and keep their propellants from boiling away in the space environment.

While the system is designed to be fully reusable, the Starship upper stage uses most of its propellant getting into Earth orbit. NASA wants to use a variant of the Starship to carry astronauts to the lunar surface in 2028 and multiple Super Heavy-tanker flights will be needed to refuel the lander in Earth orbit before it can head for the moon.

SpaceX plans to begin orbital fueling tests in the next several Super Heavy-Starship flights. But the rocket's development has taken longer than initially expected and the space agency is now hedging its bets, saying it's open to using Blue Origin's Blue Moon Mark 2 lander depending on which spacecraft is ready in time.

title: SpaceX launches first-of-its-kind Starship test flight
summary: The SpaceX Super Heavy-Starship was designed from the ground up to be fully reusable in a bid to lower launch costs.
story: SpaceX launched its huge Starship rocket on the program's 15th test flight Friday, a 22-hour mission that was meant to feature planned launch pad catches of both the booster and the Starship's upper stage.

However, after the booster sent the Starship on its way to orbit as planned, a problem of some sort prevented a return-to-the-launch-pad capture. Instead, the rocket made a splashdown off the Texas Gulf Coast, exploding in a spectacular fireball moments before hitting the water.

SpaceX managed to catch a Super Heavy booster during three previous test flights, using giant mechanical arms on the launch gantry to snag the rockets as they descended tail first on the power of three of their 33 Raptor engines. But the flight plans always include a splashdown option if an issue crops up preventing a safe capture.
It was not immediately known what triggered the diversion Friday or the explosion before splashdown.

It was a disappointment for SpaceX workers who had hoped the Super Heavy-Starship rocket's 15th test flight would be the first to demonstrate full reusability in an orbit-class rocket. The company still plans to attempt its first-ever launch pad catch of a Starship upper stage Saturday at the conclusion of the mission.

Loaded with 8 million pounds of supercold liquid oxygen and methane fuel, the rocket's 236-foot-tall first stage, powered by 33 methane-burning Raptor engines, roared to life and majestically propelled the booster away from SpaceX's "Starbase" launch site on the Texas Gulf Coast at 5:47 p.m. ET.
Arcing away to the southeast, the Super Heavy booster propelled the rocket out of the thick lower atmosphere before falling away about 2 minutes and 20 seconds after liftoff.
Technical problem forced SpaceX to divert booster to Gulf Coast

While the 171-foot-tall Starship continued the climb to space using six Raptors of its own, the booster flipped around and fired up a set of Raptors to reverse course and head back to the launch site.

But a little more than 6 minutes after liftoff, flight controllers ordered a diversion to a Gulf Coast splashdown because of a technical problem. Long-range cameras captured the big booster slowly descending to the Gulf, shrouded in steam and then a fireball as residual propellants ignited.

The Starship, meanwhile, followed a suborbital trajectory, ensuring a safe ocean splashdown in case of problems, while giving SpaceX flight controllers time to assess its health before committing to a final push to orbit.

But no issues were found and after an 18-minute coast, a single Raptor reignited for a short 10-second burn to push the craft into its planned orbit. Eight and a half minutes after that, the first of 26 upgraded version 3 Starlink internet satellites was expected to be pushed out into space to fly on its own.

For the rest of the flight, controllers planned to closely monitor the Starship, periodically assessing its health to make sure it could be safely de-orbited in case of problems that might prevent a safe return-to-launch-site capture at the same pad where it launched Friday atop the Super Heavy booster. It will be SpaceX's first attempt to get a Starship back to its pad for possible refurbishment and relaunch.

"During this prolonged coast phase, flight control teams have several options to end the mission early and return Starship to pre-cleared areas of the Pacific Ocean if needed," SpaceX said in a blog post. "These locations include early- and late-mission splashdown options around Hawaii and a mid-mission splashdown opportunity several hundred kilometers off the coast of Chile. These precleared areas ... provide a safe place to land Starship if any conditions arise that may preclude the ability to perform a safe reentry."
Starship's upper stage slated to reenter Earth's atmosphere and land at Starbase on Saturday

One hour after a final "return check" Saturday, a single Raptor is expected to fire at 3:21 p.m. Eastern time to lower the far side of the Starship's orbit deep into the atmosphere for a 56-minute belly-first reentry and return to the Texas Gulf Coast.

"During reentry, Starship can alter its flight path by moving its four control flaps," the company said. "This will permit Starship to maintain a safe and known trajectory while guiding itself with high precision control toward Starbase."
As it descends, the Starship will carry out "a series of small turns in its trajectory to intentionally fly over sparsely populated areas of northern Mexico and southern Texas," SpaceX said.
Starship will avoid major cities in the Rio Grande Valley and pass to the north of South Padre Island before heading "out over the Gulf of America as it makes its final turn south towards Starbase."

Nearing the launch pad, the 171-foot-tall Starship will fire three Raptors to flip upright. Once the maneuver is complete, one Raptor will be shut down as the rocket descends between the gantry's mechanical arms. Finally, with just one engine firing to slow the rocket to a near stop, the mechanical arms will move in to snag the spacecraft.

But all of that depends on a problem-free descent. If any problems develop that might lead to an uncontrolled landing, flight controllers can ensure a vehicle breakup before it has any chance to reach a populated area.

"During reentry, flight controllers will have several options to end the reentry early and safely by intentionally tumbling Starship to ensure that it breaks up in the atmosphere before reaching land," SpaceX said. "There is also a late-reentry option to send Starship into the Gulf ... if any of its systems or the tower itself encounter an issue after reentry that would preclude a safe catch at Starbase."
SpaceX calls development of a fully reusable rocket "the holy grail of rocketry," opening the door to airplanelike cadence where a vehicle flies again rapidly.

NASA is counting on a variant of the Starship to carry Artemis astronauts to the lunar surface in 2028. But the rocket's development has taken longer than initially expected and the space agency is now hedging its bets, saying it is also open to using Blue Origin's Blue Moon Mark 2 lander depending on which spacecraft is ready.

title: Nvidia board members are cool on restoring Jensen Huang as CEO
summary: Nvidia's board isn't considering rehiring Jensen Huang as CEO despite an online petition that has drawn more than 180,000 signatures.
story: Nvidia board members are not interested in reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO or in any other role at the chipmaker, according to a source directly familiar with their thinking.

Huang stepped down from Nvidia on Thursday amid an investigation into his extramarital affair with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies suspect was spying for China. His departure from the chipmaker he co-founded more than three decades ago came within days of the relationship becoming public.

At the same time, thousands of Nvidia employees and technology executives, including Elon Musk, have signed a petition asking the chipmaker to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO, with the organizers arguing that he "may have been forced out without due process and without even a few days to make his case."

The push to reinstate Huang comes as the company named Colette Kress, Nvidia's chief financial officer, as its interim CEO and said it would seek a permanent replacement. Nvidia's stock has tumbled in the past week amid the controversy, chopping more than $500 billion from its market valuation.

"For thirty-three years, Jensen poured his heart and soul into building Nvidia," according to the petition, which described itself as an "independent, volunteer campaign" that is "not affiliated with, authorized by or endorsed by Nvidia Corporation or Jensen Huang."

The petition added, "He bet it on ideas that most of the industry dismissed, carried it through years when the bets looked foolish, and stayed long enough to see them change how the world computes ... That deserves more than gratitude after the fact. It deserves fairness now."

The petition has gained more than 180,000 signatures, including from what it says are more than 9,000 Nvidia employees representing about one in five company workers. Executives, including Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney and Shopify CEO Tobias Lutke, have also signed the petition, according to its website.
"A petition is underway to reinstate Jensen and I'm signing it too," Musk wrote on X on Friday.
At the same time, Huang is said to be discussing his return to Nvidia with allies, the Financial Times reported on Sunday.
President Trump suggested to reporters on Monday that he would support Huang returning to Nvidia.
"I would not mind seeing that," Mr. Trump said. Later, the president said he recommended former Apple CEO Tim Cook as Nvidia's next leader.
Long-shot bid

Huang's return to Nvidia is a long shot, according to Wall Street analysts. On Sunday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called for the chipmaker to hire its next CEO from outside the company, arguing that the company needs a major leadership shakeup amid questions about whether sales of its chips to companies in Singapore and other Asian countries circumvented U.S. export controls and ended up in China.
"We will see if Nvidia intentionally ignored the warning signs of these shell companies, many of them in Singapore," Bessent said on Fox News on Sunday.

Given Bessent's push for Nvidia to look outside the company for its next leader, Huang's return appears unlikely, according to Vital Knowledge analyst Adam Crisafulli, who told investors in a research note that the "odds of him being reinstated seem quite low."
Dan Ives, a well-known tech stock analyst at Yorkville Ives, downplayed the likelihood that Huang would resume his duties at Nvidia.

"Any talk of a damaged Jensen coming back to Nvidia is ridiculous in our view given the legal/board/DC scrutiny/moral compass/China tentacles," he said in a note to investors. "For the company, the best path forward is with a new external CEO or Colette [Kress]."
Prediction market users aren't giving much credence to the idea of Huang's return, with Kalshi traders assigning only a 10% chance of the former CEO returning to that role.
Nvidia shares are poised to continue their decline on Monday, with the stock down $2.39, or 1.5%, to $160.46 in early trading.
Investors will be tuning into Nvidia's earnings call on Tuesday afternoon to hear more about the company's guidance in the wake of Huang's departure.

"The critical question in the immediate term is what management has to say about the 70% sales growth guidance for next fiscal year — does Nvidia reiterate confidence in that or withdraw it given uncertainty about export rules in Washington," Crisafulli said.
