title: Supreme Court rejects case on Trump's bid to cut grants related to DEI
summary: Two federal agencies had moved to cancel grants to researchers at the University of California that they said did not align with President Trump's policies on DEI.
story: Washington — The Supreme Court on Monday declined to hear a case involving the Trump administration's termination of grants awarded to University of California researchers that it said did not align with President Trump's priorities, including on diversity, equity and inclusion.

By turning away the appeal from the Trump administration, the Supreme Court leaves intact a lower court decision that found the cancellation of the millions in academic funding from the National Endowment for the Humanities and National Science Foundation likely violated the First Amendment.

The Justice Department had warned that if the high court allowed the decision from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit to stand, as it now has done, it would clear the way for taxpayer dollars to go to research projects promoting DEI initiatives.

The case stems from the first days of Mr. Trump's second term, when he signed executive orders that instructed federal agencies to cancel grants related to certain topics, including DEI. The legal fight involves grants from the NEH and the NSF to University of California researchers, which the Trump administration terminated because they were not consistent with the president's priorities on DEI.

Lawyers for the University of California said that from January to June 2025, the Trump administration cut off more than $324 million in grants to that university system alone. They said the two agencies carried out Mr. Trump's executive orders on funding for DEI-related programs by conducting keyword searches of grant applications, and then canceled awards that used words like "diversity," "climate change" and "gender ideology."

Grant recipients began receiving letters informing them that their funding had been terminated in April 2025. Several months later, six researchers at the University of California who received grants from the Environmental Protection Agency, NSF and NEH filed a lawsuit and sought a court order requiring their grants to be reinstated.

A federal district court sided with the plaintiffs in a June 2025 decision and certified a provisional class covering University of California researchers who had grants terminated under Mr. Trump's executive orders targeting DEI-related initiatives.

U.S. District Judge Rita Lin said that the Trump administration had terminated the grants en masse for touching on issues it said were prohibited and ruled that the funding was likely terminated based on the perceived viewpoint expressed in the research. She ordered the Trump administration to reinstate grants from the NSF, NEH and EPA.
The 9th Circuit upheld the district court's preliminary injunction in May and agreed that the grant terminations likely violated the First Amendment's prohibition on viewpoint discrimination.

The Trump administration, it said, "has not merely exercised its power to choose the programs it funds but has instead terminated individual grants in existing programs based on the perceived viewpoints of individual speakers."

While the case proceeded, the plaintiffs reached a settlement related to the EPA grants, leaving only the awards from the NSF and NEH at issue. The Trump administration said there was approximately $59 million remaining on the grants, which will expire as late as November 2029.

title: Trump says he may meet with North Korea's Kim Jong Un in China
summary: President Trump said he may meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un on his China trip this week.
story: Washington — President Trump said he may meet with North Korean dictator Kim Jong Un during his trip to Asia this week.

As he left the White House Monday morning for a summit in the Philippines, which will be followed by a trip to China, Mr. Trump told reporters the meeting with Kim would take place in China — if it happens. No meeting with Kim has been confirmed by the White House. The president said whether the meeting happens is up to Chinese President Xi Jinping. Mr. Trump will meet with Xi, along with Russian President Vladimir Putin, later this week.

"We'll be with President Xi," the president told reporters on the White House South Lawn. "He was here a month ago. And we're also going to meet with President Putin. And we may meet with Kim Jong Un, also. So that'll be good. We could — we have a chance to accomplish a lot."
The president said he doesn't know if Kim will come.
"He may come," Mr. Trump said of Kim. "I don't know. That's up to President Xi."
Mr. Trump has met with the North Korean leader in person three times, all during his first term in office. He is the only sitting U.S. president to have met with Kim.
This is a developing story and will be updated.

title: Raye leads the 2027 Grammy nominations. See the list.
summary: English singer-songwriter Raye is up for 11 awards at the 2027 Grammys, followed by Spanish singer Rosalía​ with nine nominations.
story: English singer-songwriter Raye leads the 2027 Grammy Award nominations, the Recording Academy announced Monday.

Raye is up for 11 awards at February's ceremony: record, song and album of the year — the first time she's been nominated in those big categories — as well as songwriter of the year non-classical, a variety of pop categories and music video.
Her 11 nods also mean she has tied Beyoncé's record at the 2025 Grammys for the most nominations in a single year by a female artist.
Speaking of Bey: She continues her reign as the most-nominated artist in Grammy history, scoring her 100th nod for "Morning Dew (Donk)" in the R&B solo performance category.

Raye, who is riding the success of her critically acclaimed album "This Music May Contain Hope," has 15 Grammy nominations across her career. She's never won one, though she was previously recognized by the Recording Academy with the noncompetitive Harry Belafonte best song for social change award.

Spanish singer Rosalía, fresh off her album of the year win at the 27th annual Latin Grammy Awards on Thursday for her avant-garde "Lux," follows Raye with nine nominations. She's a first-time nominee in all the categories she's up for: record, song and album of the year as well as pop solo performance, alternative music performance, alternative music album, Latin song, global music performance and music video.

Following her are Miranda Lambert, Olivia Rodrigo, Phoebe Bridgers and first-time nominee Ella Langley, who are tied with seven nods each. Bruno Mars, Leon Thomas and 2026's best new artist winner Olivia Dean have six nominations each.
Taylor Swift's nomination is her fifth consecutive studio album to be nominated for album of the year, something only one other artist has ever done: Kendrick Lamar.

Only recordings commercially released in the U.S. between Aug. 31, 2025, and Aug. 28, 2026, were eligible for nominations. The final round of Grammy voting, which determines the winners, will take place between Dec. 10 and Jan. 7.
The 2027 Grammy Awards will air Feb. 7 at 7 p.m. Eastern, live on ABC for the first time since 1972, from the Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles. It will also stream on Disney+ and Hulu.

title: High court rejects challenge to Maryland gun ban in sensitive places
summary: The Supreme Court left in place a lower court decision that upheld the measure banning guns in sensitive places.
story: Washington — The Supreme Court on Monday turned away a challenge to Maryland laws that prohibit firearms in sensitive places like schools, parks and government buildings.
In rejecting the appeal from a group of Maryland residents and gun rights groups, the high court leaves in place a lower court decision that upheld the rules.
The Supreme Court last year struck down a Hawaii law that required concealed-carry permit holders to receive permission before bringing their firearms onto private property open to the public.

At issue in the case were a set of Maryland laws that limit the places where guns can be carried in public.  The state prohibits firearms from being brought on school property, at public demonstrations and on public transit, as well as in parks, museums and casinos.

Another set of limits was enacted in 2023, in the wake of the Supreme Court's landmark 2022 decision that recognized for the first time that the Second Amendment protects the right to carry a gun outside the home. Under the new restrictions, people are prohibited from carrying firearms at daycare and medical facilities, government buildings or other places where the public gathers for "entertainment, educational enrichment or other collective social pursuits."
On the same day Maryland's latest restrictions were signed into law, two sets of plaintiffs filed lawsuits arguing they violated the Second Amendment. The suits targeted 10 categories of places.

The two cases were consolidated, and a federal district court declined to block the limits on museums, health care facilities, public transit, state parks, entertainment venues, school grounds and government buildings. But the district court ruled in favor of the plaintiffs as to public demonstrations and places that sell alcohol for on-site consumption.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit went on to rule that all of the challenged restrictions are consistent with the Second Amendment. The appeals court applied the Supreme Court's new test for evaluating the constitutionality of gun regulations, which it laid out in its 2022 decision. Under that framework, the government must show that a firearms restriction is consistent with the nation's historical tradition.

In addition to pointing to historical analogues of some of Maryland's regulations, the 4th Circuit said the Supreme Court has twice, in decisions from 2008 and 2010, asserted that laws forbidding guns in government buildings and on school grounds are allowed.

The Maryland residents and gun rights groups appealed to the Supreme Court and argued that its intervention is needed to help lower courts better define the historical limits on the right to have guns in public as more and more states are enacting location-specific limits.

"The constitutionality of these so-called 'sensitive place' bans is among the most critical questions facing the judiciary in the wake of" the Supreme Court's 2022 decision, they wrote in their petition. "If, as Maryland maintains and the Fourth Circuit below held, the right to carry a firearm 'in public' does not include public locations that are owned by the government, or where First Amendment protected activity is being carried out, or where people go to eat and to drink or gather for amusement and recreation, then it is hard to know what the right to carry a firearm 'in public' actually protects."

But Maryland Attorney General Anthony Brown argued that the state's sensitive-place laws are consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearms regulation, and therefore constitutional. He noted that there is a "rich American tradition" of barring guns in certain locations, including those that are "confined and crowded."
"This Court endorsed such 'longstanding' bans in schools, legislative assemblies, polling places, and courthouses, while recognizing that this list was non-exhaustive," Brown wrote in a filing.

In the years since the Supreme Court laid out its new test for determining the legality of gun regulations, it has been confronted with a number of challenges to longstanding firearms laws. In 2024, the Supreme Court upheld a federal law that prohibits people subject to domestic violence restraining orders from having guns.

In an opinion authored by Chief Justice John Roberts, the eight-justice majority said the "appropriate analysis" under its new historical tradition standard "involves considering whether the challenged regulation is consistent with the principles that underpin our regulatory tradition."
Then, in its last term, a unanimous Supreme Court said the Second Amendment does not allow the government to prosecute a person who is an occasional marijuana user.

title: Right whale population drops, alarming scientists
summary: The population of one of the world's rarest whales has fallen after trending upward in recent years, worrying scientists who fear the animal could still be at risk of extinction.
story: Portland, Maine — The population of one of the world's rarest whales has fallen after trending upward in recent years, worrying scientists who fear the animal could still be at risk of extinction.

The North Atlantic right whale now numbers 382 animals, according to a consortium of scientists that released its annual population estimate for them on Monday. That represents about a 2% decline from last year's estimate of 384, which was an increase of 2.1% from the previous year and showed the continuation of a prior slow but steady climb in the whales' population.

The whales were decimated by centuries of commercial whaling that mostly ended in the 1930s. The enormous animals have been slow to recover, and today are threatened by entanglement in fishing gear and collisions with ships.

Those threats, combined with a warming ocean, have conspired to hold the population down, said Heather Pettis, chair of the North Atlantic Right Whale Consortium. Pettis said the warming of the ocean has caused the whales' food — tiny organisms called copepods — to move, and the whales have followed them into areas of ocean not protected from ship strikes and entanglements.

"We know that this population can and will move around to find food and if we aren't protecting them throughout their range, we may see another situation where we have this tremendous decline again," Pettis said.

The whales' population fell about 25% from 2010 to 2020 during a time when years of poor reproduction coincided with high mortality. Recent years have been slightly more encouraging, but scientists and conservationists have warned that the whales need years of high birth counts coupled with new protections to have a chance to rebuild.
Stronger safeguards needed, environmental groups say

The loss in population last year underscores the need to spare the whales from entanglements and ship strikes, said Nora Ives, a marine scientist on the environmental group Oceana's right whale campaign.

Oceana was one of several environmental groups that opposed a proposal in Congress to delay new right whale protections until 2035. The proposal, which has passed the House of Representatives, is intended to protect commercial fishing interests from regulations that members of the industry describe as burdensome.

"The latest numbers are disappointing and make the road to recovery longer for critically endangered North Atlantic right whales. This iconic whale will not escape extinction if its population cannot grow," Ives said.

The right whales, which can weigh 150,000 pounds, give birth off the Carolinas, Florida and Georgia in the winter and venture north to feeding grounds off New England and Canada. Large groups of the animals that sometimes include a fifth of the entire population are sometimes seen off Massachusetts in spring. Last year was one of the most successful calving seasons on record, with more than 20 babies born.

The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration has said the last nine years have also been a time of unusually high numbers of injuries and deaths for the whales. The population is down to just 73 reproductive females, which makes replenishing the stock difficult.

They were hunted heavily because they tend to live fairly close to shore and floated when killed, and they yielded a high volume of oil. Some sources say they got their common name from the perception that they were the "right" whale to hunt.

title: Thanksgiving travel likely to dip a bit due to prices, AAA says
summary: Pricey plane tickets and expensive gasoline are expected to keep some Americans from traveling this Thanksgiving, but not enough to make much difference in airport security lines and highway traffic, AAA says.
story: Pricey plane tickets and expensive gasoline are expected to keep some Americans from traveling this Thanksgiving, but not enough to make much difference in airport security lines and highway traffic, AAA said Monday.
The auto club federation predicted that 81.5 million people would travel at least 50 miles from home between the Tuesday before Thanksgiving and the Monday after the holiday.

That's about 121,000 fewer than traveled domestically over Thanksgiving last year, or a one-tenth of a percent decline, AAA said in its annual forecast. If proven accurate, the small drop would end three years of record-setting Thanksgiving travel that followed the COVID-19 pandemic, according to AAA's calculations.

"After three years of record highs, the number of travelers is slightly lower partly because of higher travel costs this year. But travelers won't notice much of a difference," AAA Travel Vice President Stacey Barber said in a statement.

AAA prepared its forecast weeks before problems with U.S. air traffic control communications and radar feeds on Friday prompted the Federal Aviation Administration to impose a nationwide ground stop that lasted more than four hours and disrupted weekend flights.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Federal Aviation Administrator Bryan Bedford said they expected air traffic to normalize well before the start of the Thanksgiving travel rush.
AAA doesn't think Friday's unusually long ground stop will have a major impact on Thanksgiving travel unless it happens again, spokesperson Aixa Diaz said.
"Travelers are resilient, and from what AAA has seen in the past, it takes a lot to keep holiday travelers home," Diaz wrote in an email Sunday.

As in past years, AAA expects the vast majority of holiday travelers to opt for car trips over flights. Meanwhile, it expects buses, trains and cruise ships combined will serve 4% more passengers than last year.
Gasoline could set a Thanksgiving Day price record.

Gasoline prices have fallen over the past week, but motorists can expect to pay more than last year heading to and from Thanksgiving destinations, AAA's forecast said. Regular gas averaged $3.82 a gallon on Sunday compared to $3.08 a year earlier, AAA said.
If prices hold, gasoline would be more expensive this Thanksgiving Day than any previous. AAA's previous Thanksgiving Day record was $3.58 in 2022.

For people opting to rent vehicles, AAA car rental partner Hertz says it expects the Tuesday and Wednesday before Thanksgiving to be the busiest pickup days, with Orlando, Phoenix, Las Vegas, Atlanta and Denver the cities with the highest demand based on advance bookings.
Air travel outlook
Last November, a government shutdown that led the FAA to order flight cuts at 40 of the busiest U.S. airports created extra stress for airline passengers with Thanksgiving week tickets.
Air travelers who didn't cancel their plans were rewarded; Congress ended the longest shutdown in history, and the FAA lifted its order 10 days before the holiday.

This year, fuel prices that surged during the U.S. war with Iran are a concern. The overall inflation that influenced this month's midterm elections may also have made some Americans more cautious about venturing far afield for their Thanksgiving meals.

With U.S. airlines spending more on jet fuel, airfares were more than 22% higher in September than the same month a year earlier, according to the most recent government data. Carriers also raised fees for checked bags.

Visa's economic research group said an analysis of September credit card transactions revealed that spending on plane tickets and related travel for trips starting between Nov. 1 and Jan. 15 was down from a year earlier for households of every income level except those earning more than $200,000.
Aviation analytics firm Cirium said Thanksgiving flight bookings were running 1.6% behind last year as of late October.
Compared to last year, round-trip domestic flights booked through AAA for the Thanksgiving period were 17% more expensive, averaging $800 per ticket.

AAA expects nearly 6 million people to fly from Nov. 24 through Nov. 30, about 12,000 fewer than last year. Three Florida cities — Orlando, Fort Lauderdale and Miami — are the top three domestic destinations for Thanksgiving flights, the auto club said.

Theme parks and cruise vacations are the main reasons the Sunshine State is so popular this time of year, AAA says, adding that Detroit and Dallas are also in the top 10 since the cities are hosting Thanksgiving football games.

Other organizations have come up with different projections based on the data they reviewed. Trade organization Airlines for America said it expected U.S. carriers to serve more passengers during the same seven-day period, though it didn't specify if that includes international flights.
The group said airfares had risen much more modestly than jet fuel prices this year.

title: Fewer foreign students studying at U.S. universities, study shows
summary: Fewer international students are studying at U.S. universities as the Trump administration cracks down on immigration and reshapes higher education, a study shows.
story: Fewer international students are studying at U.S. universities as the Trump administration cracks down on immigration and reshapes higher education, data released Monday shows.

Overall, U.S. campuses saw a 9% decrease in international enrollment this fall compared with last year, according to a survey from the Institute of International Education. And the number of new students entering the United States for the first time fell by 15%.

"No one aspires to send their kids to get educated in the U.S.," said Veena Dubal, general counsel for the American Association of University Professors, whose father traveled from India to attend Tuskegee University, then the Tuskegee Institute, in the late 1960s on a student visa.
"It feels like an unsafe place. That's the message that the Trump administration has been sending to families all over the world and they're listening."

Last year, the enrollment decreases were partially offset by large numbers of students who stayed in the U.S. for temporary work after graduating. But after months of speculation, the Department of Homeland Security proposed requiring schools to pay a $70,000 fee for every student who participates in the optional practical training program.
Although the rule hasn't been finalized, participation in the program, known as OPT for short, dropped 6% this fall, according to the survey.

The proposed rule, which is expected to face legal challenges, is part of wider DHS efforts that include terminating the legal status of thousands of international students, along with detaining and deporting many of them.

And this summer, the administration finalized a rule that will prevent international students from staying in the U.S. for more than four years without approval from the federal government, although a judge has temporarily blocked it.
DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin has said the changes were intended to crack down on loopholes that international students were exploiting by extending their studies.
Although the U.S. remains the top destination for international students globally, the changes are having an effect, college leaders told the IIE.

Among more than 800 U.S. colleges and universities surveyed this fall, 88% blamed the visa application process and 70% blamed travel restrictions for the enrollment drops. And if OPT options are limited, 95% of schools predicted that international students would likely look to another country, according to the survey, which offers an early look at trends before full data is released next year.
Other factors in foreign enrollment decline

Politics aren't the only reason students are looking elsewhere, said Mirka Martel, head of research, evaluation and learning for the institute. Its survey found more global competition for international students and the rising cost of a U.S. degree also contributed.

Fanta Aw, the executive director and CEO of NAFSA, an association that represents international education, said students also are worried about research funding. Last year, the Trump administration began dismantling the federal grant-giving process and attempting to exert more political influence over what projects get funded.

"They're saying to themselves, 'Too much uncertainty in the United States. It's too difficult, and you know, more importantly, we have many more choices today than we did 10 years ago. Why subject ourselves to this?'" Aw said, noting that students are going to places like China.

NAFSA, in partnership with the international education technology company JB International, found that amid the enrollment decline, international students' contributions to the U.S. economy dropped by $2.4 billion this fall.
Schools' coffers feeling the effects
American colleges and universities heavily recruit students from overseas as a source of tuition revenue. So the drops have punched big holes in tuition revenue at some schools.

At Cleveland State University, international enrollment has dropped by 46% in two years, from 1,542 in fall 2025 to 828 this fall. And fewer than 50 new international students started this fall, said Provost Nigamanth Sridhar, who estimated that the budgetary impact ranges from $2 million to $4 million.
Decades ago, he arrived in the U.S. on an F-1 student visa and participated in OPT. Eventually, he went through the process to become a naturalized citizen.

"I am here in this position, in this job, because I had the opportunity to come to the United States as an international graduate student and then decided to stay here and build a career," said Sridhar, who is from India. "So international education is personal to me."

The biggest drops were at the graduate level. This fall's data shows a 15% drop in international graduate enrollment, compared to a 3% decrease at the undergraduate level. The report also found declines in international students from India, which sends more students to the U.S. to study than any other country.

Sarah Spreitzer, vice president at the American Council on Education, which represents college and university presidents, said substantial immigration bills are unlikely while Donald Trump remains president. But she said congressional oversight might halt new policies targeted at international students.
"Those types of things could provide more certainty for our international students that there's not just going to be these sudden or unexplainable changes," Spreitzer said.

title: Officials received years of warnings before FAA ground stop
summary: For years, audits flagged billions of dollars thrown at non-competitive contracts beset with delays, amid repeated technology breakdowns.
story: Government watchdogs have warned for years of the risk of technical failures involving decrepit air travel systems like the one that grounded all planes across the country on Friday, according to federal audits and past congressional testimony.

Audits flagged billions of dollars thrown at non-competitive contracts beset with delays, amid repeated technology breakdowns. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the fault that led to Friday's five-hour halt may trace back to one router that was supposed to be replaced in 2006.
"We're investigating that right now," Duffy said Sunday on CBS News' "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan." "This goes back decades."
One company that has been in charge of the aging telecommunications infrastructure for the last quarter-century is L3Harris.

The Federal Aviation Administration has poured billions of dollars into the company's contracts since 2020. A 2024 audit by the Office of the Inspector General found that since awarding the original contract in 2002, the FAA made 10 extensions that were "improperly authorized" (as well as one that was proper), adding 57 months and $1.5 billion in spending.

The inspector general warned the FAA "may be repetitively using these noncompetitive extensions for convenience and administrative ease," adding that it "risks paying more than the Agency should and receiving less than the best-quality results."

These concerns by government watchdogs can be traced back two decades. Just four years after Harris Corporation, now part of L3Harris, was awarded the contract in 2002 to modernize and operate the FAA's telecommunications infrastructure, an audit warned that the program was falling behind schedule. A follow-up report in 2008 identified continuing concerns about reliability problems that disrupted air traffic control operations.

A year later, in 2009, more than 800 flights were delayed after a telecommunications outage. The DOT IG investigated the incident and found that the FAA had failed to adequately oversee Harris Corporation and also had not developed sufficient safeguards for overseeing privately operated systems despite increasingly shifting more services to the private sector to reduce costs.

Despite these issues, the FAA awarded Harris another $291 million contract in 2012 to update its outdated air traffic control voice communications equipment. The project was ultimately terminated in 2018, after running into repeated delays and technical problems, with $160 million spent on the unsuccessful program.

Duffy acknowledged in a press conference following last week's outage that the government could not immediately move away from L3Harris, saying he was "stuck with L3Harris" until a new system could be built.

"Many of our contractors, many of our partners, they take our money and they provide really poor service to us," Duffy said, as he raised questions about whether the outage was caused by contractor error or faulty equipment.

Eric Soskin, transport inspector general under the Biden Administration, told CBS News that some of the FAA's equipment was now so old that one manufacturer of replacement parts had been out of business for over a decade.

"When you have systems as old as the ones that we have in place now, the knowledge of how those systems work… may even have been lost to retirements or memory," he said. "If only we had succeeded in getting a full rollout of next-gen technologies a decade ago, I bet whatever the cause was here wouldn't have happened."
But a September report from the Office of the Inspector General also warned that moving ahead with upgrades too quickly could also cause disruptions.

L3Harris did not immediately respond to CBS News' request for comment regarding the inspector general's criticisms, but said in a statement on Saturday that the company is working "in close coordination with the FAA" and has completed 70% of the switch from old copper lines to fiber cables for the Agency's communications.

"We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation's air travel," the statement said. "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously."

Even as L3Harris faced scrutiny over its performance, the company spent millions seeking to influence federal policy, including efforts to secure additional funding for modernizing the infrastructure it has operated for more than two decades.

It has paid $23.9 million to lobbyists since 2020, including $2.51 million this year, according to Senate records. Disclosures show it lobbied Congress on FAA modernization funding every year. L3Harris has also lobbied the FAA directly.

Ballard Partners, which has had deep ties to the White House, has at times been among the lobbying firms it retained. Other firms employed lobbyists who previously worked on congressional appropriations committees that play a large role in decisions on FAA funding, the records show.

Last April, L3Harris penned a letter urging congressional leaders of the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee to advance an air traffic control modernization proposal that initially called for $15 billion in federal spending.

Two of the lawmakers addressed in the letter had previously received campaign contributions from the company's political action committee, including Chairman Rep. Sam Graves, a Missouri Republican, whose campaign received $10,000 during the 2021-2022 election cycle, and Democrat Rick Larsen, of Washington, whose campaign received $5,000 during the 2023-2024 cycle.

Four days after the letter was sent, Graves publicly unveiled the committee's proposal to provide billions in additional funding for air traffic control modernization. Congress ultimately approved $12.5 billion for FAA modernization as part of President Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill Act, including $4.75 billion for telecommunications upgrades.
Graves and Larsen did not respond to CBS News' requests for comment.

In testimony to the House Appropriations Committee this March, Deputy Inspector General Mitch Behm cited a repeated pattern across 50 audits of cost increases and schedule overruns, largely blaming a failure to nail down design decisions and a lack of a clear plan.
Other government watchdogs have also been calling out crumbling infrastructure around aviation communications.

In 2024, the Government Accountability Office found 51 of the FAA's 138 air traffic systems unsustainable, citing outdated functionality and missing spare parts, with 54 more potentially unsustainable.

The Transportation Department says it is putting its $12.5 billion to good use, including replacing handwritten paper systems with electronic ones at 25 control towers, upgrading five facilities from using floppy disks, and modernizing 469 tower radios, but says that the funds are narrowly allotted by Congress with little room to choose what it spends on.

Soskin told CBS News that Friday's outage "confirms the importance of pushing ahead with the technology upgrades," but added that "FAA and DOT need to supervise these projects carefully, and make sure they are getting highly capable systems that are reliable, and that are procured properly so that they're good value for taxpayers."

"The transfer needs to be handled carefully," the former inspector general said. "It may be that some disruptions like this are unavoidable, in which case FAA and other leaders need to do a good job of explaining to travelers why they happen, and why the end result is worth the trouble."

title: 4 NFL officials work 2 games each due to ground stop, a rarity
summary: Four NFL officials worked two games Sunday — a rarity stemming from Friday's nationwide ground stop ordered by the FAA that threw airlines' schedules into complete disarray.
story: Cincinnati — Don Willard did something on Sunday that the NFL hopes doesn't ever have to be duplicated — refereeing two games in one day.

Willard was the referee Sunday afternoon for the Miami Dolphins' game against the Indianapolis Colts in Indianapolis before he and three other members of the crew made the 114-mile trip to work the prime-time contest between the Pittsburgh Steelers and Cincinnati Bengals.

The reshuffling happened after the Federal Aviation Administration called for a nationwide ground stop Friday. The stop caused consternation and chaos for professional and college teams throughout the country and even resulted in moving at least one college football game from Saturday to Sunday.

NFL officials audibled by reassigning game officials for this week's matchups to stadiums closer to cities where they reside so they could drive, and Willard was asked to take over as the lead ref for the two games.

Willard usually works NFL games as a side judge. About an hour before kickoff in Indianapolis, he did the traditional microphone check and then he handled the coin toss duties typically reserved for referees.
Willard wasn't the only one doing double duty Sunday.

Umpire Terry Killens, field judge Jabir Walker and side judge Justin Larrew also jumped in a minibus and made the two-hour drive down I-74 to work the game in Cincinnati. It's the first time this officiating crew has worked together.
The four officials arrived in Cincinnati at 6:39 p.m., giving them some time to prepare before the 8:20 p.m. kickoff.

There were two instant replay reversals during the first half. A 23-yard completion to Pittsburgh's Germie Bernard was overturned when replay saw Bernard's toe was just out of bounds. An interception by Cincinnati's Jordan Battle was also reversed when a second look showed the ball hit the ground.
However, the crew called only 12 penalties in a game that usually sees a lot of flags because of the intensity of the Steelers-Bengals rivalry.

"I thought they did a great job managing a very difficult game, very testy game, obviously by both sides. So hats off to those guys for what they pulled off today. I know it was a long day for them," Bengals coach Zac Taylor said.
League officials didn't make any of the four officials who did double duty available to the media for either of Sunday's games.
NBC Sports rules analyst Terry McAulay, who worked three Super Bowls, said during Sunday night's "Football Night in America" pregame show that what the crew did was extraordinarily challenging.

"At a high level, it's a brand-new crew working together to work this game tonight that did not have at all the normal preparation - studying tendencies, studying formation style of play, and especially for this game, studying matchups on both sides of the ball. AFC North divisional games are brutal to officiate," he said. "Just working one NFL football game for three hours is incredibly mentally exhausting. When it's done, you're mentally drained. These guys have to do it now twice in one day. They don't have the normal recovery time. I know when I did it, my recovery time was never less than four hours."
The Dolphins didn't have any travel issues, a team spokesman said.

title: Siblings of man run over by ICE agent say it was "intentional"
summary: Miguel Parra Hernandez was hit by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent Mario Alberto Morales in Houston on Oct. 10.
story: Houston — The siblings of a Mexican construction worker run over last month by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent in an unmarked SUV allege the incident that left their brother with severe injuries was "intentional."
"It was not an accident," Miguel Parra Hernandez's sister, Carmen Parra, told CBS News in an exclusive interview. "The videos show everything."
Rodolfo Parra said he cried when he saw videos depicting the Oct. 10 incident that left his brother with a broken leg and hip injuries.
"You can hear all my brother say, 'Ah, you broke my leg. Ah, you're breaking my leg,'" Rodolfo Parra said.
The siblings described 48-year-old Parra Hernandez as a "hardworking" family man who has lived in the U.S. for 34 years, since leaving Mexico in the 1990s as a teenager.
"My brother is not a criminal," Carmen Parra said.

Mario Alberto Morales, the ICE officer who struck Parra Hernandez with his vehicle, was indicted in late October by a Texas grand jury on a felony charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon. Morales' attorney has called the incident an "accident," while ICE has denounced the prosecution as a "political stunt."
"He says he's done"

While Parra Hernandez does not have a criminal history and was not the target of the ICE operation the day he was hit and detained, he remains in the agency's custody, recovering from his injuries. ICE has not disputed that Parra Hernandez lacks a criminal record, but says the Mexican national is in the U.S. illegally and subject to deportation.
Parra Hernandez's siblings claim their brother's mental and physical health has deteriorated while in ICE custody, so much so that he's suffered from suicidal ideation.
"He says he's done," Carmen Parra said. "He wants to just go to sleep and not wake up because he says, 'I'm done in this life.' But we love him."

In a letter to acting ICE Director David Venturella and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Friday, a group of Democratic lawmakers led by Rep. Lizzie Fletcher accused ICE of obstructing efforts from Parra Hernandez's family and counsel to talk to him and rejecting food brought by relatives.
"The treatment of a long-time community member is unacceptable and a violation of his constitutional rights," the lawmakers said, demanding Parra Hernandez's release.
Representatives for ICE did not respond to questions about Parra Hernandez's health and treatment, and the allegations in the lawmakers' letter.

Parra Hernandez's siblings said he was on his way to work on Oct. 10 when he and a co-worker were approached by ICE agents. Surveillance video shows the two men running out of a white truck and attempting to flee, before an ICE vehicle appears to strike Parra Hernandez from behind.

In a statement following the incident, ICE claims Parra Hernandez ran in front of the vehicle. But Sean Teare, the Harris County district attorney, alleges the ICE agent "aggressively steered his vehicle into Parra Hernandez."
Houston limits cooperation with ICE
Parra Hernandez's hospitalization is one of several ICE-related controversies that Houston Mayor John Whitmire said have spread fear in the Houston area and prompted him to take action.

Following the stunning Republican losses in Texas and across the country on Election Day, Whitmire blocked Houston police officers from contacting ICE when they stop someone who may be in the U.S. without a valid immigration status.

"We do not collaborate unless the person is a really bad person. We're not concerned about someone that got pulled over for a traffic violation, or someone over a noise ordinance," Whitmire told CBS News. "We are going after the bad guys that have committed a new offense, a new danger to our community."
Whitmire said local officials can still work with ICE when someone in the U.S. illegally is booked in jail for criminal conduct.

He argued his executive order is designed to lower "fear and anxiety" in the community, referencing the fatal shooting of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a Mexican immigrant killed by an ICE agent over the summer during an attempted vehicle stop. The deadly shooting remains under investigation.
Since the policy change in Houston, officials in Austin and San Antonio have announced similar proposals.

Whitmire said he's taking a risk with his directive, citing the threat that Republican Gov. Greg Abbott's administration could sue Houston. But Abbott will soon be replaced by Gina Hinojosa, the first Democrat to be elected Texas governor in decades, and Whitmire said he can "guarantee" she will not force him to work with ICE.
He also acknowledged the move may prompt the Trump administration to withhold federal funds from Houston.
"Of course, I'm concerned about the Trump administration every day, but you have to use your good judgment," he said.
This story published first on CBS News at 8:54 p.m. on Nov. 15, 2026.

title: U.S. loses measles elimination status as cases surge nationwide
summary: The United States has lost its official measles elimination status for the first time in 26 years. Here's what to know.
story: The United States has lost its measles elimination status, researchers with knowledge of the decision confirmed to CBS News partner KFF Health News on Saturday.

The decision from the Pan American Health Organization came after the U.S. recorded over 5,400 measles cases so far this year — more than double last year's total. The Pan American Health Organization is a regional office for the World Health Organization, covering North and South America. The agency is set to hold a news conference on Tuesday.
A country is considered as having eliminated the measles if there are "no locally transmitted measles infections or outbreaks lasting 12 months or longer," according to the World Health Organization.

The United States did not meet that standard for the first time since 2000. According to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, about a third of this year's measles cases are linked to outbreaks that began in 2025 and continued to spread.

After a 30-year record of 2,242 cases last year, the CDC has tallied 5,412 cases to date in 2026, resulting in more than 590 hospitalizations and at least six measles-related deaths, with some states reporting additional fatalities.

The biggest outbreak has been in Pennsylvania, where state health officials have reported more than 1,500 cases and seven deaths associated with the disease this year. Wisconsin reports two children have died and New York had its first measles death in more than 30 years.
Measles cases have been confirmed so far this year in 45 states and Washington, D.C.

Sen. Bill Cassidy, a Republican from Louisiana who is also a doctor, said health officials, including Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., should be doing more to promote the importance of vaccination to protect against measles.

"Speaking as a physician, you may decide not to be vaccinated because it's your free will, but the child who's too young to be vaccinated is vulnerable if you come into that child's presence, and we're seeing children die from measles who are too young to be vaccinated," Cassidy said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."
"So if you've not been vaccinated, you could be the person that brings death to another. That's something to remember."
What does it mean to lose measles elimination status?

A country or region loses its measles elimination status once its population immunity lowers enough that there is sustained spread of the disease, CBS News medical correspondent Dr. Céline Gounder explained. When a country has measles elimination status and a high rate of vaccination, a case of measles or small outbreak will soon fizzle out. But when there are this many gaps in the population's immunity, there can be "ongoing chains of transmission," Gounder said.

"It means that we're at risk of being exposed to measles and getting measles if we're not vaccinated," Gounder said. "It means ERs and pediatricians need to consider measles in anyone with a fever and rash, whether they've traveled overseas or not. And we may now become an exporter of measles to other countries."
Dr. Omer Awan, a trained epidemiologist and senior public health contributor for Forbes, said that the loss of measles elimination status is a setback to the nation's public health infrastructure.

"It's frustrating and heartbreaking ... because we have the tools to fight this. The tool is the MMR vaccine, which we know is 97% effective at preventing the onset of measles," Awan said. "It'd be one thing if we didn't have the tools to fight this, but the tools are at our disposal, we just aren't using the tools that can help us mitigate the spread and beat measles."
How can the U.S. regain measles elimination status?
A country earns measles elimination status by ensuring there is no local spread of the disease or outbreaks that last for more than a year.

PAHO says that the best way to maintain the elimination of measles is maintaining a vaccination rate of 95% or higher. Countries should also have sensitive surveillance systems to detect cases quickly, laboratory capacity and a guaranteed rapid response to outbreaks. Data about these trends must be submitted to and verified by the organization.

For the U.S. to curb outbreaks and regain measles elimination status, it needs to return to higher rates of vaccination, Awan said. He said battling misinformation and ramping up vaccination campaigns would be key to that effort.
Data shows childhood vaccination rates have declined in many communities around the U.S. in recent years, often below the threshhold needed to help ward off measles outbreaks.
Gounder also noted that lawmakers can create policies that lead to increased vaccination rates.

"States set the school vaccine rules. Nine states made opting out of vaccination easier in 2025. States ending nonmedical exemptions saw kindergarten vaccination rise 2 to 4 points," Gounder said. "Most legislatures reconvene in January. Your state lawmakers will write next year's exemption rules."
Measles in the U.S.

The United States started collecting national data on measles in 1912, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. About 6,000 measles-related deaths were reported each year in the first decade of that data collection.

In the decade between 1953 and 1963, nearly all children in the U.S. caught measles before they turned 15, with an estimated 3 to 4 million people infected each year and tens of thousands hospitalized, according to the CDC. In those years, 400 to 500 people, mostly children, died of measles annually.
Then in 1963, the measles vaccine first became widely available. The numbers began a sharp decline and several generations of Americans grew up without ever encountering measles.
By 1981, reported measles cases had dropped by 80% compared to the previous year, the CDC said. The country was officially declared as having eliminated measles in 2000.

The U.S. maintained its elimination status for over 25 years. That didn't mean there were no cases at all — in 2015, an outbreak that spread among unvaccinated people was traced back to overseas visitors at Disneyland in Southern California, and a 2018-19 outbreak in New York was eventually contained by public health measures including curtailing vaccine exemptions. But those spikes were just a fraction of the spread now being seen in the U.S.

The nation recorded 2,242 measles cases in 2025, according to CDC data, linked to 48 separate outbreaks. The CDC reported 245 hospitalizations, mostly in children, and three measles deaths last year. Infections were confirmed in at least 44 states. It was the most cases the country had seen in over three decades.
That record was shattered in 2026, when the U.S. recorded more than double that number of cases by October — a total that topped 5,000 earlier this month.
Almost all of the cases have been in people who were not vaccinated. Measles-related deaths have been reported in Pennsylvania, New York and Wisconsin.

The CDC said 43 new outbreaks — defined as three or more related cases — have been reported so far in 2026, while about a third of the cases reported this year are tied to outbreaks that have been ongoing since 2025.
Who is at risk from measles?

Measles is one of the most contagious infectious diseases. Those who are unvaccinated for the disease are most at risk of getting it. CDC data shows that 96% of people infected with measles in 2026 did not get vaccinated for measles or were unsure of their vaccination status; only 2% of cases were in people who'd been fully vaccinated.
While many people recover, measles can cause severe infections in the lungs and brain that can lead to cognitive issues, deafness or death.
Medical research has shown that two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine is extremely safe and effective at protecting against measles.

Some people — including babies, pregnant women or people with weakened immune systems — cannot get vaccinated for measles, so they rely on population immunity to keep the disease from spreading. Awan said that these groups of people will bear "the brunt of the consequences" of increased measles spread.
"They will be the ones that are most vulnerable to getting infected and experiencing the complications," such as pneumonia or encephalitis, Awan said.

title: SpaceX pulls off first Starship recovery from orbit in spectacular fashion
summary: It was the first recovery of a Starship from orbit, a major milestone for a rocket SpaceX founder Elon Musk says will dramatically lower launch costs.
story: After a 22-hour stay in space, a SpaceX Starship rocket plunged back to Earth Saturday, enduring the blazing heat of reentry while homing in on its Texas Gulf Coast launch site, flipping vertical at the last moment and settling into the grasp of two huge mechanical arms on its launch gantry.

Throngs of SpaceX employees gathered nearby cheered and applauded as the rocket restarted three of its six methane-fueled Raptor engines to flip upright, rapidly slowing to a near hover as the robot arms moved in for a mechanical embrace, catching the rocket a moment before engine shutdown.

"This is so incredible to see!" said SpaceX commentator Jessie Anderson. "One of the most incredible and historic engineering feats of all time has just happened right in front of our eyes. Congratulations to our teammates at SpaceX, and to everyone who supported the Starship program."

It was the first such recovery of a Starship from orbit — previous test flights ended with planned ocean splashdowns — marking a major milestone in SpaceX's drive to develop the first fully reusable orbit-class rocket, a vehicle company founder Elon Musk says will dramatically lower the cost of launching payloads to Earth orbit, the moon and, eventually, Mars.

The Starship was launched atop a Super Heavy booster Friday using the same pad at SpaceX's Starbase facility on the Texas coast. Standing 407 feet tall, the two-stage rocket is the most powerful launcher ever built, generating some 16 million pounds of thrust at liftoff from 33 first-stage Raptor engines.
After propelling the Starship upper stage out of the lower atmosphere, the Super Heavy first stage attempted its own return to the launch site for capture by the gantry's mechanical arms.

Going into the giant rocket's 15th test flight, SpaceX had successfully recovered the first-stage boosters used in three previous launches. But the Super Heavy launched Friday was diverted to an offshore splashdown because of a guidance problem. The vehicle ran out of fuel and exploded moments before hitting the water.

While a disappointment to the SpaceX team, Musk said in a posting on the social media platform X the problem was a "slight underperformance of engines," adding that "these early ships and boosters are already outdated by improved designs in production or on the test stand."
"This booster loss does not change our timeline to reach high volume, fully reusable Starship flights," he said.
The Starship upper stage did not disappoint.

Beaming down crystal-clear views from cameras mounted on its steering fins, the spacecraft's belly, covered in heat-shield tiles, glowed red as the ship heated up in a fireball of atmospheric friction.

Crossing the Baja Peninsula and then northern Mexico, the big rocket rapidly descended before flying just north of the launch site, banking and dropping belly first out of low clouds, restarting its engines to flip upright and then falling at an angle toward the gantry, slowing to a near standstill as the arms closed around it.

"The room behind me going absolutely insane," SpaceX commentator Dan Huot said from the mission control center. "These people have done so much to earn this. ... I mean, that was the missing link. That was the holy grail of spaceflight, plummeting through fire to be snatched out of the air by steel. We caught a Starship, and now everything changes."

But SpaceX will need to successfully launch and recover a large number of Super Heavy-Starships to demonstrate the statistical reliability needed for crewed flights. And the company will need to demonstrate its ability to autonomously refuel Starships in Earth orbit and keep their propellants from boiling away in the space environment.

While the system is designed to be fully reusable, the Starship upper stage uses most of its propellant getting into Earth orbit. NASA wants to use a variant of the Starship to carry astronauts to the lunar surface in 2028 and multiple Super Heavy-tanker flights will be needed to refuel the lander in Earth orbit before it can head for the moon.

SpaceX plans to begin orbital fueling tests in the next several Super Heavy-Starship flights. But the rocket's development has taken longer than initially expected and the space agency is now hedging its bets, saying it's open to using Blue Origin's Blue Moon Mark 2 lander depending on which spacecraft is ready in time.

title: Family Dollar to pay $63M after FTC says it overcharged customers
summary: The discount retailer failed to honor prices displayed on store shelves, on price tags and in ads, the FTC and multiple states alleged.
story: Family Dollar has agreed to pay $63 million to settle allegations that it routinely overcharged customers by millions of dollars.
The Federal Trade Commission and 17 U.S. states accused the budget retailer of failing to honor prices displayed on store shelves, on price tags and in advertisements.

A proposed order bans Family Dollar from misleading customers on prices and requires the company to adopt what the FTC described as a "pricing accuracy program" that is independently assessed and certified annually.

"Today's order will ensure Family Dollar stops deceiving consumers about its prices and returns money to consumers harmed by these practices," Christopher Mufarrige, director of the FTC's Bureau of Consumer Protection, said in a statement on Thursday.
Family Dollar operates more than 7,000 stores across 48 U.S. states and Washington, D.C. The Chesapeake, Virginia-based company did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the settlement.

The FTC and the states' complaint alleged that pricing inaccuracies are widespread at Family Dollar stores and that the retailer failed to correct errors. Customers regularly reported being charged higher prices at the register than those displayed on goods' price tags, in stores, on the retailer's website and in its mobile app, according to the complaint.
The states include Alabama, Arkansas, Colorado, Florida, Iowa, Illinois, Kansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Nebraska, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Tennessee, Utah and Wisconsin.
In October, the FTC and 20 states sued another discount retailer, Dollar General, over allegations of similar deceptive pricing practices. The litigation is ongoing.
Customer refunds and discounts
The proposed order requires Family Dollar to establish a $40 million fund to compensate eligible customers.

The retailer will notify customers of their eligibility for reimbursement through in-store notices and online. Eligible customers include anyone who made a purchase at a Family Dollar store from Jan. 1, 2023, to Oct. 1, 2026.

The order also establishes a separate $20 million discount program for customers. Under the program, Family Dollar must offer customers 15% off a range of goods for two days. State plaintiffs will receive $3 million to be divided among them.
The retailer must create a pricing accuracy program to ensure that it regularly monitors and verifies prices and trains employees to identify and correct pricing discrepancies.

title: Iran rules out nuclear site inspections until war ends
summary: Iran says it will not let U.N. inspectors return to assess damaged nuclear sites until the war with the U.S. is "permanently ended."
story: What to know about the Iran war today:

A senior Iranian official said Sunday that Tehran will not allow International Atomic Energy Agency inspectors to return to examine damaged nuclear facilities until the war has "permanently ended." IAEA inspectors visited Iran's Bushehr nuclear plant in September but have not gained access to other sites targeted by the U.S. since the war started.Yemen's Houthi rebels have forced government-allied forces to pull back from areas along the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Bahraini officials said the weapons were intercepted, and the U.S. military denied a similar claim from Iran late last week.

A senior Iranian official said Sunday that Tehran will not allow International Atomic Energy Agency inspectors to return to examine damaged nuclear facilities until the war has "permanently ended." IAEA inspectors visited Iran's Bushehr nuclear plant in September but have not gained access to other sites targeted by the U.S. since the war started.

Yemen's Houthi rebels have forced government-allied forces to pull back from areas along the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The Iran-backed Houthis have fought for months to consolidate their control over the waterway - a key route for Saudi oil and gas exports.

Hostilities around the Persian Gulf have also increased in recent days, with attacks on commercial vessels continuing and Iran claiming another attack targeting a U.S. radar installation in Bahrain. Bahraini officials said the weapons were intercepted, and the U.S. military denied a similar claim from Iran late last week.

title: U.K. mulls changing sexual consent laws after Russell Brand case
summary: Britain's government will consider adopting staggered ages for sexual consent in the wake of "appalling" stories of "abuse of power by powerful men."
story: London —  Britain's government is considering changing the U.K.'s laws on the legal age of sexual consent as a woman who claims she was raped by convicted sex offender Russell Brand campaigns to criminalize sex between adults and 16- or 17-year-olds.

British Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden said over the weekend that "appalling" stories of "abuse of power by powerful men" had emerged last week, warranting consideration of a new law that would set out different ages of consent depending on the ages of the individuals involved.

Already practiced by several other nations, the merits of this staggered age of consent approach have "been raised and will be discussed" by the government, McFadden said, adding that he "can't tell you what the conclusion of that would be, but the last week has certainly put that up in lights."

A day after Brand was sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison for rape and sexual assault, fellow British television personality and author David Walliams was named as the subject of multiple allegations of grooming young girls and harassing female colleagues.

Under current U.K. law, an adult of any age can have sex with a consenting person 16 years old or older. If a staggered system were imposed, it could make it illegal for anyone 18 or older, for instance, to have sex with individuals aged between 16 and 18, regardless of whether they gave verbal consent.

There is plenty of precedent: In eight U.S. states —   Idaho, Louisiana, Massachusetts, Mississippi, Missouri, Nevada, North Dakota and Florida, where Brand was living before he was jailed — the age of consent varies depending on the age gap between the two people.

In Idaho, for example, if one person is under 16 and the other is 18 or older, or if the victim is 16 or 17 years old and the perpetrator is at least three years older, it is classed as rape. "Lewd contact with a child" younger than 16 is a crime regardless of the perpetrator's age.
In most U.S. states, the age of consent has a "close-in-age" exception for people under 18 who engage in mutually consentual sexual acts.

In Canada, where the age of consent is 16, the staggered-age system includes more detailed, age-dependent exemptions. For people aged 12-13, the partner must be less than two years older; age 14-15, the partner must be less than five years older, and between 16-17, people are generally seen as able to give consent, unless their sexual partner is in a position of trust or authority toward them.
Austria, Belgium, France, Ireland and South Africa also have close-in-age exemptions.
Mia Latter, now 37, has accused Brand of raping her when she was 16 and he was 30, and she is now campaigning for a staggered age of consent to be introduced in Britain.

Latter, whose allegations were not part of the case that saw Brand convicted last week of raping and sexually assaulting other women, abandoned her anonymity as an accuser of the celebrity in an interview published over the weekend by The Sunday Times. She told the newspaper she was speaking out to help "protect teenagers from being groomed by older men or women."

"I don't want to criminalize teenagers having sex with each other," she said. "If you're between the ages of 16 and 18, it seems reasonable that you can have relationships with each other, and [teenagers] are always going to. But … if you're in your thirties, forties and fifties and you're trying to have a relationship with someone under the age of 18, it [should be] a criminal offense."
Brand protested his innocence from jail on Sunday in a statement read out by his wife Laura.

The prime minister's office said Monday that the comments were under investigation, as "prisoners are strictly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims and speaking to the media is only permitted in exceptional circumstances."

title: Trump heads to Asia for Putin, Xi summit; possible Kim meeting
summary: President Trump is setting off on a multi-day swing in Asia, where he's scheduled to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and China's President Xi Jinping for a highly anticipated summit.
story: Washington — President Trump is setting off Monday for a multi-day swing in Asia, where he's scheduled to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and China's President Xi Jinping for a highly anticipated summit later this week.
Ahead of his departure, Mr. Trump called it a "big trip" and said he may also meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in China.

The meeting between Mr. Trump, Xi and Putin, which marks the first between the three leaders, is expected to center on decreasing the proliferation of nuclear weapons, the White House said, and comes as the wars in Iran and Ukraine remain in focus.

Mr. Trump said Monday they would discuss denuclearization, which he called a "tough subject," as well as Iran and Ukraine, although an official said over the weekend that Ukraine was not expected to be discussed.

The president will first head to the Philippines, where the annual Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit is being held. Mr. Trump will meet with Japan, India and Australia on security in the Indo-Pacific on Tuesday. He's also scheduled to sign a trade deal with Thailand and attend a dinner with leaders of the Southeast Asian nations and other regional leaders, the White House said.

On Wednesday, the president is set to hold a state visit and lunch banquet with Philippine President Bongbong Marcos at the presidential palace, before departing for Shenzhen, China. There, he'll meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit with APEC leaders, and on Thursday, hold the meeting with Putin and Xi.
Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk is expected to join the president on the trip, according to a senior White House official, but will not be part of the meeting with Putin and Xi.

Mr. Trump's trip to Asia comes after he visited China in May for a summit with Xi, where he touted making "fantastic trade deals" and acknowledged a shared desire to end the U.S.-Iran conflict. Xi also visited the U.S. in September, marking his first visit to the White House in over a decade, as the two countries extended a tariff truce.

"I think the president does intend to talk about Iran in the trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin," a senior U.S. official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told reporters on a call.
It will be Mr. Trump's third face-to-face meeting with Xi this year.

As for Putin, Mr. Trump and the Russian president last met in Alaska in August 2025 for a high-stakes summit on ending the war in Ukraine. But the talks failed to yield a ceasefire that the U.S. was seeking. Mr. Trump is not expected to speak about the 4 ½-year war in Ukraine during the summit.

Mr. Trump's trip to Asia also coincides with issues back at home, including the recent revelations regarding an affair between Jensen Huang, the former CEO of chipmaker Nvidia, and a suspected Chinese spy. Beijing has said it was not involved.

Huang, who has a relationship with Mr. Trump, traveled on Air Force One during his May trip to China, and he and his wife were at the head table when Mr. Trump hosted Xi in Washington for a state dinner in September. White House officials said they do not think the Nvidia situation will loom over the trip.

"We do not negotiate American export controls. These are national security matters that we develop in the administration ... and we don't expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we're there," an official said.

When asked Monday if Secretary of State Marco Rubio told him that the woman with whom Huang was having an affair, Alice Huang, was suspected of being a spy, Mr. Trump said he didn't know if she was, saying "I haven't heard that." Mr. Trump also said it "isn't a bad idea" for Jensen Huang to be reinstated at Nvidia, but he also added that he recommended Apple's Tim Cook for the job.

Both Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick are traveling with the president. Bessent last week accused Lutnick of failing to prevent China from getting some of Nvidia's most advanced chips.
Mr. Trump told reporters before he left that he was not considering replacing Lutnick.

title: Drawing China close, is Kim Jong Un bracing to confront the U.S.?
summary: As North Korea and China draw closer together, is Kim Jong Un ramping up for a confrontation with the U.S.?
story: Dandong, China — With a pair of binoculars and a camera hanging around his neck, retired Chinese government official Mr. Yang leaned against a fence on a boardwalk that meanders through the city of Dandong, peering across the wide Yalu River that separates China from North Korea.

He came to visit from Dalian, about 200 miles away, despite the temperature hovering just above freezing, to catch a glimpse of life inside China's heavily sanctioned, nuclear armed neighbor nation. But the main attraction he came to see is the massive new bridge towering over Dandong, which now links the two countries.
"The bridge is good, but it's only for trucks and cars, not for the trains," he complained. "But this is good for trade, and I do hope this means relations improve with North Korea."

At almost two miles long and four lanes across, the new Yalu River Bridge is a feat of engineering. The Chinese side was finished 12 years ago, but North Korea only recently completed its section, with leader Kim Jong Un making a surprise appearance for the official opening on Oct. 24.

As CBS News visited the new river crossing, a large group of tourists arrived from Fujian province, more than 1,000 miles to the south, to pose for photos in front of the impressive piece of infrastructure.

"This will enhance the friendship between China and North Korea for sure, but we hope that North Korea will open up to the West," tour group leader Mr. Sun told CBS News. "North Korea was an isolated country, and this shows they're trying to join the world."
That may be a message China's government is keen to encourage, but the recent actions and rhetoric from the Kim regime in Pyongyang suggests otherwise.
Kim Jong Un ramping up for a confrontation?
Since the beginning of October alone, North Korea has test-fired more than a dozen missiles — the most concentrated series of such launches by Pyongyang since 2023.
Kim has personally observed some of the launches, accompanied by his teenage daughter Kim Ju Ae, widely viewed as his potential successor.

Former U.S. State Department official Robert Carlin, who has half of a century of experience as a North Korea analyst, believes Kim could be preparing to take steps that will inevitably end in confrontation with the U.S.

"It's part of a pattern of preparations to get ready for what he (Kim) thinks he wants to do. So he's testing new systems, and there's been a flurry of them. They can test in private — they do it all the time —   so they want to make these visible for some reason," Carlin told CBS News. "When you put that together with the pretty aggressive probing along the demarcation line, the high-level statements with warnings and threats … we have to take seriously the possibility that KJU [Kim] is preparing something, putting himself into position for the moment he thinks the winds are at his back, the situation is ripe for him to make some sort of move against U.S. assets in the region and against South Korea."

President Trump has been pushing for a new meeting with Kim for months, citing what he considers his good personal rapport with the North Korean leader, and there has been speculation the two leaders could meet while Mr. Trump is in China this week to attend the APEC summit.

He fueled that speculation himself Monday as he departed for Asia, saying it would be up to the Chinese hosts of the summit, but telling reporters when asked about a possible meeting: "Yes, we might have Kim Jong Un."

Mr. Trump met three times with Kim during his first term, including two historic summits aimed at getting the North Korean leader to agree to steps toward his nuclear-armed country denuclearizing, but the discussions went nowhere.

Since then, Kim has only expanded his nuclear arsenal. South Korean intelligence agencies believe Pyongyang could now have as many as 120 nuclear warheads. Kim has made it clear, meanwhile, that he will only agree to a new round of negotiations if the U.S. first and formally recognizes North Korea as a nuclear state.
Burgeoning ties with Russia and China

While longstanding international sanctions against his country over its nuclear weapons program remain in place, since the failed talks with Mr. Trump, Kim has projected a sense of being emboldened — of no longer leading a nation ubiquitously dismissed as an international pariah.
The relationship with China, while at times strained, has been a constant, and it has helped Kim push the image of North Korea as a global player, rather than a "hermit kingdom."

Since Vladimir Putin ordered the ongoing, full-scale invasion of Ukraine more than four years ago, Pyongyang has also proven a dependable ally to Russia. North Korea has sent a constant stream of munitions to replenish Moscow's depleted stocks, as well as thousands of soldiers to fight on the front lines. In return, Moscow has sent financial and technological assistance, helping North Korea further develop its nuclear weapons program.

The city of Dandong is a symbol of the China-North Korea bond. Hundreds of thousands of Chinese troops marched across the original Yalu River bridge to fight alongside North Korean soldiers in the Korean War. Almost 3 million Chinese soldiers were deployed to fight in that conflict between 1950 and 1953.

The city was bombed by U.S. forces due to its strategic position on the vital North Korean supply line, and the old Yalu River Bridge was destroyed. Renamed "Broken Bridge," it became a war relic and tourist attraction in its own right.

In the center of Dandong, overlooking the old Broken Bridge and the nearby Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge, a smaller piece of infrastructure that facilitates cross-border rail and one-lane road traffic with the North Korean city of Sinuiju, local businesses sell Korean outfits along with trinkets and souvenirs, cashing in on Chinese fascination with the neighbors.

Grocery stores sell liquor in bottles that look like grenades, mortars and bullets, while hotels positioned along the river, facing North Korea, offer telescopes and binoculars in bedrooms for guests to peer across the Yalu into apartments and farmland on the far side. On some sections of the river, North Korea is only about 1,000 feet away.

Using our own long lens, CBS News was able to see people in North Korean apartments at night. At first light, the North Korean side became a hive of activity as people headed out to the fields and greenhouses to work.
George, a 16-year-old student, said he was visiting Dandong because of his passion for Chinese and North Korean history.

"North Korea is trying to get better connections with China, and China is opening to Western countries more and more, and if those things continue to happen, maybe North Korea will be opening to Western countries the same as China," he said.
As for the increasing tension on the Korean Peninsula, George dismissed the concerns.
Kim Jong Un, he said, is just "trying to tell the Western countries and the whole world that the DPRK is powerful enough to join the global stage right now."

While in Dandong, CBS News visited a restaurant and met a North Korean waitress who said she had been living in China for a year — one of as many as 80,000 North Koreans living and working in the city, all of whom are strictly monitored and not permitted to assimilate with the local Chinese population.
She told CBS News she missed home and hopes to return one day to North Korea, and she praised Kim Jong Un as a father to her country.
