title: AI phishing scams turn your social posts against you
summary: University of Texas at Arlington researchers reveal how AI analyzes public Instagram posts to craft spear phishing emails that feel personal.
story: Kurt Knutsson, the 'CyberGuy', weighs in on warnings of rising AI cyber threats after Bill Gates sounds the alarm. Gates warns of negative surprises within a year and cautions that the world is not prepared for AI upheavals.

You post a few photos from a concert on Instagram. The next day, an email arrives that appears to be from the venue, offering you access to exclusive photos from the show. It mentions the artist you saw and even references the night you attended. Sounds legitimate, right? You might be tempted to click without giving it a second thought. But what if that email came from a scammer who used artificial intelligence to study your social media posts?

That's the alarming possibility researchers at the University of Texas at Arlington have uncovered. Their study shows how widely available AI tools can gather personal details from public social media accounts and turn them into highly convincing phishing emails. Even more concerning, the technology can generate these personalized messages at a scale that once required far more time and effort. Think about the photos and updates you've shared recently. Could someone use those details to convince you an email is legitimate? According to this research, the answer could be yes.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
AI-POWERED CYBERATTACKS FUEL 'BLACK OCTOBER' FEARS
Public social media profiles can reveal personal details that scammers use to create convincing AI-generated phishing emails. (Anna Barclay/Getty Images)
How AI phishing scams use your social media posts

You've probably seen your share of phishing emails. Maybe someone claims there's a problem with your bank account or a package couldn't be delivered. Many of these scams follow familiar patterns, and we've become pretty good at spotting the obvious ones. But AI is giving scammers a much more personal approach. Researchers at the University of Texas at Arlington studied a technique known as context-aware spear phishing. In plain English, it means using details about someone's everyday life to create a scam that feels like it was written specifically for them.

Let's say you recently returned from a vacation in Brazil. You posted photos of the hotel and tagged a few places you visited. A scammer could use AI to analyze those posts and generate an email that appears to come from your hotel. The message might thank you for staying and offer a discount on your next visit. Everything seems to line up with your actual trip. However, the link could lead to a fake website designed to steal your password or credit card information.

Shirin Nilizadeh, an associate professor in UTA's Department of Computer Science and Engineering who led the study, explained why this is so concerning. "Anyone can be the attacker, and that makes it scarier," Nilizadeh said. And she's right. Someone using these tools may need very little personal knowledge about you. Your public posts can provide much of the information needed to create a believable message.
Researchers show how AI turns personal details into convincing scams

The research team, which included graduate student Elham Pourabbas Vafa and researcher Sayak Saha Roy, examined how AI could analyze public social media activity and generate personalized phishing emails. According to the research paper, the team studied 200 public Instagram accounts. They found that as few as 10 posts from an individual could provide enough information to create highly targeted messages.

The researchers evaluated more than 18,000 AI-generated emails and compared them with thousands of real-world phishing messages. The AI tools pulled information from travel photos and public updates about upcoming events. They also examined personal concerns people had shared online. From there, the technology created emails that appeared relevant to each person's recent experiences. The researchers even tested how AI could customize subject lines, sender names and links to make the messages more believable.

Consider something as simple as posting that you're excited about an upcoming concert. A scammer could use that information to send a fake ticket confirmation or an offer for upgraded seats. If you had recently complained about a delayed flight, an email offering compensation might arrive at just the right moment. These examples show how easily familiar details could be turned against someone. In a user study, participants generally rated the AI-generated emails as more convincing and less suspicious than the real-world phishing examples used for comparison.

However, the researchers evaluated people's reactions to the messages in a controlled setting. They did not measure how many people would actually click the malicious links during a real attack. Even with that limitation, the results raise serious concerns about how easily personal information can be used to manipulate someone's trust.
Why personalized phishing emails are getting harder to spot

One of the most unsettling parts of this research is that scammers may never need to hack your social media account. If your profile is public, they can potentially collect details you've already shared with the world. And those details can make an otherwise suspicious message feel familiar.

An email mentioning a restaurant you visited yesterday might seem harmless. So could a message referencing a concert you attended over the weekend. When the timing and details are accurate, people may be less likely to question where the message came from. That's the advantage scammers are hoping to exploit.

This research adds another concern because AI can automate much of the work involved in creating personalized messages. There's also the problem of how polished these emails can sound. We're used to looking for spelling mistakes and awkward wording. AI can produce professional-sounding messages, so those traditional warning signs may be missing. You could receive an email that looks perfectly normal, references something you actually did and still comes from someone trying to steal your information.
A SCAMMER HAS YOUR NAME, PHONE NUMBER AND ADDRESS. WHAT CAN THEY ACTUALLY DO?
Scammers can use AI to analyze your online activity and send personalized messages designed to trick you into clicking malicious links. (NickyLloyd via Getty Images)
AI safety filters missed most phishing requests

Now, you might assume AI companies already have safeguards that prevent people from using their tools to create phishing scams. They do. But the researchers found that those protections had significant weaknesses. The team tested three widely used AI safety tools: Llama Guard, ShieldGemma and WildGuard. These systems attempt to recognize harmful requests before an AI model responds.

With their default settings, the tools detected only 0% to 19% of the requests to create personalized phishing attacks. That's a pretty troubling result, especially considering how quickly AI can generate these messages.

The researchers then explored whether more specific instructions could help the safety systems recognize these attacks. The improvement was substantial. After researchers adjusted the safeguards to identify context-aware phishing attempts, detection rates reached as high as 99% in their tests. That's encouraging because it suggests stronger safeguards are possible. However, those results came from a research setting. They don't guarantee that every malicious request would be blocked in the real world.

The researchers also left the exact instructions used to generate their phishing emails out of the public paper. They wanted to avoid providing criminals with a ready-made guide. Nilizadeh is urging AI companies to take these threats seriously and improve their protections against targeted social engineering attacks.
How to protect yourself from AI phishing scams

These findings show how easily scammers could turn everyday social media posts into convincing emails. You don't need to stop sharing your life online, but it's worth being more thoughtful about what strangers can see. And there are several practical ways to protect yourself if a suspicious message reaches your inbox.

Start by checking who can see your posts on Instagram, Facebook and other social media platforms. If your accounts are public, strangers may be able to view your photos and personal updates. Consider limiting access to approved followers and reviewing older posts that reveal more than you'd like. You can follow our guide on how to change your Instagram privacy settings. Keep in mind that people can still share or screenshot content from private accounts.

Posting vacation photos while you're still away can reveal where you are. The same goes for announcing upcoming travel plans or tagging yourself at an event. Consider waiting until you're home to share certain experiences. Also, check location tags and other details in your photos before posting them publicly. You don't need to stop sharing the things you enjoy, but a little discretion can make it harder for strangers to follow your activities.

If an email arrives from a hotel or another business referencing something you recently did, don't assume it's legitimate. Open the company's official app or type its website address into your browser instead of clicking the email link. You can also contact the business through a phone number you've independently verified. Be especially suspicious when a message asks you to sign in, provide payment information or respond urgently. Even a familiar-looking sender address can be spoofed.

Strong antivirus software can help protect your devices if you encounter a phishing attack. Some security tools can warn you about known dangerous websites and detect malware hidden in suspicious attachments or downloads. That's valuable protection if you accidentally click something malicious. However, antivirus software cannot guarantee that every phishing website will be blocked, especially if you voluntarily enter your information. Keep your security software updated and turn on its available protection features. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.
FAKE CHATGPT BILLING EMAILS CAN STEAL YOUR LOGIN
Even a simple photo shared online could give scammers clues to make a phishing email seem legitimate. (iStock)

Scammers can learn more about you than you might realize. Data brokers and people-search websites may expose your home address, phone number and other personal details that criminals could use to make phishing emails more convincing. A personal data removal service can help find that information and request its removal from covered websites. While no service can erase everything about you online or remove your public social media posts, it can help reduce the personal information available to scammers. You can also request removals yourself for free, although doing so across multiple websites can take time. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com.

A scammer who steals one password may try using it to access other accounts. That's why every important account should have a unique, strong password. A trusted password manager can help you create and store them. Enable multifactor authentication wherever possible, preferably with an authenticator app or security key. Passkeys can offer even stronger phishing resistance on supported services. And never share a verification code with someone who contacts you unexpectedly.

Security updates help close vulnerabilities that criminals can exploit. Turn on automatic updates for your phone, computer and browser whenever possible. It's also worth checking that your email provider's spam and phishing filters are active. Gmail, Outlook and other major email services already block many suspicious messages, although some attacks can still get through. If you receive a suspicious email, use the built-in option to report it as phishing.
Know what to do if you click a suspicious link
Accidentally clicking a phishing link doesn't automatically mean your device has been compromised. However, if you think you've encountered a scam, here's what to do next.

Stop interacting immediately: Close the suspicious page. Don't enter personal information or download anything from the website.Scan your device: If you downloaded a file or suspect malware, run a security scan using strong antivirus software.Change compromised passwords: If you entered a password, change it immediately through the legitimate website using a trusted device.Review account activity: Check for unfamiliar logins or suspicious transactions. Sign out of unrecognized sessions and enable multifactor authentication.Contact your bank: If you shared financial information, notify your bank or credit card company immediately. Ask them to help secure your accounts.Report the scam: Report suspicious emails through your email provider and file a report with the Federal Trade Commission at reportfraud.ftc.gov/.
Stop interacting immediately: Close the suspicious page. Don't enter personal information or download anything from the website.
Scan your device: If you downloaded a file or suspect malware, run a security scan using strong antivirus software.
Change compromised passwords: If you entered a password, change it immediately through the legitimate website using a trusted device.
Review account activity: Check for unfamiliar logins or suspicious transactions. Sign out of unrecognized sessions and enable multifactor authentication.
Contact your bank: If you shared financial information, notify your bank or credit card company immediately. Ask them to help secure your accounts.
Report the scam: Report suspicious emails through your email provider and file a report with the Federal Trade Commission at reportfraud.ftc.gov/.
One final suggestion. When an email seems unusually well-timed or knows something personal about you, give it a second look. That little bit of hesitation could prevent a very expensive mistake.
Kurt's key takeaways

I think most of us understand that sharing personal information online comes with some risk. But this research takes that concern in a direction many people probably haven't considered. You could share a perfectly innocent photo from dinner or a weekend getaway and later receive an email that seems to know exactly where you've been. I can see how someone might trust that message, especially if it arrives at the right time and looks like it came from a familiar business. That's what worries me. AI is making it easier for criminals to use our own experiences to earn our trust. And they may be able to do it without spending much time researching us individually. I'm encouraged that the researchers found ways to improve AI safety filters. I'd like to see companies put those findings to work. In the meantime, I think we all need to be a little more careful about what we post publicly and a lot more skeptical of unexpected emails, even when the details seem right.

title: Elderly homeowner’s hired help turns into squatter nightmare made worse by blue state laws: report
summary: Jordy Smith, 76, said a fake plumber locked her out of her San Diego home and rented rooms to over a dozen people before Squatter Squad intervened.
story: Law enforcement was seen confronting a group of alleged squatters inside a home in California after a homeowner alleges she hired a "plumber" who then took over her home and reportedly rented it out to strangers. (Squatter Squad)
An elderly woman said a man posing as a plumber took over her home in California and began renting it out to more than a dozen people – many of them appearing to be homeless.
The situation had been brewing for more than two years before law enforcement finally removed the group after blue state laws complicated the issue, according to the homeowner and those helping her.
Jordy Smith, 76, opened up about the situation that took over her life in the City Heights neighborhood of San Diego, where she reportedly hired this man to repair pipes.
He then allegedly locked her out of the home and was renting it out to a revolving door of people, according to KGTV.
A homeowner said a plumber she hired to repair her home took it over, locked her out and rented it out to strangers. (Squatter Squad)
ALLEGED MALIBU SERIAL SQUATTER FEATURED IN NEW DOCUSERIES AFTER YEARS OF HOMEOWNER COMPLAINTS
Smith told a reporter that she temporarily moved from her home after she broke a hip and invited the unnamed "plumber" to make the repairs while she was gone.
"He just took over and, like, before we knew it, there was like 15 people," she said.
HOW THE 'SQUATTER HUNTER' IS FIGHTING HOME TAKEOVERS WITH TECH

In a post on social media, Squatter Squad, which is a "squatter removal and prevention" company that was hired to remove the group, said, "Boats were showing up. RVs were moving onto the property. More people were staying there. The contractor had started inviting others onto the property, renting out rooms and even charging people for RV space."
Squatters took over the homeowner's house, and she said she tried for two years to remove them. (Squatter Squad)
Smith said she later discovered the man was not a licensed plumber and had transferred the home’s utility accounts into his name before allegedly beginning to rent out rooms to others.
NYC LANDLORD PLEADS FOR HELP AS '9-YEAR-SQUATTER' CONTINUES TO DRAIN HIM DRY IN COURT SAGA: 'TWILIGHT ZONE'
She and her partner found themselves locked out of their own home.
Scads of trash and debris fill the property's yard. (Squatter Squad)
"I couldn’t sleep at night. I mean, it just seemed like we’d never get back home," she said.
SAN FRANCISCO HOME WITH HISTORY OF SQUATTERS UNDER CONTRACT FOR $1.3 MILLION
Attempts to confront the people living inside reportedly went nowhere, with Smith saying occupants would lock the door and refuse to speak with them.
Squatter Squad told KGTV that squatter issues are "often treated as civil matters," making it difficult for homeowners to remove them.

"The issue isn’t whether legitimate tenants deserve protection. They absolutely do. We need a system that protects legitimate tenants while also providing property owners and law enforcement with a clear, efficient process for addressing unlawful occupancy."

title: New Orleans cruise ship disaster timeline reveals tanker's troubled past and frantic final minutes
summary: The Atlantic Asphalt tanker lost steering just minutes before slamming into the docked American Heritage cruise ship in New Orleans on Friday.
story: Fox News correspondent Christina Coleman joins 'Hannity' to break down the tanker collision with a river cruise ship in New Orleans. Coleman says at least 129 passengers were rescued and none critically injured.

A timeline of Friday's horrific crash between a cruise ship and tanker in New Orleans reveals how the massive vessel lost steering control just minutes before slamming into a docked cruise ship, raising questions about the tanker's troubled safety history.

The collision between a cruise ship and tanker caused the passenger vessel to take on water before capsizing around 22 minutes later, which sent passengers and crew scrambling to get off the ship. While 32 people were hospitalized, no deaths were reported. Federal investigators are working to find out what caused the tanker's steering failure.
Here's a timeline of the New Orleans boat crash on Friday (All in Central Time):
NEW ORLEANS BOAT CRASH CALLED ‘MIRACLE ON THE MISSISSIPPI’ AS EVERYONE IS ACCOUNTED FOR, OFFICIALS SAY
A map shows the point of impact in the Port of New Orleans collision. (Fox News)

The American Cruise Lines vessel arrived near the Port of New Orleans after completing a Mississippi River cruise that lasted several days. The boat was docked for two hours before the collision and was in the process of beginning to let passengers disembark, according to officials. Around 200 people were on the ship.
The Atlantic Asphalt, which carried 19 crew members and a local river pilot, departed from Lower 9 Mile Anchorage, located near Mississippi River mile marker 83.
Its destination was an oil facility in Reserve, Louisiana.
According to the NTSB, the tanker suffered a steering casualty which left its rudder fixed in the starboard position, causing the vessel to make a turn toward the Mississippi River's east bank.
It's not yet clear what caused the steering malfunction.

According to the NTSB, crew on the tanker issued various emergency commands such as a whistle, requests for assistance, commands to deploy anchors, emergency orders and radio warnings before colliding with the American Heritage.

First responders work the scene by the riverboat American Heritage after it capsized following a collision with the tanker Atlantic Asphalt on the Mississippi River near the Port of New Orleans on Nov. 13, 2026, in New Orleans, La. (Michael DeMocker/Getty Images)
The Atlantic Asphalt collided with the American Heritage cruise ship near the Port of New Orleans.
Shortly after the tanker crashed into the American Heritage, it began taking on water as passengers and crew tried to evacuate. The ship also began to tilt toward the river's middle course.
TWO DEAD, INCLUDING INFANT, AFTER BOAT CAPSIZES IN NEW YORK HARBOR; 12 RESCUED
A massive rescue operation consisting of Coast Guardsmen, police, firefighters and other first responders also began, with other tugboats and commercial vessels also coming to assist.

Video shows the American Heritage river cruiser after a tanker struck the docked vessel in New Orleans. (WVUE)

title: Lindsay Clancy to be retried for murder in killing of three children
summary: Lindsay Clancy's murder retrial in the strangling deaths of her three children is set for March 29 after her first trial ended with a deadlocked jury.
story: Massachusetts Judge William Sullivan denies Lindsay Clancy's motion for acquittal, pushing the high-profile murder case toward a November 2 hearing.
A Massachusetts judge set March 29 as the start date for Lindsay Clancy's retrial on murder charges in the strangling deaths of her three young children.

The former nurse's first trial ended on Sept. 4 with a jury deadlocked 11-1, with only a single juror voting to find her guilty of murder. The others sided with her defense, which argued that she should not be found criminally responsible due to mental illness.

Judge William Sullivan repeatedly told the parties to pick a date in March or April. Prosecutors had wanted May at the start and later pushed for the end of April. Sullivan ultimately chose the late March date.
LINDSAY CLANCY PROSECUTORS FACE DILEMMA: RETRIAL OR PLEA DEAL IN CASE INVOLVING 3 STRANGLED CHILDREN

Lindsay Clancy looks at jurors as Judge Sullivan asks them to start deliberations for a sixth day during her murder trial on Thursday, Sept. 3, 2026, in Plymouth, Mass. (Pool Photo by Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger)
"You've all done retrials, and generally, the sooner it is the case is retried, the better it is for all parties," he said.
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

Although prosecutors did not specifically address whether they intend to seek the same charges, Clancy's defense lawyer, Kevin Reddington, said he anticipated that they plan to move forward on the same counts of first-degree murder.
SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS
Lesser charges could open the door for a plea deal or even a bench trial, according to legal experts.

Reddington told Fox News' Bryan Llenas in September that if prosecutors reduced the top charge to second-degree murder, he would opt for a bench trial — one without jurors — in the hope that she receives probation as punishment.

Callan, left, Dawson and Cora Clancy. The three children were killed at their Duxbury, Massachusetts, home in January 2023. (Lindsay Marie Clancy/Facebook)
GOT A TIP?

"I would like to see [Plymouth County District Attorney Tim Cruz] reduce it to a second-degree so we could possibly waive a jury and try the case before a judge," he said. "I would see Tim determine that the case should not go forward and dismiss it, or in the alternative fashion, something where Lindsay gets the mental, physical help that she needs rather than criminal prosecution — because I would not ever, ever in a million years have that woman go to Framingham State Prison."
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

Jack Lu, a retired Massachusetts judge and law professor, said a bench trial would use significantly fewer resources than a second jury trial. Prosecutors could seek second-degree murder charges if they decide her mental illness prevented her from forming the intent required for first-degree murder, he said.
Because of Sullivan's looming retirement, any delays could force the second trial to be held in front of a new judge.

"Perhaps this will be the unusual murder trial that goes off without a hitch," he told Fox News Digital. "For example, have the attorneys double-checked and locked in the availability of experts? This could delay the trial."
He also questioned whether Clancy's retrial should take priority over other cases in the same court.
"My answer: It should not," he said Monday.

Patrick Clancy exits Plymouth Superior Court, Plymouth, Mass., Monday, July27, 2026. (David McGlynn for Fox News Digital)
"It appears to be pushing aside older murder trials," Lu said. "I agree with the prosecutor on this point: ‘It is unfair to them.’ Them is victims and defendants in other murder cases."
Assistant Plymouth County District Attorney Jennifer Sprague had raised other cases slated for trial in her argument for a May trial date, but Sullivan set it for March over her objection.

On Jan. 24, 2023, Clancy's ex-husband Patrick Clancy came home to find her critically injured in their backyard and their three young children — Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months — strangled to death inside.
LINDSAY CLANCY DEFENSE FILES MOTION TO DISMISS UNDER DOUBLE JEOPARDY GROUNDS, WITH FOCUS ON HOLDOUT JUROR

Prosecutors said Clancy attempted to take her own life after killing the children while her husband was out doing errands. Her injuries left her paralyzed. She's been held at a Massachusetts hospital as her case plays out.
Clancy's defense had unsuccessfully raised double jeopardy concerns, which Sullivan dismissed last week.

title: Trump border crackdown drives encounters to record October low as zero-release streak hits 18 months, DHS says
summary: Border Patrol recorded just 8,288 southwest border apprehensions in October, marking a stunning 95% drop from the Biden administration's average.
story: Rep. Pat Fallon sounds the alarm on lawmakers potentially softening their stance on immigration policy and border security. Fallon contrasts the record high of over 200,000 illegal crossings per month under former President Joe Biden with the successful enforcement strategies implemented by President Donald Trump. Fallon emphasizes that protecting citizens requires a strong presidential will rather than congressional action.

Border Patrol agents caught fewer illegal immigrants at the southwest border in all of October than they did in just five days of the same month under former President Joe Biden in 2024, according to new federal figures.

The sharp drop comes as the Trump administration reports 18 straight months of zero releases at the border and the lowest nationwide encounter total ever recorded for the opening month of a fiscal year.
"President Trump unleashed the full strength of DHS to secure the border and enforce the law," Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said. "The results speak for themselves."
TRUMP DHS HITS 16 STRAIGHT MONTHS WITH 0 RELEASES AT THE BORDER

U.S. Customs and Border Protection Air and Marine Operations officers conduct a helicopter demonstration of their rapid response capabilities during a joint exercise at the border between El Paso, Texas, and Ciudad Juárez, Chihuahua, Mexico, on Aug. 13, 2026. (Herika Martinez/AFP via Getty Images)
"Under President Trump’s leadership, we will continue to deliver the most secure border in American history and save American lives," Mullin added.

Border Patrol recorded 8,288 apprehensions along the southwest border in October, down 95% from the Biden administration’s monthly average and 97% from its December 2023 peak, according to the Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Customs and Border Protection.
TRUMP ADMIN MARKS 15 STRAIGHT MONTHS WITH ZERO BORDER RELEASES AS APPREHENSIONS PLUNGE 94%
A construction vehicle builds the border wall near Sunland Park, New Mexico, in 2026. (Christian Torres/Getty Images)

The numbers stand in sharp contrast to the surge retired Yuma Sector Border Patrol Chief Chris Clem described in an October interview with Fox News Digital, when he recalled overwhelmed agents and migrants spilling into surrounding communities.

"They just started walking through the agriculture fields. They started running through town," Clem said, recalling December 2021. "They started going to the food bank. They started knocking on people’s doors at all hours of the night."
CBS REPORT MARVELS AT ONCE-CHAOTIC SOUTHERN BORDER CROSSING HAS GONE QUIET UNDER TRUMP CRACKDOWN

In Yuma alone, Clem said daily arrivals climbed from roughly 25 in December 2020 to more than 1,000 a year later. During one particularly difficult three-day stretch in December 2021, daily arrivals approached 1,500, he said.
"The agents, their heads were in the right place. They knew they had to do the job," Clem said. "But when you’re outnumbered, literally 100 to one, it’s very difficult."
DHS TOUTS MILLIONS OF ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT DEPARTURES AS BORDER CROSSINGS DROP 94% UNDER TRUMP
U.S. Border Patrol agent Nicole Ballistrea watches over the U.S.-Mexico border fence in Nogales, Arizona. (John Moore/Getty Images)
The latest southwest border apprehension total fell 7% from September, carrying the decline into the first month of fiscal year 2027.
Nationwide, CBP recorded 27,890 encounters in October, also down 7% from September. That was the lowest October total on record and the lowest for any month since February, the agencies said.
TRUMP HITS DRAMATIC MILESTONE IN MASSIVE DEPARTURE FROM BIDEN BORDER PLAN: 'WHAT A DIFFERENCE'

The new figures follow preliminary DHS data showing 98,708 southwest border apprehensions for all of fiscal year 2026, roughly 95% below the Biden administration’s annual average of more than 1.8 million.
Clem credited stronger border enforcement and the prospect of deportation with changing the calculation for people considering crossing illegally.
TRUMP ADMINISTRATION'S IMMIGRATION PUSH FUELS ICE'S BIGGEST ARREST MONTH IN AGENCY HISTORY

A U.S. Border Patrol checkpoint on Interstate 19, about 20 miles north of the Mexican border. Agents stop all northbound traffic, looking for undocumented immigrants and drug smugglers. Dogs help in the search. (Jim West/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)
"They know that they’re not gonna be processed and released, which was the status quo under the Biden-Harris administration," he told Fox News Digital in the October interview.
He said enforcement inside the country reinforced that message by making clear that getting past Border Patrol did not eliminate the possibility of arrest and removal.
ICE ARRESTS MORE THAN 100 ALLEGED GANG MEMBERS IN SINGLE WEEK, INCLUDING VIOLENT MS-13, TDA SUSPECTS: DHS
"When you combine the strong border posture, as well as the strong and robust interior enforcement, it’s a recipe for success," Clem said.
CBP Commissioner Rodney S. Scott credited Trump and Mullin with giving the agency an "unprecedented level of control over our borders."
MULLIN TELLS RUTHLESS PODCAST THAT THE TRUMP ADMINISTRATION HAS APPREHENDED 2,210 TERRORISTS
Secretary Markwayne Mullin shakes hands with President Donald Trump, left, after his swearing in. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)
"We know more about who and what is entering our homeland than at any time in our nation’s history," Scott said in the latest announcement.
"America is safer because we are enforcing the rule of law, keeping threats out of our communities and putting the security of the American people first," he added.
The decline in border apprehensions came as CBP reported a jump in the weight of drugs seized nationwide.

Seizures of cocaine, methamphetamine, heroin, fentanyl and marijuana collectively rose 44% from September, according to the agencies. Officers and agents seized 14,745 pounds of methamphetamine and 9,032 pounds of cocaine in October, increases of 59% and 60%, respectively.
The release did not include a separate October total for fentanyl.
Still, Clem cautioned in October that lower apprehension numbers did not eliminate threats from smugglers or people trying to evade detection.
"There are always gonna be that risk where somebody does sneak through. Who is that person?" he said.
"We have an immigration issue we need to address," Clem said. "We need to find a way to retain and recruit those that are here, that are foreign nationals that want to contribute."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"But none of that should matter when it comes down to securing the border," he added. "We should always be looking at keeping America safe."

title: Illinois ethanol plant bomb investigation: Person of interest in custody
summary: FBI Springfield, Illinois, is leading the manhunt after a credible explosive device was found at BioUrja Renewables in Peoria, sparking evacuations.
story: The ‘Big Weekend Show’ panel discusses a bomb found at an ethanol plant in Illinois and the ongoing investigation.
A person of interest is in custody Monday in an investigation into who left a bomb near an ethanol facility in Peoria, Illinois, a police spokesperson confirmed to Fox News.
The FBI, whose Springfield, Illinois, office is leading the ongoing investigation, confirmed "law enforcement activity" in Peoria County.

The explosive device found at BioUrja Renewables on Friday led to evacuations within a one-mile "blast radius" and triggered nearly a 24-hour emergency response. A large facility the size of 44½ football fields and a large area that was evacuated suggested a potentially major threat to public safety.

"I can just tell you it was deemed a credible threat," Peoria Police Chief Brad Dixon told reporters at a briefing Saturday, noting that forensic testing is still underway to determine the exact composition of the device. "There's an extensive criminal investigation going on."
Dixon declined to call the device a "bomb" despite the facility reporting to police it had received a bomb threat.
IED NEAR ALABAMA RESERVOIR DETONATED AFTER OFFICIALS WARN OF 'UNPRECEDENTED' CRITICAL INFRASTRUCTURE THREAT

Federal investigators have taken over the probe and manhunt for someone who left a "credible threat" and called in a bomb scare at a sprawling Illinois ethanol plant that spans 44½ football fields. (FBI Springfield Office)

Authorities warned that because the facility houses large quantities of ethanol and other highly combustible chemicals, an ignition could have triggered a massive explosion far larger than the device itself.

FBI Special Agent Ryan Presley said the investigation remains in its preliminary stages, declining to release further details about a potential motive or suspect. A Sunday morning news conference held by the Springfield office was postponed until at least Monday.

"While the area has been cleared and no additional suspicious devices have been located, the FBI encourages the public to remain alert and share any relevant information they may have," Springfield FBI posted Saturday to X.
WAVE OF SCHOOL BOMB THREATS ROCKS KENTUCKY AMID SUSPECTED ROBOCALL SCHEME, POLICE SAY

"We will work tirelessly to identify the individual responsible and bring them to justice," Presley added, noting the FBI has provided bomb technicians, investigative and intelligence resources to local authorities before taking over the lead of the investigation.
The incident began Friday afternoon when workers at the Peoria plant reported a bomb threat they received to police. Roughly an hour later, crews located a suspicious package near the facility.

Peoria Mayor Rita Ali warned of a potentially catastrophic event because, she told WMBD-TV, BioUrja is "a plant that has ethanol and highly combustible types of chemicals, and so that’s what alarms us."
CAR LOADED WITH EXPLOSIVES SLAMS INTO LAVISH PORTLAND SOCIAL CLUB, BOMB SQUAD STILL PULLING OUT LIVE DEVICES

By Saturday afternoon, officials from the Peoria Police Department, the FBI and the U.S. Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives completed their search of the facility and confirmed no other items of concern were found. Bomb technicians rendered it safe, Peoria police said.

The evacuation order was lifted Saturday, almost a full day after the device was discovered Friday close to the ethanol plant in Peoria, a city of about 110,000 people, about 150 miles southwest of Chicago. Bomb technicians rendered it safe, Peoria police said.
"We understand that this is a disruptive process for our residents and guests," Dixon said. "We’re asking for the public’s patience while we work to make this area safe."
No injuries were reported, and no arrests have been made.
ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT ALLEGEDLY MADE BOMB THREAT ON FLIGHT, DHS SAYS

"#FBISpringfield is now leading the investigation following the identification of an explosive device found at BioUrja Renewables on Friday, Nov. 13," the Saturday X post began. "While the area has been cleared and no additional suspicious devices have been located, the FBI encourages the public to remain alert and share any relevant information they may have related to this ongoing situation by immediately calling 9-1-1, 1-800-CALL-FBI, or online at http:// tips.fbi.gov.

"Tipsters may elect to remain anonymous," it added. "The FBI continues to work closely with local, state, and federal law enforcement partners, to include @ATFHQ, @ILSecOfState, @ILStatePolice, the Peoria County Sheriff’s Office, Peoria Fire Department, and @peoria_police, to identify the individual(s) responsible and will hold them fully accountable under the law. All releasable investigative updates will be shared via official FBI Springfield social channels."

Because the BioUrja Renewables plant sits directly on the banks of the Illinois River, the one-mile evacuation zone extended across the waterway. Coast Guard Capt. Brandy Parker confirmed the agency established a safety perimeter blocking all vessel traffic between mile markers 160 and 164 while bomb technicians rendered the device safe and searched the facility.

The Illinois River, a major tributary of the Mississippi, is a major commercial shipping corridor. The Coast Guard is responsible for securing inland navigable waterways and waterfront industrial facilities against terrorism, sabotage and hazardous material spills — especially given the catastrophic environmental and safety risks if an explosion had ignited the plant's ethanol reserves.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Parker serves as the sector commander for U.S. Coast Guard Sector Upper Mississippi River. The safety shutdown came the same weekend Coast Guard crews far south in Sector New Orleans were forced to close a stretch of the lower Mississippi River after the asphalt tanker Atlantic Asphalt collided with a docked cruise ship carrying 129 passengers near the Port of New Orleans.
Fox News' Janelle Benham, The Associated Press and Reuters contributed to this report.

title: Mamdani guts elite NYPD tactical unit, backs 'civilian-led approach' to responding to protests
summary: Zohran Mamdani disbands the NYPD Strategic Response Group and unveils a civilian-led dialogue team to handle New York City protest response.
story: NYC ICE official Kenneth Genalo blasts Mayor Zohran Mamdani and sanctuary policies, warning they force agents into dangerous street arrests and put public safety at risk.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced the disbanding of the NYPD's Strategic Response Group (SRG) on Monday, saying the city will now pursue a "civilian-led approach" to responding to protests.

Mamdani made the announcement alongside Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch, stating that the SRG's counterterrorism functions will be folded into an existing command, while a brand-new organization will now lead protest response, the Community Dialogue and De-escalation Division (CDDD).

The CDDD, which will lie within the Mayor's Office of Community Safety, will work to "improve the NYPD's protest response" via a specialized "dialogue team," known as the First Amendment Support Team (FAST), they said.

"The CDDD will not have weapons or arrest powers. FAST will consist of 30 uniformed officers trained in communication and de-escalation. The NYPD will also establish a new Patrol Support Division (PSD), a unit within the NYPD’s Patrol Services Bureau, with vetted officers who will spend most of their time on patrol-related duties and receive specialized crowd management training to support responses to demonstrations," the mayor's office said in a statement.
NYC MAYOR ZOHRAN MAMDANI SAYS HE WON'T FIRE NYPD COMMISSIONER JESSICA TISCH DESPITE SOCIALIST PRESSURE
The NYPD Strategic Response Group (SRG) monitors a crowd outside 26 Federal Plaza on Oct. 21, 2025 in New York City. (Photo by Adam Gray/Getty Images)

"During our campaign, I promised New Yorkers that we would disband the Strategic Response Group and separate counterterrorism from protest response, and today we are delivering on that promise," Mamdani said in a statement.
MINNEAPOLIS PROGRESSIVES TURN ON GEORGE FLOYD-ERA PUBLIC SAFETY OVERHAUL, PUSH TO DISMANTLE OFFICE
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch speak at a Sunday morning news conference after a spate of weekend shootings in Brooklyn. (Kyle Mazza/Anadolu)

"New Yorkers exercising their constitutional right to protest should not be met with the same police response as a terrorism threat. We are establishing a new, civilian-led approach that prioritizes dialogue, engagement and de-escalation," he added.

The reforms also impose new restrictions on the tools police are allowed to use when responding to protests, including codified bans on kettling, long guns and tear gas. Pepper spray will also not be used as a crowd management tool, and "long-range acoustic devices" will be limited to 90 decibels.
MAMDANI, NYPD GIVE SECURITY UPDATE AHEAD OF JEWISH HIGH HOLY DAYS, 9/11 25TH ANNIVERSARY

NYPD officers detain a demonstrator during a protest amid a two-week ceasefire in the U.S.-Israeli conflict with Iran, along Third Avenue in the Midtown area of New York City on April 13, 2026. (Shannon Stapleton/Reuters)

Under the previous structure, the NYPD said the SRG responded to citywide mobilizations, civil disorders and major events and was a "critical asset" during parades, protests and the papal visit. SRG personnel were "also deployed to areas requiring an increased police presence due to increased crime or other conditions" and "mobilizes for shootings, bank robberies, missing persons, demonstrations, or other significant incidents," according to the department.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Tisch noted at a March budget hearing that the SRG did not typically deal with peaceful protests, but was deployed for protests that involved criminal activity. She also noted that in 2025, the NYPD facilitated 4,255 protests and the SRG was available at 245 of them, or roughly 6%.
Anders Hagstrom is a reporter with Fox News Digital covering national politics and major breaking news events.

title: Young paraglider dies after reported emergency sends him crashing into field during Illinois flight
summary: Officials are investigating a fatal paragliding incident involving a 21-year-old man from a Chicago suburb who shared his aerial adventures and daring stunts online.
story: Giovanni Lopez’s death remains under investigation as officials await an autopsy to determine the cause and manner of death.(Giovanni Lopez/Facebook)
An Illinois paraglider died in a weekend crash after reportedly experiencing an emergency mid-flight.
Officials on Saturday identified the victim as Giovanni Lopez, 21, of Woodridge, a southwest suburb of Chicago.
Lopez frequently documented his paragliding adventures and daring aerial maneuvers on social media.
The Kendall County Coroner’s Office said it was notified around 3:40 p.m. Saturday of a possible fatality in Plainfield, an area dotted with farm fields southwest of Chicago.
CLIMBER STRANDED ON 6-INCH LEDGE AT 11,000 FEET AS 46 MPH WINDS GROUND RESCUE HELICOPTER
Giovanni Lopez, 21, died in a paragliding incident in Plainfield, Illinois, after a reported midair emergency. (Giovanni Lopez/Facebook)
"The Kendall County Coroner’s Office was notified of a possible fatality related to a paragliding incident in the area of Ridge Road and 127th Street in Plainfield, Illinois," the office said.
Officials did not disclose the exact circumstances that led to Lopez’s death.
NBC Chicago reported that Lopez encountered an emergency while paragliding.
HIKER IDENTIFIED, POPULAR TRAIL CLOSED AFTER DEADLY FALL AT UTAH'S ZION NATIONAL PARK
Giovanni Lopez frequently shared videos of his paragliding adventures and daring aerial stunts on social media. (Giovanni Lopez/Facebook)
Witnesses reportedly rushed to Lopez's aid and attempted to help him until paramedics arrived and continued lifesaving efforts, the outlet said.
Upon arrival, coroner’s deputies pronounced Lopez dead at the scene.
Officials said the cause and manner of death will be determined following a forensic autopsy.
The incident remains under investigation by the Plainfield Police Department and the Kendall County Coroner's Office.
Giovanni Lopez wears a motorized propeller unit on his back as part of his paragliding equipment. (Giovanni Lopez/Facebook)

title: NTSB details warning whistles and emergency orders before tanker collision capsized New Orleans riverboat
summary: NTSB investigators detail warning whistles and emergency orders captured on the tanker's voyage recorder before the New Orleans riverboat collision.
story: NTSB investigators detail a steering problem, warning whistles and emergency anchor orders in the minutes before the Atlantic Asphalt struck the docked American Heritage in New Orleans. (Credit: WVUE)

A tanker suffered a steering problem about two minutes before slamming into a docked New Orleans riverboat Friday, federal investigators said Sunday, detailing warning whistles, calls for help and emergency orders before the collision.

The Atlantic Asphalt was heading upriver near the Crescent City Connection Bridge at about 12:26 p.m. when its rudder remained turned to the right, sending the ship toward the Mississippi River’s east bank, National Transportation Safety Board senior marine accident investigator Bart Barnum said.
The tanker struck American Cruise Lines’ American Heritage at about 12:28 p.m. The riverboat capsized in about 22 minutes, according to preliminary information presented by the NTSB.
NEW ORLEANS BOAT CRASH CALLED ‘MIRACLE ON THE MISSISSIPPI’ AS EVERYONE IS ACCOUNTED FOR, OFFICIALS SAY
NTSB team surveying the wreckage. (NTSB)
Investigators downloaded more than nine hours of data from the tanker’s voyage data recorder, including bridge audio, rudder angle, engine RPM, course and speed.

The recordings captured sounds consistent with the ship’s whistle, warnings and requests for assistance over its marine radio, commands to deploy anchors and emergency shiphandling orders, Barnum said.
11-NIGHT CARIBBEAN CRUISE ABRUPTLY CANCELED AFTER COAST GUARD DETAINS SHIP
Officials described the steering problem as a "steering casualty," but cautioned that the term does not establish what went wrong.
"It could be many different things. That is something that we are investigating very closely," Barnum said.
AT LEAST 6 PEOPLE INJURED AFTER BOSTON DUCK BOAT OVERTURNS NEAR ENTRANCE TO POPULAR TOURIST ATTRACTION
Tugboats surround the Atlantic Asphalt tanker in New Orleans following its collision with the docked American Heritage river cruiser on Nov. 13, 2026. (Kat Ramirez for Fox News Digital)

NTSB board member John DeLeeuw said investigators have data on the tanker’s speed but are still analyzing it before releasing it publicly. Video showed anchors were down, but investigators are still determining which ones were deployed and how far, he said.

The findings follow a frantic rescue effort that officials said left everyone aboard the American Heritage alive. Roughly 100 people were pulled from the Mississippi River, while responders evacuated more than 80 before the vessel overturned, Port of New Orleans Harbor Police Chief Melanie Montroll said Saturday.
TWO DEAD, INCLUDING INFANT, AFTER BOAT CAPSIZES IN NEW YORK HARBOR; 12 RESCUED
"This is a miracle. It is a literal miracle on the Mississippi," Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry said Friday.
Eight people remained hospitalized Saturday, including two in serious condition. The other six were stable, officials said.
FBI INVESTIGATES SUSPECTED HOMICIDE ABOARD MSC SEASCAPE CRUISE SHIP AFTER SUDDEN RETURN TO TEXAS
The NTSB said Sunday that 140 passengers and 50 crew members were aboard the riverboat, a total of 190.
New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno also said the American Heritage’s captain was injured but stayed aboard until passengers and crew were accounted for, becoming the last person to leave.
MOM LOSES GRIP ON DAUGHTER AS PASSENGER FERRY CAPSIZES WITH 20 PEOPLE STILL MISSING
"Every moment of the critical time [Friday], he did not want to leave his ship," Moreno said Saturday.

Coast Guard Capt. Melanie Burnham said Saturday that crews were preparing to remove 16,000 gallons of fuel before salvage operations, warning that removing the capsized vessel could take weeks. DeLeeuw said Sunday that divers had been in the water, with salvage work overseen by the Coast Guard and salvage companies.
UNLICENSED NYC BOAT OPERATOR ALLEGEDLY IGNORED SAFETY WARNINGS BEFORE MOTHER, BABY DIED IN CAPSIZING: FEDS
Port of New Orleans collision map. (Google Maps)
Interviews with American Heritage crew members were underway Sunday. Interviews with the Atlantic Asphalt’s crew were scheduled to begin Monday and continue through the week, Barnum said.

The NTSB expects to release a preliminary report within about 30 days. Sunday’s briefing was its last planned on-site news conference, DeLeeuw said, with further updates to be posted online.

title: Duffy: Investigators examining 2 routers after nationwide FAA ground stop, no signs of foreign cyberattack
summary: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy says two routers from FAA facilities in Texas and Arkansas are undergoing deep diagnostics after the ground stop.
story: Fox News correspondent Alex Hogan reports from the White House on the travel chaos resulting from a massive nationwide ground stop. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy also joins 'Fox News Sunday' to detail the latest on the investigation as he asks Congress for additional funding to modernize the agency's telecommunications network.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Sunday that two routers from FAA facilities in Texas and Arkansas are undergoing extensive testing as investigators examine whether faulty equipment or an installation problem triggered the nation's longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years.

Appearing on "Fox News Sunday," Duffy said that investigators have found no indication of a foreign cyberattack, although the FBI and other federal law enforcement partners remain involved in the probe.

"We think it was the installation or the router that was the bad actor," Duffy said. "But we're open, if we see something else, we're gonna continue to investigate with our federal partners and law enforcement."
FAA SAYS AIR TRAVEL SHOULD BE BACK TO NORMAL SUNDAY AFTER NATIONWIDE GROUND STOP

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, right, with Federal Aviation Administrator Bryan Bedford, left, speaks during a news conference at the U.S. Department of Transportation, Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Tom Brenner)

In an update posted on X, Duffy said contractor L3Harris had secured the two routers from remote FAA facilities in Texas and Arkansas and was conducting "deep diagnostics testing" at its headquarters in Florida, with engineers from the FAA, Juniper and Cisco assisting.
The investigation follows Friday's nationwide ground stop, which halted air traffic for more than four hours and contributed to disruptions affecting roughly 15,000 flights Friday and Saturday.

The fallout continued Sunday, with 3,798 flights delayed and another 1,638 canceled within, into or out of the United States as of noon ET, according to flight-tracking website FlightAware. Among the hardest-hit airports according to the provided data were Atlanta's Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport, with 376 delays, and Dallas Fort Worth International Airport, with 363 delays and 195 cancellations.

The shutdown occurred as L3Harris was replacing aging copper wiring with fiber-optic technology in the FAA's communications system. The work led to intermittent communications and radar gaps, prompting officials to halt flights nationwide.
Duffy said President Donald Trump convened federal officials on Friday as the administration investigated whether the disruption could have involved malicious interference.
"President Trump actually had the whole of government on the phone on Friday," Duffy said. "Was anyone seeing footprints? Was anyone hearing chatter? Was this a cyber attack from a foreign nation?"
"We have no indication that that was at play here," he added.
4 CRITICAL TRAVEL ISSUES FOR THOSE DELAYED AND DISRUPTED BY FAA NATIONWIDE GROUND STOP
Duffy defended the decision to issue the nationwide ground stop, emphasizing that passenger safety takes precedence when problems emerge in the FAA's communications network.
"When we have inconsistencies in our network we're going to shut it down," Duffy said.

Passengers wait at boarding gates at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in Washington, D.C. on Nov. 13, 2026, after the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a nationwide ground stop at all airports due to a communications problem. (Zina DESMAZES / AFP via Getty Images)
The transportation secretary also warned that the FAA's communications infrastructure remains outdated despite ongoing efforts to replace copper wiring with fiber-optic technology.
"We're still using an old 1980 architecture for telecom," Duffy said. "I need a brand new telecom system."
BUTTIGIEG TAKES SWIPE AT TRUMP ADMINISTRATION AMID FAA FLIGHT CHAOS
Duffy said AT&T, Verizon and Lumen are prepared to help build a replacement network, but additional congressional funding is needed to move forward.

The request has drawn scrutiny from congressional Democrats, who argue the administration has yet to spend billions already allocated for air traffic control modernization. Duffy countered that the existing funds were designated for specific upgrades, including radar, radios and electronic flight strips, rather than a new communications network.
Travelers wait at LaGuardia Airport in New York, Friday, Nov. 13, 2026, after the Federal Aviation Administration grounded flights nationwide. (AP Photo/Ryan Murphy)
Meanwhile, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said Saturday that "the worst is behind us," with air travel expected to return to normal by the end of Sunday.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The nationwide ground stop was the first since January 2023 and only the second since the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks.

title: Virginia parents charged after house party draws hundreds of teens, fireworks and alleged underage drinking
summary: Fairfax County police charged Lisa and Aubrey Vaughan after their 13-year-old sons' small backyard party spiraled into a massive gathering with fireworks and crowds.
story: Officers were speaking with homeowners in McLean, Virginia, when a loud boom drew their attention to the backyard, where dozens of teenagers were seen streaming out as another boom rang out on Nov. 6. (Fairfax County Police Department/Facebook)

A Virginia couple who say they wanted to give their 13-year-old sons a safe place to hang out with a handful of classmates ended up facing criminal charges after their backyard gathering exploded into a massive party with hundreds of teenagers, fireworks and police descending on their neighborhood.

Lisa Vaughan, 45, and Aubrey Vaughan, 55, were charged with contributing to the delinquency of a minor and maintaining a common nuisance after Fairfax County police responded to their McLean home on Nov. 6. The couple maintains their innocence, with their attorney saying an invitation intended for just 10 to 20 classmates spread to older students.
"There will be no more," Aubrey Vaughan told FOX 5 DC, referring to the party for their sons. "We're done."
COLLEGE HOMECOMING PARTY TURNS TO CHAOS AS DECK COLLAPSES, LEAVING AT LEAST 28 PEOPLE INJURED

Lisa Vaughan, 45, and Aubrey Vaughan, 55, were charged with contributing to the delinquency of a minor and maintaining a common nuisance in connection with the party. (Fairfax County Police Department)

Police responded to multiple 911 calls around 9:03 p.m. reporting an out-of-control party. Callers estimated between 100 and 300 people had gathered at the home, where responding officers encountered a large crowd and fireworks being discharged, according to police.

Aubrey Vaughan apologized to neighbors, saying he was "embarrassed" by how quickly the gathering spiraled out of control. He and his wife even had their 13-year-old sons go door-to-door to apologize after police dispersed the crowd, according to FOX 5.
Police bodycam video shared to the department's social media shows Lisa Vaughan standing outside her family's home while speaking with responding officers. (Fairfax County Police Department)

The couple had planned a small eighth-grade gathering, but the invitation circulated on Snapchat and eventually reached students at a local high school, attracting uninvited teenagers, according to the family's attorney.
Aubrey Vaughan said he had "zero idea" high schoolers would show up and that he and his wife struggled to keep them out of their backyard and home.

Police described the gathering as an "underage drinking party," but Vaughan disputed suggestions that alcohol was permitted. He told FOX 5 that the invitation explicitly prohibited alcohol and bags, and that he and his wife were home supervising the entire time.
Responding officers encountered a large crowd of teens and fireworks being discharged at the home. (Fairfax County Police Department)
Aubrey Vaughan estimated the incident lasted about 45 minutes, saying he realized things were getting out of hand roughly 10 to 15 minutes before officers arrived.

"They wanted to maintain a safe place, free from alcohol, for kids to have a good time, but they had no control about all the kids that arrived and caused chaos in their neighborhood," the couple's attorney, Alaric Piette, told FOX 5.

Piette said the parents welcomed officers and offered to let them inspect the party area, but police declined. Both parents later turned themselves in and were released on $1,000 unsecured bonds each.
FAMILIES CONFRONT CALIFORNIA 'PARTY MOM' IN COURT, CALLING HER A 'MONSTER' WHO GROOMED THEIR CHILDREN
Fairfax County Police Chief Kevin Davis acknowledged the challenges parents face when deciding whether to host gatherings at home rather than let teenagers socialize elsewhere without supervision.
"I think it's universally a bad idea to host anything at a home," Davis said, warning that large gatherings involving alcohol, drugs or reckless behavior can quickly become dangerous.

The couple maintains their innocence, with their attorney saying an invitation intended for just 10 to 20 classmates spread to older high school students who overran the party. (Fairfax County Police Department)
The police chief emphasized that "parents have to be parents" and "adults have to be adults," warning that good intentions can have unintended consequences.
Aubrey Vaughan, meanwhile, said he was grateful police helped disperse the crowd and harbors no resentment toward the responding officers.
"The lesson is just make sure you're watching Snapchat," Aubrey Vaughan told FOX 5.

Police have not announced charges against any teenagers who attended the gathering.

Transportation Sec. Sean Duffy says the situation arose when contractor L3Harris Technologies Inc. was replacing old copper wiring in the air traffic control system with new fiber wiring, causing a system overload.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy speaks during a press briefing at Department of Transportation headquarters on Nov. 14, 2026, in Washington, D.C. title: 'Purge'-masked suspect accused of killing college student at Halloween bash — before his sister helps nab him
summary: Omar Perez's sister identified him using police photos and the family's Life360 app after the University of Colorado Boulder student's killing.
story: Omar Perez, 18, is held without bond on murder charges in the death of Luca Hanlon, 19, near University Hill.

Colorado police have identified the people sought in security footage released after a Halloween party shooting that killed a University of Colorado Boulder student, as prosecutors consider additional charges.
On Thursday, Boulder Police Public Information Officer Dionne Waugh confirmed to Fox News Digital that "everyone in the photos and video we released" has now been identified.

The primary suspect, Omar Perez, 18, faces murder and related charges in the death of Luca Hanlon, 19, following a deadly confrontation at an off-campus Oct. 31 party in Boulder’s University Hill neighborhood.
Luca Hanlon, pictured in his graduation gown, poses with his family. (Facebook/Grace Crocilla Hanlon)
MASS SHOOTING AT GEORGIA BLOCK PARTY LEAVES 2 DEAD, 35 INJURED

After the arrest, detectives asked for the public's help in identifying three other people seen in video and photos from that night, including two males, one wearing an "Art the Clown" shirt and another in a red hoodie, and a female witness.
It’s unclear whether they will face charges.
"The investigation is ongoing. When and if there are additional arrests or charges, I will send out a news release," Waugh said.

Shannon Carbone, the public information officer (PIO) for the Boulder County District Attorney’s Office, told Fox News Digital that prosecutors "successfully argued in court Tuesday to have Perez held without bond."
Perez's preliminary hearing is scheduled for Feb. 10, 2027, according to the District Attorney's Office.
The Colorado Public Defender’s Office declined to comment on the case. The university did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
TEEN PREVIOUSLY CONVICTED IN SHOOTING ACCUSED OF KILLING PREGNANT MOM OF 4 INSIDE SPIRIT HALLOWEEN
The shooting

According to a Boulder police arrest affidavit, police first responded to a home off Marine Street around 9:58 p.m. on Halloween after receiving a noise complaint. Responding officers issued a nuisance-party citation, and hundreds of people left the gathering. Around 90 minutes later, at 11:28 p.m., officers returned after a call concerning gunshots fired.
Luca Hanlon was shot at a home on Marine Street in Boulder, Colorado. (Google Maps)

Witnesses told authorities that Perez had been in the group of people that left, but he returned to the residence with six others. They were asked to leave, but Perez and his group allegedly became irate, leading to a scuffle in the living room and on the front porch. A witness said Perez appeared to be wearing a SWAT uniform and a "Purge" mask.
A resident at the home put Perez in a headlock, prompting Perez to allegedly pull out a gun and open fire, the affidavit stated.
One witness told police he heard Perez threaten, "Oh, I could shoot this place up."
POLICE IDENTIFY AGENT KILLED AFTER SUSPECT OPENS FIRE NEAR COLORADO BUS, WOUNDS OTHER 3 OFFICERS
Perez shot Hanlon in the neck and another 19-year-old student in the leg. Hanlon died the following day at Boulder Community Health.
Luca Hanlon, right, is pictured with his family. (Facebook/Grace Crocilla Hanlon)
"I do not have any other updates on the second victim because of privacy. If that changes I will send out a news release," Waugh told Fox News Digital.
Sister identifies suspect
The arrest affidavit stated that Perez’s sister saw photos released by Boulder police and contacted them after recognizing her brother's clothes.

She then checked the family's "Life360" app, which tracked Perez arriving at the residence around the time of the shooting. The app also mapped his path following the shooting. Over the next several hours, Perez allegedly traveled through Westminster, Arvada, Keenesburg, and then back to Thornton.
"The defendant was arrested in Thornton. He is not a CU student and, contrary to some rumors, was not arrested on campus," Carbone told Fox News Digital.
Luca Hanlon was a student at the University of Colorado in Boulder. (Andrew Burton/Getty Images)

His sister told investigators that days before the shooting, Perez illegally purchased a 10mm Glock "on the street" and posted photos of the weapon on Instagram. She said he had replaced a revolver he "threw in some bushes" after accidentally shooting himself in the calf on Sept. 26.
The affidavit also noted that Perez and other people who accompanied him traveled in a newer red Audi sedan.
When Perez picked his sister up from work, she got into the Audi and noticed a "black purge looking mask" on the floorboard. She also told police three people were in the vehicle with Perez.

Perez allegedly told his sister that they had been beaten up earlier at a party they attended, "by four guys and his friends," the affidavit stated.
In addition to murder with extreme indifference, Perez faces first-degree assault and attempted first-degree murder charges, both with extreme indifference.
"For first degree murder, the only sentence allowed under law is life in prison without the possibility of parole. Additional charges will likely be filed," Carbone said.
Luca Hanlon
CU Boulder identified Hanlon, of Pennsylvania, as a second-year media production student in its College of Communication, Media, Design and Information.

"It doesn't feel real. He was my best friend. He was always there. If I needed a shoulder to cry, he was there, to celebrate the biggest wins in life. He was just like an all-around, stand-up, great, just model citizen," Hanlon’s friend, Jack Anderson, told Denver’s ABC 7.
"I would say he was who I aspired to be in life. He was that person."
Anyone with any information about the case is urged to contact Boulder police at 303-441-3333, or submit tips online at the police department’s Evidence Submission Portal.

title: Harvard scientist pushes back on NASA chief over mystery space object: 'It's not an asteroid'
summary: Avi Loeb challenges NASA's Jared Isaacman, arguing 1998 KY26 is not an asteroid and could be a lost Soviet spacecraft from a failed Mars mission.
story: Avi Loeb tells Fox News Digital why he believes 1998 KY26 could be the lost Soviet Phobos 1 spacecraft and says a 2031 mission could settle the mystery.

A Harvard astrophysicist behind the theory that a mysterious object speeding through the solar system could actually be a lost Soviet spacecraft is pushing back on NASA's top official, saying the object is "not an asteroid."

Known as 1998 KY26, the roughly 36-foot-wide object is believed to be a near-Earth asteroid but is accelerating in a way gravity alone cannot explain. Harvard astrophysicist Avi Loeb and his colleagues have examined whether it could instead be Phobos 1, a Soviet spacecraft that stopped communicating while traveling to Mars in 1988.
NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman weighed in on the mysterious object Thursday during an appearance on "Fox & Friends."
EIFFEL TOWER-SIZED ASTEROID APOPHIS TO PASS CLOSER TO EARTH THAN MANY SATELLITES IN 2029, NASA SAYS
"I've not seen any evidence to suggest this is...anything other than an asteroid," Isaacman said.
Two shape models show scientists' estimates of the form of near-Earth object 1998 KY26. (Credit: NASA)
Loeb challenged that assessment during an interview with Fox News Digital on Friday.
HARVARD ASTRONOMER TAPPED TO LEAD WHITE HOUSE UFO COUNCIL SAYS US GOVERNMENT 'BAFFLED BY WHAT THEY ARE SEEING'

"Well, first of all, it's not an asteroid because 1998 KY26 appears to have non-gravitational acceleration, meaning it's being pushed by some force other than gravity, and asteroids are just rocks," Loeb said.
Scientists have been trying to explain what is causing the additional acceleration.
SCIENTISTS DISCOVER POTENTIALLY MASSIVE DWARF PLANET CANDIDATE HIDING BEYOND PLUTO
One theory has been that KY26 is a "dark comet," a rocky object behaving like a comet without producing a visible cloud or tail.
An illustration shows the Soviet Phobos 1 spacecraft, which was launched toward Mars in July 1988 but lost after a faulty command caused it to shut down. (Credit: NASA)

New research from Georgia Tech has cast doubt on whether KY26 could retain enough ice to produce that effect, while other research has suggested pressure from sunlight and heat radiating from its surface could account for the acceleration.
GIANT ROBOTIC CLAWS WILL GRAB DEAD SATELLITES IN SPACE

Loeb told Fox News Digital that his team found KY26's trajectory closely resembles that of the failed Soviet mission and calculated that sunlight reflecting off Phobos 1 could produce a push consistent with the nongravitational acceleration observed in KY26.
He also pointed to recent observations indicating the object is highly reflective and rotates about once every five minutes.

A model of Phobos 1, the Soviet spacecraft that lost contact with Earth while traveling to Mars in 1988. Harvard astrophysicist Avi Loeb and his colleagues have examined whether the mysterious object 1998 KY26 could be the lost probe. (Credit: NASA)
NASA'S CHANDRA TELESCOPE REVEALS MILKY WAY'S OUTER REACHES MAY STRETCH FARTHER THAN PREVIOUSLY KNOWN
The lack of a visible cometary tail or evidence of material escaping the object is central to Loeb's skepticism of the dark-comet explanation.

"It could be a comet shedding some gas backward that is pushing it forward, but in that case we should have seen the gas," Loeb said. "We should have seen the dust because for comets we see a tail and the dust particles are being pushed away from the sun by the solar radiation."
"We don't see a cometary tail. We don't see any evidence for outgassing around this object. That's the puzzle," he added.
Loeb compared the debate over how to classify KY26 to encountering an unfamiliar animal at a zoo.
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X
Avi Loeb speaks during the SALT conference in Manhattan, New York City, on September 14, 2022. (David 'Dee' Delgado)
"If you are an expert on zebras and you see an elephant, you would say the elephant is a zebra without stripes," Loeb said. "But that's an oxymoron because it's a completely different animal."
He also argued that scientists should be willing to consider explanations outside the familiar categories of asteroids and comets when observations do not neatly fit either one.
THE NEXT FRONTIER: WASHINGTON GRAPPLES WITH ITS LATEST SPACE ODDITY
"Innovation in science requires some imagination," Loeb said. "It requires you to allow for the possibility that our knowledge is incomplete."
SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS
Fox News Digital reached out to NASA for a response to Loeb's comments and asked whether Isaacman stands by his assessment of KY26.

"In a paper published in 2025, NASA completed a comprehensive orbital analysis of near-Earth asteroid 1998 KY26 and concluded its behavior is driven by solar radiation forces," NASA told Fox News Digital. "Using recent measurements of the asteroid's shape, size, and rotation, a team led by NASA's Center for Near-Earth Object Studies determined that the asteroid's complex trajectory is due to solar radiation forces, which are the natural push of sunlight and thermal emission on its non-spherical shape.

Jared Isaacman, President Donald Trump's nominee to be National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Administrator, testifies during a Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee confirmation hearing in the Russell Senate Office Building on Capitol Hill on April 9, 2025, in Washington. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)
"This analysis demonstrates the asteroid's path isn't caused by hidden comet-like activity."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB

Loeb acknowledged that his team's theory remains unproven, but said a definitive answer could come in 2031, when the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency's Hayabusa2 spacecraft is expected to rendezvous with KY26.
SEND US A TIP
Loeb predicts the encounter could show that scientists have been looking at a piece of Soviet space history rather than an unusual natural object.
GOT A TIP?
A concept image of an asteroid passing Earth. (iStock)
"We predict that when they land on it, instead of seeing an iceberg, they will find the label ‘Made in the USSR,’" Loeb said.
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST
Loeb also acknowledged that the 2031 encounter could settle the question once and for all.
GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL

title: UPS cargo plane, Copa Airlines passenger jet collide at Miami airport, leaving 2 injured
summary: A UPS Airlines cargo plane and a Copa Airlines passenger jet collided on the ground at Miami International Airport on Saturday night, leaving two people with minor injuries.
story: A UPS cargo plane and Copa Airlines passenger jet collided at the intersection of two taxiways at Miami International Airport, leaving two people with minor injuries, officials said. (WSVN)
A UPS cargo plane and a Copa Airlines passenger jet collided on the ground at Miami International Airport Saturday night, leaving two people with minor injuries, airport officials confirmed.
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) said the wingtip of a Copa Airlines Boeing 737 struck the nose of a UPS Boeing 767 while both aircraft were taxiing around 9 p.m. local time.

Air traffic controllers had instructed the UPS crew to give way to the Copa Airlines flight, which was heading to its gate after landing, while the UPS cargo plane was preparing to depart for Bogotá, Colombia, according to the FAA.
The agency said it is investigating the collision.
AMAZON CARGO PLANE OVERRUNS MIAMI AIRPORT RUNWAY AND STRIKES 'MULTIPLE' VEHICLES; 5 DEAD, 5 INJURED
A UPS cargo plane and a Copa Airlines passenger jet collided at Miami International Airport Saturday night, leaving two people with minor injuries, according to airport officials. (WSVN)

"At approximately 9:15 p.m., an arriving aircraft and a departing aircraft made contact with each other at the intersection of two taxiways," Greg Chin, communications director for the Miami-Dade Aviation Department, said in a statement.

"Flights are being directed to other taxiways, so there is no impact to airport operations at this time. Two patients were treated on the scene by Miami-Dade Fire Rescue for minor injuries and did not require medical transport," Chin added.
Air traffic control audio reviewed by Fox News Digital captured an exchange between pilots and a controller following the collision.
A pilot aboard the Copa Airlines flight was heard saying, "Somebody just hit us."
NTSB REPORT DETAILS HOW CONTROLLER DECISION AND TECH FAILURES LED TO DEADLY RUNWAY COLLISION

A UPS Boeing 767 was involved in a collision with a Copa Airlines aircraft on a taxiway at Miami International Airport on Nov. 14, 2026. (D.A. Varela/Miami Herald/Tribune News Service via Getty Images)
"UPS 358, did you hit that aircraft?" an air traffic controller asked.
"Yeah, we went too far and he clipped us with his wing," the UPS pilot responded.
Copa Airlines said Flight CM427, arriving from Panama City, Panama, was carrying 166 passengers and six crew members when the collision occurred.
The airline said the Boeing 737's left wingtip was involved in the collision with the cargo plane while both aircraft were taxiing.
All passengers disembarked at the terminal, with two receiving treatment for apparent minor injuries, the airline added.
UPS Airlines also acknowledged the incident in a statement posted on X.
"We are aware of an incident involving one of our aircraft on the ground in Miami," the company said.
4 CRITICAL TRAVEL ISSUES FOR THOSE DELAYED AND DISRUPTED BY FAA NATIONWIDE GROUND STOP

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, left, and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin appear during a news conference in the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room at the White House on Nov. 13, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Shawn Thew/EPA/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
"Our crew is safe, and we are committed to working with authorities to determine what happened. The safety of our employees and the public is our highest priority."

The collision came as U.S. airports continued recovering from Friday's nationwide Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ground stop, which disrupted thousands of flights after radar and communications systems experienced instability.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Saturday that air traffic control communications had returned to full operations, while FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said airlines expected to restore their full schedules by the end of Sunday.
